docs.text:
SAA-C03 Topic Guides — Study Index

38 exam-focused topic guides for the AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) exam. Each file follows the same teaching pattern:

The idea — the service explained from zero with a real-world analogy. Core concepts — exam-tested facts, numbers, tables, and explicit "THE trap" callouts. Question patterns — realistic exam scenarios with answers and signal keywords. Pocket card — a keyword → answer table for rapid review.

The goal is to understand why an architectural solution fits the requirements, not simply memorize service definitions.

📲 Install AWS SAAC3

📖 Suggested Reading Order

🏗️ Priority 1: Core Infrastructure

Networking and Content Delivery
  • VPC
  • Route 53
  • CloudFront & Global Accelerator
  • Direct Connect & VPN
  • Transit Gateway
  • DNS, IPv6 & Edge Infrastructure
Compute
  • EC2
  • ELB & Auto Scaling
  • Lambda
  • ECS & Fargate
  • EKS & Kubernetes
  • Elastic Beanstalk
Storage
  • S3 — storage classes, encryption, lifecycle, replication, Object Lock.
  • EBS, EFS & Instance Store — block vs file storage and ephemeral disks.
  • Storage Gateway, DataSync & Transfer Family — hybrid storage and file transfers.
  • FSx — Windows, Lustre, ONTAP, OpenZFS.
  • Snow Family — offline data transfer and edge computing.
Identity and Access Management
  • IAM — roles, policies, permissions, STS, cross-account access.

🗄️ Priority 2: Databases

Database Services
  • RDS & Aurora
  • DynamoDB
  • ElastiCache
  • Other Databases

⚡ Priority 3: Serverless and Application Integration

Application Services
  • API Gateway
  • SQS, SNS & Kinesis
  • EventBridge & Step Functions
  • Application Development & Integration

🔐 Priority 4: Security and Identity

Security Services
  • KMS & CloudHSM
  • Secrets Manager & Parameter Store
  • WAF, Shield & Security Services
  • Cognito
  • Directory Services
  • Certificates

📊 Priority 5: Monitoring, Management and Governance

Monitoring and Operations
  • CloudWatch, CloudTrail & Config
  • Systems Manager & Operations
Infrastructure and Governance
  • CloudFormation
  • Organizations & Control Tower
  • Service Catalog & Trusted Advisor
  • Well-Architected Framework
  • Specialized Services & Governance
Cost Management
  • Cost Management

📈 Priority 6: Analytics, AI and Data Integration

Analytics and Data
  • Data Lakes, ETL & Data Integration
  • Analytics, Big Data & Streaming
  • AI & Machine Learning One-Liners

📦 Priority 7: Migration and Disaster Recovery

Migration and Resilience
  • Disaster Recovery
  • Migration, Messaging & Disaster Recovery

🎯 Priority 8: Final Review

Exam Preparation
  • Exam Traps & Key Patterns
  • Elimination Rules

🧠 How to Use These Guides First pass: Follow the suggested reading order. Focus on the analogies and understand what each service solves. Second pass: Cover the answer columns in the pocket cards and quiz yourself using the keywords. After practice tests: For every incorrect answer, revisit that topic's Question Patterns section. Identify the signal words or constraints you missed. Exam morning: Review guides 36 and 38, then skim the pocket cards. Reinforce what you know rather than trying to learn everything from scratch. 📊 Official Exam-Domain Weights Exam domain Weight Design Secure Architectures 30% Design Resilient Architectures 26% Design High-Performing Architectures 24% Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%

These weights apply to the official exam domains, not individual AWS services. Use them to balance your preparation rather than predict the frequency of specific service questions.

docs.text:
1. First pass: read in the suggested order above — the analogies do the heavy lifting.
  2. Second pass: cover the pocket cards' right columns and quiz yourself from the keywords.
  3. After practice tests: for every miss, come back to that topic's "Question patterns" section — the crack explanations show which signal words you skipped.
  4. Exam morning: skim guide 36 (traps) and each guide's pocket card only. Nothing new on exam day.

docs.title: Section 1: IAM — Identity and Access Management
The idea
docs.text:
IAM controls who can access AWS resources and what they are allowed to do.

IAM is:

  • Global — not tied to a Region.
  • Free — there is no additional charge for IAM itself.
  • Based on identities, policies, and credentials.

The most important distinction:

Authentication = Who are you? Authorization = What are you allowed to do?

IAM mainly handles authorization, while authentication can come from IAM itself or from an external identity system through federation.

docs.title: Users, groups, and roles
docs.text: Identity What it is Typical use IAM User A specific AWS identity with long-term credentials Individual AWS identities when federation is not being used IAM Group A collection of IAM users Give multiple users the same permissions IAM Role An identity that is assumed and provides temporary credentials AWS services, applications, federation, and cross-account access

docs.title: IAM user
docs.text:
An IAM user can have:

  • Console password
  • Access keys
  • Permissions through identity-based policies

Access keys are long-lived programmatic credentials used by tools such as the AWS CLI and SDKs.

IAM User
├── Access keys
│   → authenticate programmatic API requests
│
└── IAM policies
    → authorize what the user can do

Access keys are long-lived credentials, so they should not be used when a role can be used instead.

Access keys = credentials, not permissions.

docs.title: IAM group
docs.text:
A group is only a collection of IAM users.

A group cannot contain:

  • another group
  • a role

A role cannot be attached to a group; groups are used to attach policies to multiple IAM users.

Groups are mainly used to manage permissions for multiple IAM users.

docs.title: IAM role
docs.text:
A role does not represent one permanently logged-in person.

A principal assumes the role, and AWS provides temporary credentials.

Common examples:

EC2 → IAM role
Lambda → execution role
ECS task → task role
User → assumed role
Account A → role in Account B
Federated user → IAM role

docs.title: Golden rule
docs.text:
AWS workload needs AWS permissions → use an IAM role, not hard-coded access keys.

For example:

EC2
 ↓
IAM instance role
 ↓
Temporary credentials
 ↓
S3 / DynamoDB / SQS / etc.

Do not:

EC2
 ↓
Hard-coded access key
 ↓
S3

The same principle applies to Lambda, ECS, and other AWS services that support IAM roles.

docs.title: IAM policies
docs.text:
Policies are JSON documents that define permissions.

Basic structure:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::company-bucket/reports/*"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Important policy elements
docs.text: Element Meaning Effect Allow or Deny Action API operations such as s3:GetObject Resource The AWS resource affected, usually identified by an ARN Condition Optional conditions such as MFA, source IP, VPC, TLS, tags, etc. Principal Who the policy applies to; mainly seen in resource-based policies

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::company-bucket/alice/*"
}

This grants access to objects under:

s3://company-bucket/alice/

but not:

s3://company-bucket/bob/

docs.title: Resource tags and ABAC
docs.text:
IAM policies can use resource tags in conditions to control access based on resource attributes.

This is called Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC).

Example:

UAT EC2:
Environment = UAT

Production EC2:
Environment = Production

An IAM policy can allow access only when:

ec2:ResourceTag/Environment = UAT

Result:

UAT employee
    ↓
IAM policy
    ↓
Environment = UAT
    ↓
Can manage UAT instances
    ✕
Cannot manage Production instances

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Restrict employees to EC2 instances based on tags."

→ IAM policy Condition + ec2:ResourceTag/... → ABAC

This is preferable to separating instances into VPCs when the requirement is who is authorized to manage which resources.

Remember:

Tags identify resources; IAM Conditions use those tags to control access.

docs.title: Policy types
docs.text: Policy type Attached to Purpose Identity-based policy User, group, or role Defines what that identity can do Resource-based policy Resource such as S3 bucket or SQS queue Defines who can access the resource Permissions boundary IAM user or role Maximum permissions that identity can have SCP AWS Organizations account or OU Maximum permissions allowed in the account Session policy Role session Further restricts permissions for a specific session S3 ACL S3 bucket/object Legacy access-control mechanism; generally prefer policies

docs.title: Grant vs ceiling
docs.text:
This distinction is heavily tested:

  • Identity policy → can grant permissions.
  • Resource policy → can grant permissions.
  • Permissions boundary → limits maximum permissions; grants nothing by itself.
  • SCP → limits maximum permissions; grants nothing by itself.
  • Session policy → further limits a role session.

Think:

Identity permissions
        ∩
Permissions boundary
        ∩
SCP
        ∩
Session policy

An applicable explicit Deny can block the request.

docs.title: How AWS evaluates permissions
docs.text:
The basic rules are:

  1. Everything starts as implicitly denied.
  2. An applicable Allow can grant access.
  3. An applicable explicit Deny always wins.

Common reasons an apparently allowed request fails:

  • Explicit Deny
  • SCP
  • Permissions boundary
  • Session policy
  • Resource policy restrictions
  • Incorrect trust policy when assuming a role

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
A policy saying:

Allow s3:GetObject

does not necessarily mean the request will succeed.

Another applicable policy can still deny it.

docs.title: STS and temporary credentials
docs.text:
AWS Security Token Service (STS) provides temporary AWS credentials.

Temporary credentials consist of:

  • Access key ID
  • Secret access key
  • Session token

They expire automatically.

The most important STS operation for the exam is:

sts:AssumeRole

Typical flow:

Principal
   ↓
AssumeRole
   ↓
AWS STS
   ↓
Temporary credentials
   ↓
Access AWS resources

docs.title: Why use temporary credentials?
docs.text:
They:

  • expire automatically
  • reduce the need for long-lived access keys
  • are suitable for applications, federation, and cross-account access

A role session can have a configured duration within AWS-supported limits; the exact maximum depends on the type of role/session and configuration. For exam questions, focus primarily on temporary vs long-lived credentials rather than memorizing one universal duration.

docs.title: IAM roles have two important policies
docs.text: A role has two separate concepts that must not be confused.

docs.title: 1. Permissions policy
docs.text:
Defines:

What can the role do?

Example:

Allow:
s3:GetObject
s3:PutObject

docs.title: 2. Trust policy
docs.text:
Defines:

Who can assume the role?

Example:

EC2 service
Account A
SAML identity provider
OIDC identity provider

This is a critical exam distinction.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A role might allow:

s3:GetObject

but its trust policy might only allow:

ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com

An EC2 instance cannot simply use that role.

docs.title: Exam pattern
docs.text:
"The role has the required permissions, but the principal cannot assume it."

Check the:

Trust policy

docs.title: Federation
docs.text:
Federation allows users to authenticate using an external identity system instead of creating a separate IAM user for every person.

Typical external identity systems include:

  • Active Directory
  • Microsoft Entra ID
  • Okta
  • Other corporate identity providers

The important idea is:

The corporate directory authenticates the user; AWS provides authorization through roles and temporary credentials.

docs.title: Direct federation with AWS
docs.text:
This is especially important for questions involving:

  • corporate AD/LDAP
  • SSO
  • temporary AWS credentials
  • no IAM user for every employee

Typical architecture:

Corporate AD / LDAP
        ↓
Identity Provider (IdP)
        ↓
SAML / federation
        ↓
AWS STS
        ↓
IAM Role
        ↓
Temporary credentials
        ↓
AWS resources

The external identity provider confirms the user's identity.

AWS then gives the user temporary credentials associated with an IAM role.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The corporate directory does not become an AWS IAM user database containing 1,200 IAM users.

Instead:

1,200 corporate users
        ↓
External identity system
        ↓
Federation
        ↓
IAM roles
        ↓
Temporary AWS credentials

This is one of the most important federation patterns for SAA.

docs.title: Non-SAML LDAP: Custom Identity Broker
docs.text:
Sometimes the on-premises identity store is LDAP-based but cannot use SAML.

In this case, a custom identity broker can act as the bridge between LDAP and AWS.

Typical architecture:

On-premises LDAP
        ↓
Custom identity broker
        ↓
AWS STS
        ↓
Temporary AWS credentials
        ↓
AWS resources

The broker:

  1. Authenticates the user against LDAP.
  2. Determines which IAM role the user should use.
  3. Calls STS.
  4. Returns temporary AWS credentials to the user.

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
On-premises LDAP + not SAML-compatible → Custom Identity Broker + STS

Do not confuse this with IAM Identity Center. The key clue is that the existing identity store is not compatible with SAML.

docs.title: Small question
docs.text:
A company needs to integrate its on-premises LDAP directory with AWS. The existing identity store is not compatible with SAML. Which approach provides the most appropriate integration?

→ Develop an on-premises custom identity broker and use AWS STS to issue temporary credentials.

docs.title: Federation protocols
docs.text: Two important federation technologies appear in AWS questions.

docs.title: SAML 2.0
docs.text:
Common for:

Corporate workforce
        ↓
AD / Entra ID / Okta
        ↓
SAML
        ↓
AWS

SAML is commonly associated with enterprise workforce SSO.

docs.title: OIDC
docs.text:
OpenID Connect is commonly used for:

  • web/mobile authentication
  • workloads
  • GitHub Actions and other external systems
  • Kubernetes/EKS workload identity scenarios

For SAA, remember the broad distinction:

Enterprise workforce SSO → commonly SAML
Modern application/workload federation → commonly OIDC

docs.title: IAM Identity Center
docs.text:
IAM Identity Center is AWS's workforce SSO service.

It is particularly useful when employees need access to:

  • multiple AWS accounts
  • AWS applications
  • business applications

Typical architecture:

Corporate IdP
      ↓
IAM Identity Center
      ↓
AWS accounts
      ↓
Permission sets
      ↓
IAM roles

It can integrate with external identity providers such as:

  • Microsoft Entra ID
  • Okta
  • other SAML-compatible IdPs
  • Active Directory environments

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Employees need one login to access multiple AWS accounts."

Think:

IAM Identity Center

docs.title: Direct federation vs IAM Identity Center
docs.text: Do not treat these as the same thing.

docs.title: Direct federation
docs.text:
The application/workflow directly uses federation and STS to obtain temporary AWS credentials.

Corporate IdP
    ↓
Federation
    ↓
STS
    ↓
IAM role
    ↓
AWS resources

This is especially relevant to scenarios such as:

"Corporate AD users need temporary AWS credentials to access an S3 bucket."

docs.title: IAM Identity Center
docs.text:
AWS provides a centralized workforce SSO experience:

Corporate IdP
    ↓
IAM Identity Center
    ↓
AWS accounts
    ↓
Permission sets / roles

This is especially relevant to:

"Employees need SSO access to multiple AWS accounts."

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text: Question wording Likely answer Corporate users need temporary AWS credentials Federation + STS Existing AD users should access AWS without IAM users Federation One login to many AWS accounts IAM Identity Center Centralized employee access across AWS accounts IAM Identity Center S3 access for thousands of corporate users Federation + roles + STS External application users sign in with Google/Facebook Cognito

docs.title: IAM Identity Center vs Cognito
docs.text: These are commonly confused.

docs.title: IAM Identity Center
docs.text:
For:

Employees / workforce users

Company employee
      ↓
Corporate IdP
      ↓
AWS accounts

docs.title: Amazon Cognito
docs.text:
For:

Application users / customers

Example:

Mobile app
    ↓
Cognito
    ↓
Application user

If a question says:

Customers sign in to a web/mobile application using Google, Facebook, Apple, or username/password.

Think:

Cognito

If it says:

Employees need SSO into AWS accounts.

Think:

IAM Identity Center

docs.title: Cross-account access
docs.text:
Suppose:

Account A = auditors
Account B = production

Auditors in Account A need temporary access to Account B.

The standard solution is:

docs.title: Account B
docs.text: Create a role with the required permissions.

docs.title: Account B trust policy
docs.text: Trust Account A.

docs.title: Account A
docs.text:
Allow its users to call:

sts:AssumeRole

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Account A user
      ↓
AssumeRole
      ↓
STS
      ↓
Temporary credentials
      ↓
Role in Account B
      ↓
Account B resources

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
"Users from another AWS account need temporary access."

Think:

Cross-account IAM role + trust policy + STS

Do not create shared IAM users or exchange long-lived access keys.

docs.title: ExternalId and third-party access
docs.text:
When a third-party AWS account assumes your role, the trust policy can require an:

ExternalId

This helps protect against the confused deputy problem.

Typical scenario:

Your AWS account
      ↓
Role
      ↑
Third-party SaaS / partner

The third party provides the expected ExternalId when assuming the role.

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
"Third-party service needs to assume a role on behalf of customers."

Think:

ExternalId

docs.title: Permission boundaries
docs.text:
A permissions boundary defines the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can receive.

It does not grant permissions by itself.

Example:

Identity policy
      +
Permissions boundary
      =
Effective permissions

If the identity policy allows:

s3:*

but the boundary only allows:

s3:GetObject

the identity cannot use the permissions outside the boundary.

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
"Developers can create roles, but those roles must never exceed a predefined maximum."

Think:

Permissions boundary

docs.title: Service Control Policies (SCPs)
docs.text:
SCPs are part of:

AWS Organizations

They define the maximum available permissions for accounts or organizational units.

An SCP:

  • does not grant permissions
  • restricts what an account can do
  • can affect IAM users and roles
  • can restrict the account root user

Example:

Organization
    ↓
OU
    ↓
Account
    ↓
SCP denies certain services

Even if an IAM policy says:

Allow

the SCP can still prevent the action.

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
"The account is in AWS Organizations and an action is blocked despite an IAM Allow."

Think:

SCP

docs.title: Permissions boundary vs SCP
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

Permissions boundary SCP Scope One IAM user/role AWS account / OU Grants permissions? No No Purpose Maximum permissions for an identity Maximum permissions allowed in an account AWS Organizations required? No Yes

Think:

Permissions boundary → one identity
SCP                  → whole account / OU

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
MFA adds another authentication factor.

A policy can require MFA using:

aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent

Example concept:

Allow EC2 termination
ONLY IF
MFA is present

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text:
"Users must provide MFA before performing a sensitive action."

Think:

aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent

docs.title: Root user
docs.text:
The root user is the identity associated with the AWS account's original email address.

Root has extremely broad permissions and should not be used for normal administration.

Best practices:

  • Enable MFA.
  • Do not create root access keys.
  • Do not use root for daily work.
  • Use an appropriate administrative identity instead.
  • Use root only for tasks that specifically require it.

docs.title: Important SCP nuance
docs.text:
An SCP can restrict the root user in member accounts of an AWS Organization.

The management account is different; SCPs do not restrict the permissions of its root user in the same way.

docs.title: IAM Access Analyzer and credential tools
IAM Access Analyzer
docs.text:
Helps identify resources that are accessible from outside the intended trust boundary.

Typical exam wording:

"Which IAM tool identifies resources shared with external principals?"

Answer:

IAM Access Analyzer

docs.title: IAM credentials report
docs.text:
Provides information about IAM users and their credentials, such as:

  • password usage
  • access key age
  • MFA status

Useful for finding stale credentials.

docs.title: IAM access advisor
docs.text: Shows service permissions/usage information that can help identify unused permissions.

docs.title: S3-specific IAM concepts
docs.text: S3 commonly uses both identity-based and resource-based policies.

docs.title: Identity policy
docs.text:
Attached to:

User / Group / Role

Example:

Role
 ↓
Allow s3:GetObject

docs.title: Bucket policy
docs.text:
Attached to:

S3 bucket

It can specify:

Principal

For example:

Principal = specific IAM role

Bucket policies are especially important for:

  • cross-account access
  • restricting access to specific principals
  • enforcing S3 security requirements

docs.title: S3 prefixes and per-user access
docs.text:
S3 does not have traditional folders in the same way a filesystem does.

What looks like a folder is generally an object key prefix.

Example:

company/
  alice/
    document1.pdf
    document2.pdf

  bob/
    document3.pdf

Policies can restrict users to a particular prefix.

For example:

arn:aws:s3:::company/alice/*

This pattern commonly appears together with federation.

docs.title: Full architecture
docs.text:
Corporate AD / LDAP
        ↓
Identity Provider
        ↓
Federation
        ↓
STS
        ↓
IAM Role
        ↓
IAM Policy
        ↓
S3 prefix

This is the exact pattern to recognize when a question combines:

  • corporate directory
  • SSO
  • temporary credentials
  • S3
  • per-user folders

docs.title: S3 ACLs
docs.text:
S3 ACLs are an older access-control mechanism.

For modern S3 architectures:

Prefer IAM policies and S3 bucket policies.

Do not confuse:

S3 ACL

with:

VPC Network ACL

They are completely different.

  • S3 ACL → S3 access control
  • Network ACL → subnet-level network filtering

docs.title: Common exam patterns
docs.text:
"An EC2 instance needs access to S3." → Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance.

"Lambda needs permission to read DynamoDB." → Use a Lambda execution role.

"Credentials are hard-coded in an application on EC2." → Replace them with an IAM role.

"A new IAM user will use the AWS CLI, but has no programmatic credentials yet." → Create Access Keys and attach the necessary permissions.

"A brand-new IAM user is intended to make API calls to S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, and other AWS resources." → Create Access Keys + attach the necessary permissions.

"An IAM user already has valid Access Keys/programmatic credentials, but API calls return AccessDenied." → Attach an appropriate IAM policy.

The distinction is:

Access Keys
→ authentication / programmatic credentials

IAM Policy
→ authorization / permissions

"The role has the required permissions, but the principal cannot assume it." → Check the trust policy.

"Users in Account A need temporary access to Account B." → Cross-account role + trust policy + STS AssumeRole.

"A third-party SaaS provider needs to assume your role." → Consider ExternalId in the trust policy.

"An IAM policy allows the action, but the action is denied." → Look for an explicit Deny, SCP, permissions boundary, session policy, or resource-policy restriction.

"Developers can create roles, but those roles must never exceed a defined permission set." → Permissions boundary.

"An account in AWS Organizations cannot perform an action even though IAM allows it." → Check the SCP.

"5,000 employees already have corporate AD credentials and need AWS access without creating thousands of IAM users." → Federation / IAM Identity Center, depending on the architecture described.

"Corporate users need temporary AWS credentials to access S3." → Federation + STS + IAM role.

"Employees need one login to access many AWS accounts." → IAM Identity Center.

"The corporate LDAP directory is not compatible with SAML, but users need temporary AWS credentials." → Custom identity broker + STS.

"Customers sign in to an application using Google or Facebook." → Amazon Cognito.

"Each corporate employee should only access their own S3 folder." → Use IAM policies restricting access to the user's S3 prefix, often combined with federation.

"Employees responsible for UAT must not be able to manage production EC2 instances." → Tag the EC2 instances and use an IAM policy Condition with ec2:ResourceTag/... (ABAC).

"Restrict EC2 access based on Environment=UAT or Environment=Production." → IAM Condition + resource tags → ABAC.

"A sensitive action should only work after MFA." → Condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.

"What should be done first to secure a new AWS account?" → Protect the root user with MFA, avoid root access keys, and use a proper administrative identity for normal work.

Permissions policy Who can assume the role? Trust policy Cross-account access Role + trust policy + STS Third-party role assumption ExternalId Maximum permissions for one identity Permissions boundary Maximum permissions for an AWS account/OU SCP External corporate users Federation Corporate AD/LDAP → AWS Federation / IdP LDAP not SAML-compatible Custom identity broker + STS Federation → temporary AWS credentials STS One login → multiple AWS accounts IAM Identity Center Enterprise SSO with SAML IAM Identity Center / SAML federation Application customer login Cognito Per-user S3 folder S3 prefix + IAM policy Policy attached to S3 bucket Bucket policy Legacy S3 permissions S3 ACL Resource access based on tags ABAC / IAM Condition EC2 access by tag ec2:ResourceTag/... docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is object storage.

Bucket
  ↓
Object
  ├── Data
  ├── Key
  └── Metadata

S3 is not:

  • Block storage → EBS
  • Shared filesystem → EFS / FSx

You normally replace an entire object rather than modify individual bytes.

docs.title: Important S3 facts
docs.text:
• 99.999999999% durability
  • Bucket belongs to one Region
  • Bucket names are globally unique
  • Max object size: 5 TB
  • S3 has effectively unlimited total storage

docs.title: S3 key
docs.text:
photos/2026/cat.jpg

S3 has no traditional folders; photos/2026/ is part of the key.

docs.title: S3 static website + Route 53
docs.text:
S3 can host a static website containing:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
  • Images
  • Other static files

For a custom domain, Route 53 can route traffic to the S3 website endpoint.

docs.title: Important bucket-name rule
docs.text:
When routing a domain directly to an S3 bucket configured for static website hosting, the:

S3 bucket name must exactly match the domain or subdomain being routed.

Example:

Domain:
example.com

Bucket:
example.com

For a subdomain:

Domain:
www.example.com

Bucket:
www.example.com

This is a common SAA exam requirement.

docs.title: Typical architecture
docs.text:
User
  ↓
Route 53
  ↓
A / Alias record
  ↓
S3 website endpoint
  ↓
S3 bucket

docs.title: Important Route 53 prerequisites
docs.text:
For the direct S3 website-endpoint pattern:

  • A registered domain name
  • An S3 bucket configured for static website hosting
  • The bucket name matches the domain/subdomain
  • Route 53 is hosting the DNS for the domain
  • Use a Route 53 A Alias record pointing to the S3 website endpoint

Route 53 alias records can be used for both:

example.com
www.example.com

The S3 bucket must match the record name used for the S3 website target.

docs.title: Region misconception
docs.text:
The S3 bucket does not have to be in the same Region as the Route 53 hosted zone.

Route 53 is a global DNS service.

You select the S3 bucket's Region when configuring the S3 website endpoint as the alias target.

docs.title: CORS misconception
docs.text:
CORS is not required simply to route Route 53 traffic to an S3 website.

Route 53
→ DNS routing

CORS
→ Browser cross-origin access

Do not confuse the two.

docs.title: Important HTTPS caveat
docs.text:
An S3 website endpoint does not support SSL/TLS directly.

For HTTPS, a common architecture is:

User
  ↓ HTTPS
CloudFront
  ↓
S3

With CloudFront, you can use a custom certificate and keep the S3 bucket behind CloudFront.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
The bucket-name-must-match-domain rule applies to the direct S3 website endpoint pattern.

It does not mean every S3 bucket behind CloudFront must have the same name as the user's domain.

For example:

example.com
    ↓
CloudFront
    ↓
my-company-static-assets-123

The CloudFront distribution can use a differently named S3 bucket as its origin.

Direct Route 53 → S3 website endpoint → bucket name matches domain

CloudFront → S3 origin → bucket name does not need to match the public domain

docs.title: S3 storage classes
docs.text:
Storage class Access pattern Retrieval Minimum storage S3 Standard Frequent Milliseconds None S3 Intelligent-Tiering Unknown / changing Milliseconds in active tiers None S3 Standard-IA Infrequent Milliseconds 30 days S3 One Zone-IA Infrequent + re-creatable Milliseconds 30 days S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Rare + immediate Milliseconds 90 days S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Archive Minutes–hours 90 days S3 Glacier Deep Archive Very rare / long-term Hours 180 days Important 2026 exam note

Minimum storage ≠ minimum lifecycle transition time.

For example, you can configure a lifecycle transition to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA at day 7 (or even day 0), but the object still has a 30-day minimum billable duration. Leaving earlier results in a prorated charge. The same principle applies to the Glacier classes: 90/90/180 days are minimum billable durations, not necessarily a mandatory waiting period before transitioning.

Glacier classes provide the same high durability model as S3 Standard with lower storage cost.

docs.title: 1. Access frequency
docs.text:
Frequent
→ Standard

Unknown / unpredictable
→ Intelligent-Tiering

Infrequent
→ Standard-IA / One Zone-IA

Rare
→ Glacier

docs.title: 2. Retrieval speed
docs.text:
Milliseconds
→ Standard / Standard-IA / One Zone-IA / Glacier Instant

Minutes–hours
→ Glacier Flexible

Hours acceptable
→ Deep Archive

docs.title: 3. Retention
docs.text:
Standard-IA     → 30 days
One Zone-IA     → 30 days
Glacier Instant → 90 days
Glacier Flexible→ 90 days
Deep Archive    → 180 days

Deleting/transitioning before the minimum duration can still incur charges for the remaining minimum period.

docs.title: S3 Standard
docs.text:
Use for:

  • Frequently accessed data
  • Low-latency access
  • Predictable access

Frequently accessed → S3 Standard

docs.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
docs.text:
Use when access is unknown or unpredictable.

S3 automatically moves objects between access tiers. There is a small monitoring/automation charge.

Known access schedule
→ Lifecycle

Unknown/unpredictable access
→ Intelligent-Tiering

docs.title: S3 Standard-IA
docs.text:
Use for:

  • Infrequent access
  • Immediate retrieval
  • Multi-AZ resilience

Infrequent + immediate → Standard-IA

docs.title: S3 One Zone-IA
docs.text:
Stores data in one AZ.

Use for:

  • Infrequent access
  • Re-creatable data
  • Secondary copies

Re-creatable / secondary copy → One Zone-IA

Do not use it as the only copy of irreplaceable data.

docs.title: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
docs.text:
For:

  • Rarely accessed data
  • Immediate retrieval
  • Millisecond access

Rare + immediate retrieval → Glacier Instant Retrieval

docs.title: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
docs.text:
For archival data where retrieval can take minutes to hours.

Archive + minutes/hours acceptable → Glacier Flexible Retrieval

docs.title: Retrieval options
docs.text:
Retrieval Typical time Use Expedited 1–5 min Urgent access Standard 3–5 hours Normal retrieval Bulk 5–12 hours Large, low-cost retrieval

Provisioned Retrieval Capacity guarantees capacity for Expedited retrievals and provides up to 300 MB/s per capacity unit.

Under 15-minute retrieval → Expedited

Guaranteed Expedited capacity / predictable fast retrieval → Provisioned Retrieval Capacity

Large amount + lowest retrieval cost → Bulk

docs.title: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
docs.text:
For very long-term archival:

  • Regulatory records
  • Compliance archives
  • Multi-year retention
  • Very rare access

Lowest-cost S3 storage class; retrieval takes hours.

Cheapest long-term archive → Deep Archive

docs.title: Lifecycle rules
docs.text:
Automatically:

  • Transition objects
  • Expire/delete objects
  • Delete old versions
  • Abort incomplete multipart uploads

Example:

Standard
   ↓
Standard-IA
   ↓
Glacier
   ↓
Delete

Known access schedule → S3 Lifecycle

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Keeps multiple object versions.

Version 1
Version 2

A normal delete on a versioned bucket creates a delete marker rather than immediately deleting the current version.

Delete Marker
Version 2
Version 1

Remove the delete marker and the object becomes visible again.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Once Versioning is enabled, it can be suspended, but the bucket cannot return to its original unversioned state.

Accidental overwrite/deletion protection → Versioning

docs.title: Delete marker
docs.text:
With Versioning enabled:

DELETE object
→ Delete Marker created
→ Old versions remain

But:

DELETE object?versionId=...
→ Specific version permanently deleted

Important event distinction:

Delete marker
→ s3:ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated

Permanent deletion
→ s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete

docs.title: MFA Delete
docs.text:
Adds MFA protection to certain Versioning operations.

Useful against:

  • Permanent deletion of object versions
  • Malicious deletion
  • Accidental versioning suspension

Require MFA before permanently deleting versions → MFA Delete

docs.title: S3 Object Lock — WORM
docs.text:
WORM = Write Once, Read Many

Object Lock prevents protected object versions from being overwritten/deleted during the protection period.

Object Lock requires Versioning.

S3
 ↓
Versioning
 ↓
Object Lock

docs.title: Object Lock: Governance vs Compliance
docs.text: Governance Compliance Normal users can delete? No No Authorized users can bypass? Yes No Strict immutability Less suitable Yes Admin/root bypass Possible with appropriate bypass permissions No

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
Can be bypassed with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention.

Administrators may override → Governance

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Cannot be bypassed during retention, including by administrators/root.

Nobody can bypass → Compliance

docs.title: Retention period
docs.text:
Protect until a specific date.

"Keep for exactly 5 years." → Retention period

docs.title: Legal Hold
docs.text:
Protection remains until explicitly removed.

Litigation / investigation / case closure → Legal Hold

docs.title: Object Lock vs Versioning
docs.text:
Recover old version after accidental deletion
→ Versioning

Prevent deletion/overwrite during retention
→ Object Lock

docs.title: Object Lock and replication
docs.text:
For locked-object replication:

  • Source and destination must have Object Lock enabled.
  • Retention metadata can be replicated.

Useful for compliance copies in another bucket/Region.

docs.title: Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
docs.text:
Copies objects to another Region.

Uses:

  • Disaster recovery
  • Compliance
  • Geographic separation
  • Lower latency
Region A
   ↓ CRR
Region B

docs.title: Same-Region Replication (SRR)
docs.text:
Copies objects to another bucket in the same Region.

Uses:

  • Log aggregation
  • Production → test
  • Separate accounts/buckets
  • Data isolation

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text: Standard replication requires Versioning on both source and destination.

docs.title: Existing objects
docs.text: Existing objects need replication → S3 Batch Replication

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
S3 encrypts new objects by default.

Encryption Key management Signal SSE-S3 AWS Simple server-side encryption SSE-KMS AWS KMS Key control + audit SSE-C Customer Customer supplies key Client-side Customer Encrypt before upload

docs.title: SSE-S3
docs.text: Use for simple S3 encryption without special key-management requirements.

docs.title: SSE-KMS
docs.text:
Provides:

  • Customer-managed KMS key option
  • Fine-grained permissions
  • Key controls
  • CloudTrail audit

Need to audit encryption-key usage → SSE-KMS

docs.title: S3 Bucket Key
docs.text:
Reduces KMS requests and costs for large numbers of SSE-KMS objects.

Trade-off: less granular KMS/CloudTrail visibility.

Too many KMS requests/cost → S3 Bucket Key

docs.title: SSE-C
docs.text:
Customer supplies the key with each request. HTTPS is required.

Customer manages key for each request → SSE-C

docs.title: Client-side encryption
docs.text:
Application
 ↓ encrypt
Ciphertext
 ↓
S3

Must encrypt before AWS receives the data → Client-side encryption

docs.title: Encryption in transit
docs.text:
At rest:

SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS / SSE-C / Client-side

In transit:

HTTPS / TLS

Force HTTPS with a bucket policy denying:

aws:SecureTransport = false

Force HTTPS → aws:SecureTransport

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
IAM policies
    ↓
VPC endpoint policies
    ↓
S3 bucket policies
    ↓
S3 Block Public Access

docs.title: VPC Endpoint Policy for S3
docs.text:
An S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint provides private VPC access to S3 without an Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway.

A VPC endpoint policy controls what can be accessed through that specific endpoint.

VPC
 ↓
S3 Gateway Endpoint
 ↓
Endpoint policy
 ↓
Approved S3 buckets

Different endpoints have different policies.

EC2 can access only specific S3 buckets through an S3 gateway endpoint → Gateway VPC Endpoint + endpoint policy

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
VPC endpoint policy
→ controls access THROUGH the endpoint

Bucket policy
→ controls access TO the bucket

docs.title: Bucket policies
docs.text:
Resource-based policies controlling:

  • Who can access
  • Cross-account access
  • HTTPS
  • Encryption
  • IP restrictions
  • VPC endpoint restrictions

aws:sourceVpce can restrict access to a specific VPC endpoint.

Bucket only accessible through a specific endpoint → Bucket policy + aws:sourceVpce

docs.title: S3 Requester Pays
docs.text:
Used when you share an S3 dataset with other AWS accounts and want the requester to pay the S3 request and applicable data-transfer/retrieval charges instead of the bucket owner.

Bucket owner
→ Pays for storage

Requester
→ Pays for requests
→ Pays for applicable data transfer/retrieval charges

Useful for:

  • Large datasets shared with other AWS accounts
  • Public/shared datasets where the owner does not want to pay access costs
  • Cross-account data downloads

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Requester Pays does not grant access by itself.

The requester must still have permission to access the bucket, such as through:

  • IAM policies
  • Bucket policies
  • Cross-account permissions

Requester Pays requires authenticated requests, so anonymous requests are not allowed.

docs.title: Key distinction
docs.text:
Cross-account access
→ Who is allowed to access the bucket?

Requester Pays
→ Who pays for the request/download?

You may need both when sharing data with another AWS account.

Large S3 dataset shared with another account + requester should pay access/download costs → S3 Requester Pays

docs.title: Block Public Access
docs.text:
Main protection against accidental public exposure.

Prevent public S3 access → S3 Block Public Access

docs.title: Public S3 objects
docs.text:
To make S3 objects readable by anyone on the Internet:

Bucket policy
→ Allow s3:GetObject
→ Principal: "*"

A public-read object ACL can also make an object public when ACLs are enabled, but modern S3 buckets usually use Bucket owner enforced, which disables ACLs.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Bucket policy / public-read ACL
→ controls whether the object is public

CORS
→ controls whether browser JavaScript can access a cross-origin response

So:

All S3 objects must be publicly readable → Bucket policy or public-read ACL if ACLs are enabled

CORS does NOT make S3 objects public.

docs.title: Small exam pattern
docs.text:
Public static assets readable from the Internet → Bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject to Principal: "*"

Public-read ACL → possible only when ACLs are enabled

CORS → not an access-control mechanism

Do nothing → objects are not public by default

docs.title: Presigned URLs
docs.text:
Temporary access to a private S3 object without giving AWS credentials.

Customer
 ↓
Presigned URL
 ↓
Private object

Temporary private download → Presigned URL

docs.title: CloudFront + S3: OAC
docs.text:
Origin Access Control (OAC) lets CloudFront access the S3 origin while preventing direct public S3 access.

User
 ↓
CloudFront
 ↓
S3

Users access content through CloudFront, not directly through S3 → OAC

OAC is preferred over the older OAI approach.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
If CloudFront uses the S3 REST API origin, the S3 bucket can remain private and its name does not need to match the public website domain.

example.com
    ↓
CloudFront
    ↓
private bucket: company-assets-123

Do not apply the direct S3 website-endpoint bucket-name rule to this architecture.

docs.title: S3 access logs vs CloudTrail
docs.text: S3 Server Access Logs CloudTrail data events Main purpose Detailed S3 request/access logging AWS API/object activity Typical details Requester, bucket, time, operation, referrer, response time, HTTP status/error Who performed the API action and which object/API was accessed Typical use Detailed S3 access/request logs Audit/security Destination Separate S3 bucket CloudTrail event store / delivery destination

docs.title: S3 Server Access Logs
docs.text:
Detailed records of requests made to an S3 bucket, including information such as:

  • Requester
  • Bucket/object
  • Request time and operation
  • Referrer
  • Response/turnaround time
  • HTTP status/error information

Logs should be delivered to a different bucket to avoid recursive logging.

Detailed S3 request/access details → Server Access Logs

Who performed an S3 object API operation → CloudTrail data events

Exam trap: Both can log S3 activity, but Server Access Logs are the better answer when the question lists fields such as request time, referrer, turnaround time, and error code.

docs.title: S3 Performance
docs.text: S3 automatically scales to high request rates.

docs.title: Per-prefix baseline
docs.text:
Operation Per prefix PUT / COPY / POST / DELETE ≥ 3,500 requests/sec GET / HEAD ≥ 5,500 requests/sec

There is no limit on the number of prefixes in a bucket.

docs.title: What is a prefix?
docs.text:
A prefix is the beginning of an S3 object key.

photos/2026/cat.jpg

Possible prefix:

photos/

Prefix = part of the object key, not a real folder.

docs.title: High request rates
docs.text:
To increase aggregate request throughput:

Multiple prefixes
      +
Parallel requests
      ↓
Higher aggregate throughput

Example:

1 prefix  → 5,500 GET/sec
10 prefixes → potentially 55,000 GET/sec

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
S3 automatically scales, so you do not normally need to create prefixes manually. For very high request rates, distributing requests across prefixes can improve performance.

A sudden large increase in traffic can temporarily cause:

503 Slow Down

→ retry using exponential backoff.

docs.title: Multipart upload
docs.text:
Splits large objects into parts.

Benefits:

  • Parallel uploads
  • Better performance
  • Retry individual parts

Limits:

  • Single PUT: 5 GB
  • Max object: 5 TB

Upload a very large file efficiently → Multipart upload

docs.title: S3 Transfer Acceleration
docs.text:
Improves long-distance uploads:

User
 ↓
Nearest edge
 ↓
AWS backbone
 ↓
S3

Global users uploading to one S3 bucket → Transfer Acceleration

For global downloads:

→ CloudFront

docs.title: Byte-range requests
docs.text:
Retrieves only part of an object.

Useful for:

  • Large objects
  • Parallel downloads
  • Partial retrieval

Download only part of a large object → Byte-range request

docs.title: S3 Event Notifications
docs.text:
S3 Event Notifications = trigger actions when objects change.

SQS         → queue
SNS         → notification / fan-out
Lambda      → run code
EventBridge → advanced routing

docs.title: Important events
docs.text: Event Meaning s3:ObjectCreated:* Object created s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete Deleted / version permanently deleted s3:ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated Delete marker created s3:ObjectRemoved:* All removal events

docs.title: Exam patterns
docs.text:
New object → s3:ObjectCreated:*

Permanent deletion → s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete

Delete marker → s3:ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated

All removals → s3:ObjectRemoved:*

Queue processing → SQS

Notify/fan-out → SNS

Complex routing → EventBridge

docs.title: Trap
docs.text:
DELETE on versioned bucket
→ Delete marker
→ NOT permanent deletion

DELETE specific version ID
→ Permanent deletion

docs.title: Pocket card
docs.text:
Object created → ObjectCreated:*
Permanent delete → ObjectRemoved:Delete
Delete marker → ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated
All removals → ObjectRemoved:*
Queue → SQS
Notify → SNS
Complex routing → EventBridge

docs.title: S3 Select
docs.text:
Queries one object and returns only matching data.

Part of one large CSV/JSON → S3 Select

docs.title: Athena
docs.text:
Queries many S3 objects/datasets using SQL.

Analyze many S3 files → Athena

docs.title: S3 Storage Lens
docs.text:
S3 Storage Lens = account-wide and organization-wide visibility into S3 usage and activity.

It aggregates metrics and insights across all buckets and Regions from a single dashboard.

Use it for:

  • Storage usage and growth trends
  • Cost optimization insights
  • Data protection and configuration status (including versioning status)
  • Identifying buckets that do not meet best practices
  • Organization-wide and account-wide summaries

Key points:

  • Works across all buckets and Regions automatically
  • Provides free default dashboard metrics plus advanced paid metrics
  • Can export metrics to an S3 bucket for analysis
  • Can be scoped to an AWS Organization (organization-level dashboard)

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Account/org-wide S3 visibility, metrics, or configuration status (e.g., which buckets lack versioning) → S3 Storage Lens

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
S3 Storage Lens
→ visibility, metrics, configuration insights across buckets/Regions

CloudTrail
→ API activity audit (who did what)

IAM Access Analyzer
→ external/public access analysis

docs.title: Question patterns
docs.text:
A company stores frequently accessed application data in Amazon S3 and requires low-latency access with no special archival requirements. Which S3 storage class should be used? → S3 Standard

A company cannot predict whether objects will be accessed frequently or rarely. It wants S3 to automatically optimize storage costs based on changing access patterns. Which storage class should it use? → S3 Intelligent-Tiering

A company stores backups that are accessed only occasionally but must be retrieved immediately when needed. The data must also remain resilient across multiple Availability Zones. Which storage class is appropriate? → S3 Standard-IA

A company stores thumbnails that can be regenerated from the original images. The thumbnails are rarely accessed, and the company wants a lower-cost storage class even though the data is stored in a single Availability Zone. Which class should it choose? → S3 One Zone-IA

A company stores medical images that are rarely accessed but, when requested, must be available with millisecond retrieval. Which S3 storage class should it use? → S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval

A company is archiving records that may occasionally need to be retrieved, but retrieval can take several hours. Which S3 storage class should it use? → S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval

A company must retain compliance records for many years, expects almost no access, and wants the lowest-cost S3 storage option. Which storage class should it use? → S3 Glacier Deep Archive

A company knows that objects should remain in Standard storage for 30 days, then move to IA, then to Glacier, and eventually be deleted. How can this process be automated? → S3 Lifecycle rules

A company wants protection against accidental overwrites and deletions of objects so previous versions can be recovered. Which S3 feature should it enable? → Versioning

A company has versioning enabled and deletes the current object without specifying a version ID. The company wants to understand why the previous object version still exists. What did S3 create? → Delete marker

A company must require MFA before users can permanently delete specific object versions or suspend versioning. Which feature provides this protection? → MFA Delete

A financial company must ensure that protected S3 objects cannot be deleted or overwritten during a required retention period. Which S3 feature should it use? → S3 Object Lock

A company wants authorized administrators to be able to bypass an S3 Object Lock retention period when necessary. Which retention mode should it use? → Governance mode

A company must prevent anyone, including administrators, from bypassing the retention period of protected S3 objects. Which Object Lock mode should it use? → Compliance mode

A company must retain records until a specific date, such as five years after creation. Which Object Lock mechanism should it use? → Retention period

A company is involved in a legal investigation and must keep certain S3 objects protected until the investigation is explicitly closed. Which Object Lock mechanism should it use? → Legal Hold

A company needs copies of S3 objects in another AWS Region for disaster recovery if the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which feature should it use? → Cross-Region Replication (CRR)

A company needs to automatically copy objects from a production S3 bucket to another bucket in the same AWS Region for data isolation. Which feature should it use? → Same-Region Replication (SRR)

A company enabled S3 replication but now needs to replicate objects that were uploaded before the replication rule was created. Which feature should it use? → S3 Batch Replication

A company needs server-side encryption for S3 objects and wants to control encryption keys and audit their use through AWS KMS. Which encryption option should it choose? → SSE-KMS

A company has millions of SSE-KMS encrypted S3 objects and wants to reduce the number of KMS requests and associated costs. Which feature should it enable? → S3 Bucket Key

A company wants S3 to use a customer-provided encryption key with every upload and download request. Which encryption option should it use? → SSE-C

A company requires data to be encrypted before it ever reaches AWS. Which encryption approach should it use? → Client-side encryption

A security team requires an S3 bucket to reject any request that is made without HTTPS. Which bucket-policy condition should be used? → aws:SecureTransport

EC2 instances in a private subnet must access only specific S3 buckets without using an Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway. Which solution should be configured? → S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint + endpoint policy

A company wants an S3 bucket to accept requests only when they come through a particular VPC endpoint. Which bucket-policy condition can enforce this restriction? → aws:sourceVpce

An online survey startup has 5 TB of real estate data in an S3 bucket in us-east-1. The data must be shared with a European AWS account, and the startup wants to minimize the S3 request and applicable data-transfer/retrieval costs it pays. Anonymous access must also be disabled. Which S3 feature should it use? → S3 Requester Pays

A company wants to share a large S3 dataset with another AWS account and wants the other account to pay for the S3 requests and applicable download/retrieval charges. What feature should it enable? → S3 Requester Pays

A security team wants to prevent an S3 bucket and its objects from accidentally becoming publicly accessible. Which S3 feature should it enable? → S3 Block Public Access

A company wants to make every object in an S3 bucket readable by anyone on the Internet. Which approach can grant anonymous read access to the objects? → S3 bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject to Principal: "*"

A company wants to make an S3 object publicly readable by assigning a public-read ACL. Under what condition can this work? → S3 ACLs must be enabled

A developer configures S3 CORS to allow requests from https://example.com and expects this configuration to make the S3 objects publicly accessible to everyone. Is that correct? → No. CORS controls browser cross-origin access; it does not grant S3 read permission.

A web application needs to let users download a private S3 object for a limited period without giving them AWS credentials. Which feature should be used? → Presigned URL

A company serves private S3 content through CloudFront and does not want users to access the S3 bucket directly. Which CloudFront feature should it use? → Origin Access Control (OAC)

A security team needs to determine which identity accessed a specific S3 object through API activity logs. Which AWS service should be used? → CloudTrail data events

A company needs S3 request logging and wants the logs delivered to another bucket. Which S3 feature should it use? → S3 Server Access Logs

A large electronics company wants detailed logs for every S3 request, including requester, bucket name, request time, operation, referrer, response time, and error code. Which solution should it use? → S3 Server Access Logs

A global enterprise has S3 buckets across multiple Regions and needs to identify all buckets that do not have versioning enabled. Which solution should it use? → S3 Storage Lens

An application suddenly begins receiving a very large number of S3 requests and needs higher aggregate request throughput. What architectural approach can distribute requests across S3 prefixes? → Use multiple prefixes with parallel requests

An application must upload a very large 200-GB file to S3 efficiently and be able to retry failed portions without restarting the entire upload. Which feature should it use? → Multipart upload

Users around the world upload files to one S3 bucket and uploads from distant locations are slow. Which S3 feature is designed to accelerate long-distance uploads? → S3 Transfer Acceleration

A client needs to download only a portion of a very large S3 object instead of retrieving the entire object. Which feature should it use? → Byte-range request

A company wants a Lambda function to process every newly uploaded object in an S3 bucket automatically. Which S3 mechanism should trigger the function? → S3 Event Notification

A company needs to process S3 events through a queue so consumers can process them asynchronously. Which destination should it use? → Amazon SQS

A company wants one S3 event to be delivered to multiple subscribers for fan-out processing. Which service is most appropriate? → Amazon SNS

A company needs advanced filtering and routing of S3 events to different targets based on event content. Which service should it use? → Amazon EventBridge

A company needs to retrieve only matching rows from a single large CSV object stored in S3. Which service is designed for this use case? → S3 Select

A data team needs to run SQL queries across many CSV and Parquet files stored in S3 without managing servers. Which service should it use? → Amazon Athena

A company needs urgent retrieval of archived S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval data and wants retrieval in a few minutes. Which retrieval option should it choose? → Expedited Retrieval

A company needs guaranteed capacity for Expedited Glacier retrievals rather than relying on on-demand capacity. What should it purchase? → Provisioned Retrieval Capacity

A company needs to retrieve a very large amount of Glacier Flexible Retrieval data and wants the lowest retrieval cost, while waiting several hours is acceptable. Which retrieval option should it choose? → Bulk Retrieval

A company has a static corporate website in an S3 bucket and a registered domain in Route 53. It wants Route 53 to route traffic directly to the S3 static website. Which prerequisite is required? → The S3 bucket name must match the domain name.

A company wants to use example.com as the custom domain for an S3 static website hosted directly through the S3 website endpoint. What should the bucket be named? → example.com

A company wants to host www.example.com directly from an S3 static website endpoint. What should the bucket be named? → www.example.com

A company wants Route 53 to route example.com directly to an S3 static website. Which record type should normally be used? → A Alias record pointing to the S3 website endpoint

A company wants to route an S3 static website through Route 53 and asks whether the Route 53 hosted zone and S3 bucket must be in the same AWS Region. What is the correct answer? → No. Route 53 is global; use the S3 bucket's Region for the S3 website endpoint.

A company configures CORS on an S3 bucket and expects that to satisfy the prerequisite for routing a custom domain from Route 53 to the S3 website. Is CORS required? → No. CORS is for browser cross-origin access, not DNS routing.

A company wants HTTPS for a public S3 static website using a custom domain. Can the S3 website endpoint provide HTTPS directly? → No. Put CloudFront in front of S3 and use HTTPS there.

A company uses CloudFront in front of an S3 bucket with the public domain example.com. Must the S3 bucket itself be named example.com? → No. The bucket-name matching rule applies to the direct S3 website-endpoint pattern; a CloudFront S3 origin can use a differently named bucket.
