docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Amazon EC2 lets you run virtual servers in AWS.

You choose:

  • Instance type → CPU, memory, networking, and other hardware characteristics
  • Purchasing option → On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot
  • Storage → EBS, Instance Store, or network file systems such as EFS
  • Networking → VPC, subnet, security groups, ENIs, IP addresses

docs.title: EC2 instance lifecycle
docs.text: Action State RAM Instance Store Private IP Elastic IP Underlying host Reboot Running ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅ Usually same Stop Stopped ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅ 🔄 May change Hibernate Stopped ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ 🔄 May change Terminate Terminated ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌* Removed

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text:
Reboot restarts the operating system; the EC2 instance remains the same instance.

Use it to:

  • restart the OS
  • restart services or recover from software problems
  • avoid entering the stopped state

RAM is not preserved as a hibernation snapshot.

Exam clue: “Restart the OS without stopping the EC2 instance.” → Reboot

docs.title: Stop → Start
docs.text:
Stopping moves the instance to stopped; starting it again boots the OS normally.

  • RAM is not preserved.
  • Common for off-hours/dev-test shutdowns and applications that do not need to run continuously.
  • The default public IPv4 address can change after stop/start.
  • Use an Elastic IP for a persistent public IPv4 address.

Exam clue: “Application runs only during business hours; stop it outside those hours to reduce cost.” → Stop

docs.title: Hibernate
docs.text:
Hibernate is like stop, but preserves RAM contents by saving RAM state to the root EBS volume; the state is restored when the instance starts.

Hibernation must be enabled when the EC2 instance is launched. You cannot enable or disable hibernation after launch.

Typical clues:

  • long startup time
  • preserve in-memory state
  • resume where the application left off
  • pre-warm an application
  • stop during off-hours but resume quickly

docs.title: Critical exam trap
docs.text:
Hibernation must be enabled when the EC2 instance is launched.

You cannot enable or disable hibernation after launch.

Therefore:

“Enable hibernation on the existing EC2 instance.” → Incorrect

“Launch/migrate the application to an EC2 instance with hibernation enabled.” → Correct

docs.title: Important requirements
docs.text:
• Available only for supported EC2 configurations.
  • Root volume must be an appropriate encrypted EBS volume with enough capacity for the instance RAM contents.

docs.title: Cost concept
docs.text:
• While hibernated in stopped, there are no EC2 instance usage charges once it reaches stopped.
  • Storage and other applicable resource charges still apply.
  • During the hibernation transition through stopping, EC2 instance usage is billed.

Exam clue: “Stop the instance to save cost, but startup takes several minutes; resume much faster.” → Use EC2 hibernation

Remember: Hibernation must be configured at launch.

docs.title: Terminate
docs.text:
Termination permanently removes the EC2 instance; it cannot be restarted.

Storage:

  • EBS volumes with DeleteOnTermination are deleted.
  • EBS volumes configured to remain are preserved.
  • Instance Store data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated; it is not persistent storage.

Exam clue: “Permanently remove the EC2 instance.” → Terminate

docs.title: Lifecycle memory rule
docs.text:
Reboot    = restart the OS
Stop      = shut down
Hibernate = shut down + preserve RAM
Terminate = delete the instance

docs.title: Lifecycle comparison
docs.text: Feature Reboot Stop/Start Hibernate Terminate Same EC2 instance ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ OS restarts ✅ ✅ ❌ — RAM preserved ❌ ❌ ✅ ❌ Instance Store preserved ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ Becomes stopped ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ Can start again ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ Saves compute cost while idle ❌ ✅ ✅ — Fast resume of application state ❌ ❌ ✅ ❌ Permanent removal ❌ ❌ ❌ ✅

docs.title: Exam decision rule
docs.text:
Restart OS
→ Reboot

Shut down temporarily / save compute cost
→ Stop

Shut down + preserve RAM + resume faster
→ Hibernate

Permanently remove
→ Terminate

docs.title: EC2 billing by instance state
docs.text: State Instance usage billed? pending ❌ running ✅ stopping ❌ stopped ❌ shutting-down ❌ terminated ❌

docs.title: Important exception: Hibernation
docs.text:
During hibernation, instance usage is billed while the instance is in stopping.

Normal Stop:
running → stopping → stopped
             ❌          ❌

Hibernate:
running → stopping → stopped
             ✅          ❌
  • Normal stop → stopping = not billed
  • Hibernate → stopping = billed
  • Once hibernation reaches stopped, EC2 instance usage charges stop; EBS storage charges still apply.

docs.title: Reserved Instance trap
docs.text:
A Reserved Instance (RI) is a billing commitment, not an EC2 instance lifecycle object.

Stopping or terminating an EC2 instance covered by an RI:

  • stops that EC2 instance's usage charge
  • does not stop/cancel the RI commitment

AWS states that Reserved Instances applied to terminated instances continue to be billed until the end of their term according to the payment option.

EC2 instance stopped/terminated
→ EC2 instance usage charge stops

Reserved Instance
→ RI commitment continues

docs.title: Decommissioned application + unused RI
docs.text:
Example:

Application decommissioned
→ EC2 instance no longer needed
→ Standard RI has 8 months remaining

Actions:

  1. Terminate the unused EC2 instance

  2. stops EC2 instance usage charges

  3. do not keep an unnecessary instance running

  4. Sell the unused eligible Standard RI in the Reserved Instance Marketplace

  5. transfers the unused RI commitment after the sale

  6. eligible customers can resell unused Standard EC2 Reserved Instances

docs.title: RI Marketplace rule
docs.text:
RI type Can be sold in RI Marketplace? Eligible Standard RI ✅ Convertible RI ❌

Other eligibility conditions apply; not every Standard RI can necessarily be listed.

docs.title: SAA exam trap
docs.text:
“Application was decommissioned but the company still has Reserved Instances.”

Think:

Unused EC2 instance
→ Terminate EC2 instance

Unused eligible Standard RI
→ Sell in Reserved Instance Marketplace

Do not choose:

  • Stop the RI → no RI lifecycle operation like this
  • Terminate the RI → you terminate the EC2 instance, not the RI commitment
  • Cancel the RI → active RIs generally remain commitments for their term; eligible Standard RIs can instead be sold through the Marketplace

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
EC2 instance
= actual compute resource

Reserved Instance
= pricing commitment applied to eligible usage

docs.title: SAA memory rule
docs.text:
Stop EC2
→ stops EC2 usage charges
→ RI charges continue

Terminate EC2
→ stops EC2 usage charges
→ RI commitment continues

Sell eligible Standard RI
→ transfers the RI
→ removes your RI commitment after sale

docs.title: Instance families
docs.text:
An instance type such as m7g.2xlarge contains:

m7g.2xlarge
││ │  │
││ │  └── size
││ └───── architecture / processor family
│└─────── generation
└──────── instance family

docs.title: Instance family quick reference
docs.text: Type Main use Storage optimized I/O-intensive databases, NoSQL, high disk throughput Compute optimized CPU-intensive applications, batch processing, HPC Memory optimized RAM-intensive applications, in-memory databases, caching General purpose Balanced workloads, web/app servers, general databases

docs.title: Main families
docs.text: Family Purpose Common exam keywords M General purpose, balanced CPU/memory web/app servers, general workloads T Burstable general purpose occasional CPU spikes, dev/test, CPU credits C Compute optimized CPU-intensive, batch, HPC R Memory optimized in-memory DBs, caches, real-time analytics X Very high memory SAP HANA, very large in-memory DBs I Storage optimized high IOPS, low-latency local NVMe, NoSQL D Storage optimized, dense HDD distributed file systems, data warehousing, large sequential datasets P GPU optimized ML training, deep learning G GPU optimized graphics, video rendering, ML inference Inf AWS Inferentia-based ML cost-efficient ML inference Trn AWS Trainium-based ML ML training

docs.title: Graviton
docs.text:
A g suffix (m7g, c7g, r7g) indicates an AWS Graviton processor based on ARM architecture.

Typical clues:

  • best price-performance
  • reduce compute cost
  • sustainability
  • Linux/application is ARM-compatible

Trap: Do not choose Graviton merely because the question says “newer generation”; the workload must be ARM-compatible.

docs.title: Enhanced Networking
docs.text:
Enhanced Networking provides:

  • higher bandwidth
  • higher packets per second (PPS)
  • consistently lower inter-instance latency
  • no additional charge on supported EC2 instance types

Main technologies:

ENA
→ modern / Nitro instances

EFA
→ HPC / AI/ML + not work with t3a.medium + Windows issue

Older technology:

Intel 82599 VF
→ older Xen-based instances

docs.title: ENA — Elastic Network Adapter
docs.text:
ENA is the standard enhanced-networking interface for Nitro-based EC2 instances.

Nitro EC2 → ENA → higher bandwidth, higher PPS, lower latency.

ENA also supports Windows EC2 when the required ENA driver is installed.

Exam clue: “Modern EC2 needs higher bandwidth, higher PPS, and lower inter-instance latency.” → Enhanced Networking with ENA

Example: A Windows app on t3a.medium needs higher bandwidth/PPS/lower latency → ENA. t3a is Nitro-based.

docs.title: EFA — Elastic Fabric Adapter
docs.text:
EFA is specialized networking for HPC and AI/ML workloads.

It provides very low-latency, high-throughput communication and can bypass much of the traditional OS networking stack for supported applications.

Typical use cases:

  • HPC clusters
  • CFD simulations
  • MPI-based workloads
  • tightly coupled distributed computing
  • distributed AI/ML training

docs.title: EFA vs ENA
docs.text:
ENA
= general enhanced networking
= normal VPC IP networking

EFA
= specialized HPC / AI/ML networking
= very low latency + high throughput
= OS-bypass capability for supported applications

EFA with ENA provides both normal IP networking and EFA capabilities on supported instances.

Term What it is Key exam clue EFA Network interface designed for HPC HPC + low latency + high throughput + OS-bypass ENA Enhanced networking for EC2 General high-performance networking, not the specific HPC OS-bypass clue ENI Virtual network interface Basic VPC networking: IPs, security groups, etc. VIF Virtual interface for Direct Connect On-premises ↔ AWS connectivity too

docs.title: Critical exam trap
docs.text:
Do not choose EFA merely because the question says HPC.

Check:

HPC
→ Does the instance type support EFA?
→ Does the OS support EFA?

Source guide example:

Windows + t3a.medium + higher bandwidth/PPS/lower latency → ENA, not EFA.

The guide states that EFA is not supported on Windows instances.

docs.title: Exam clues
docs.text:
• “HPC application requires very low-latency communication between EC2 instances.” → EFA
  • “Improve HPC networking performance.” → EFA
  • “Windows EC2 instance needs enhanced networking.” → ENA

docs.title: Cluster Placement Group + EFA
docs.text:
For tightly coupled HPC workloads, EFA is often combined with a Cluster Placement Group.

The two solve different problems:

Cluster Placement Group
→ places instances close together

EFA
→ specialized high-performance networking

docs.title: Intel 82599 VF
docs.text:
The Intel 82599 Virtual Function (VF) is the older enhanced-networking technology used by certain older Xen-based EC2 instance families.

Supported families in the guide:

  • C3
  • C4
  • D2
  • I2
  • M4, excluding m4.16xlarge
  • R3

docs.title: Easy memory
docs.text:
Modern / Nitro
→ ENA

HPC / AI/ML
→ EFA

Older Xen
→ Intel 82599 VF

docs.title: Enhanced Networking decision rule
docs.text:
Modern / Nitro EC2
→ ENA

HPC / AI/ML + supported instance
→ EFA

Older Xen-supported instance
→ Intel 82599 VF

docs.title: EC2 Remote Access Ports
docs.text:
For direct connections to EC2 instances, the protocol determines the inbound Security Group port.

Connection Typical OS Port SSH Linux TCP 22 RDP Windows TCP 3389

docs.title: Exam memory
docs.text:
Linux + SSH
→ TCP 22

Windows + Remote Desktop (RDP)
→ TCP 3389

A Security Group must allow the required inbound port from the appropriate source IP/range.

Windows EC2 + Remote Desktop connection failing + public IP and routing already correct → check inbound TCP 3389 in the Security Group

Linux EC2 + SSH connection → check inbound TCP 22

Important: Security Groups control whether traffic is allowed; they do not encrypt the traffic.

docs.title: Purchasing options
docs.text:
Key questions:

  • How long will the workload run?
  • Is usage predictable?
  • Can the workload be interrupted?
Option Commitment Typical use On-Demand None Short-term or unpredictable workloads Reserved Instances 1 or 3 years Predictable, steady EC2 usage Savings Plans 1 or 3 years Predictable spending with more flexibility Spot None Interruptible, fault-tolerant workloads Dedicated Host Host-level allocation Hardware visibility, certain BYOL requirements Dedicated Instance Dedicated hardware Hardware isolation without host-level control

docs.title: On-Demand
docs.text:
Use when:

  • workload duration is uncertain
  • usage is short-term
  • no long-term commitment is desired
  • interruption is not acceptable

Trap: Do not assume every workload lasting less than one year must be On-Demand. Consider whether long-term commitment makes economic and operational sense.

docs.title: Reserved Instances
docs.text:
Best for predictable, steady EC2 usage.

Example:

Application server
→ 24 hours/day
→ 365 days/year
→ predictable capacity

docs.title: Standard RI
docs.text:
• Larger discount, less flexibility.
  • Can be sold in the Reserved Instance Marketplace if eligibility requirements are met.

docs.title: Convertible RI
docs.text:
• More flexible configuration changes, smaller discount.
  • Can be exchanged for another Convertible RI with different attributes during the term.
  • Cannot be sold in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

Exam clue: “Workload is steady, but instance family/configuration may change.” → Convertible RI

docs.title: Standard vs Convertible
docs.text: Feature Standard RI Convertible RI Higher potential discount ✅ ❌ Modify certain attributes ✅ ✅ Exchange for different RI configuration ❌ ✅ Sell in RI Marketplace ✅ ❌ Best when Usage predictable, config stable Usage predictable, config may change

docs.title: Savings Plans
docs.text:
Compute Savings Plan EC2 Instance Savings Plan Flexibility Highest Lower Commitment $/hour of compute usage $/hour for a specific EC2 family + Region Instance family Can change Must stay in the family Region Can change Must stay in the Region Instance size Can change Can change within family OS / tenancy More flexible More limited Services EC2, Fargate, Lambda EC2 only

Savings Plans are based on a committed spend per hour, not a specific instance reservation.

docs.title: Compute Savings Plan
docs.text:
Most flexible. Can apply across:

  • EC2 instance families
  • EC2 Regions
  • Fargate
  • Lambda

Exam clue: “Long-term savings + maximum flexibility to change instance families, Regions, Fargate/Lambda.” → Compute Savings Plan

docs.title: EC2 Instance Savings Plan
docs.text:
Less flexible, usually larger discount.

Commitment is tied to:

  • a specific instance family
  • a specific AWS Region

Example:

m7i family
us-east-1

docs.title: Capacity reservation vs discount
docs.text:
A common exam trap: confusing discounts with guaranteed capacity.

A pricing commitment does not automatically reserve EC2 capacity.

Requirement:

“Guarantee EC2 capacity in a specific Availability Zone.”

Think:

  • On-Demand Capacity Reservation
  • or a Zonal Reserved Instance, where applicable

A regional RI is primarily a billing discount and does not guarantee capacity in a particular AZ.

Regional RI = discount + AZ flexibility, no capacity reservation.

Zonal RI = discount + capacity reservation in that AZ.

Savings Plans are also billing commitments, not capacity reservations.

docs.title: Spot Instances
docs.text:
Spot Instances use spare AWS capacity and can be reclaimed by AWS.

Good for interruptible workloads:

  • batch processing
  • image/video processing
  • CI/CD workers
  • distributed data processing
  • stateless workers
  • checkpointable workloads
  • flexible background jobs

AWS provides a two-minute interruption notice for Spot interruptions.

Poor choice when:

  • interruption is not tolerated
  • application is not fault tolerant
  • losing the instance causes unacceptable data loss

Exam clue: “Can be interrupted/restarted; minimizing cost is the priority.” → Spot

docs.title: Common cost pattern
docs.text:
For:

  • predictable baseline usage
  • unpredictable additional demand

a common architecture is:

Predictable baseline
→ RI / Savings Plan

Additional flexible capacity
→ Spot / On-Demand

Example:

100 instances normally required
→ 80 covered by Savings Plan
→ 20 added using Spot when possible

Exact combination depends on interruption tolerance.

docs.title: Dedicated Host vs Dedicated Instance
docs.text: Both provide physical hardware isolation from other AWS customers.

docs.title: Dedicated Host
docs.text:
Provides visibility/control over the physical host.

Relevant for:

  • BYOL
  • per-socket licensing
  • per-core licensing
  • host-level visibility
  • physical host placement requirements

Exam clue: “Software is licensed per socket or per physical core.” → Dedicated Host

docs.title: Dedicated Instance
docs.text:
Provides hardware isolation without the same host-level visibility/control.

Exam clue: “Only hardware isolation is required for compliance.” → Dedicated Instance

docs.title: Placement groups
docs.text:
Placement groups control how EC2 instances are placed on underlying AWS infrastructure.

Placement group Placement Main goal Typical workload Memory Cluster Close together in same AZ Low latency + high network throughput HPC, tightly coupled workloads Together Spread Each instance on separate underlying hardware Individual failure isolation Small number of critical instances Individuals apart Partition Groups/partitions on separate underlying hardware Group-level failure isolation Kafka, Cassandra, Hadoop, HDFS Groups apart

docs.title: Cluster placement group
docs.text:
Instances are placed closely together within a single AZ.

Provides:

  • very low network latency
  • high network throughput

Best for:

  • tightly coupled HPC
  • very fast instance-to-instance communication

Trade-off:

  • concentrated failure domain
  • Cluster placement group gives 'insufficient capacity' if hardware has no more room for additional instances in the same cluster placement group. Stop and restart all instances → then launch new ones

Exam clue: “Lowest network latency between EC2 instances.” → Cluster Placement Group

docs.title: Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)
docs.text:
EFA is specialized EC2 networking for HPC and AI/ML workloads.

It provides lower and more consistent latency and higher throughput than traditional TCP networking for supported workloads.

Typical use cases:

  • HPC clusters
  • tightly coupled distributed computing
  • MPI-based applications
  • distributed AI/ML training

docs.title: EFA vs Cluster Placement Group
docs.text:
Cluster Placement Group
→ puts instances close together
→ low latency / high throughput

EFA
→ specialized high-performance networking
→ HPC / AI/ML communication

For HPC:

EC2
+
Cluster Placement Group
+
EFA

The guide states AWS recommends a cluster placement group for EFA-enabled HPC workloads, although it is not an absolute requirement for every EFA deployment.

docs.title: Multiple EFAs
docs.text:
Some supported multi-network-card EC2 instance types can use multiple EFA network interfaces to maximize network bandwidth.

Do not memorize “EFA can only be attached once.”

Instead:

Multiple EFAs may be possible on supported instance types, but EFA remains an HPC/AI/ML performance feature.

docs.title: Critical exam trap
docs.text:
EFA does not provide DDoS protection.

For DDoS protection, do not choose EFA merely because the application is HPC.

HPC performance
→ EFA
→ Cluster Placement Group

DDoS protection
→ AWS Shield
→ AWS WAF
→ CloudFront
→ resilient load-balanced architecture

docs.title: Exam clues
docs.text:
• “HPC application requires very low-latency communication between EC2 instances.” → EFA
  • “Tightly coupled HPC workload requires low latency and high network throughput.” → Cluster Placement Group + EFA
  • “Improve HPC networking performance.” → EFA
  • “Protect a public application from DDoS attacks.” → Shield / WAF / CloudFront, not EFA

docs.title: Easy memory rule
docs.text:
EFA = HPC network performance
Cluster = EC2s close together
Shield = DDoS protection
WAF = web request filtering

docs.title: Spread placement group
docs.text:
Instances are placed on distinct underlying hardware to reduce correlated hardware failures.

Best for:

  • a small number of critical instances
  • workloads where each instance needs an isolated failure domain

A spread placement group supports a limited number of instances per AZ.

Exam clue: “A few critical instances must not share the same underlying hardware.” → Spread Placement Group

docs.title: Partition placement group
docs.text:
Instances are divided into logical partitions; each partition uses separate underlying hardware.

Best for large distributed systems such as:

  • Hadoop
  • Cassandra
  • Kafka
  • HDFS

Supports large numbers of instances and provides partition information through EC2 instance metadata, allowing topology-aware applications to distribute replicas intelligently.

Exam clue: “Large distributed system where instances should be separated into independent hardware groups.” → Partition Placement Group

docs.title: Easy memory rule
docs.text:
Cluster   = close together
Spread    = isolate individual instances
Partition = isolate groups of instances

docs.title: Placement group decision rule
docs.text:
Lowest latency / highest network throughput
→ Cluster

Isolate individual instances
→ Spread

Isolate groups of instances
→ Partition

docs.title: Elastic Network Interface (ENI)
docs.text:
An Elastic Network Interface (ENI) is a virtual network interface attached to an EC2 instance.

A VPC Interface Endpoint is an AWS PrivateLink endpoint that creates ENIs inside your subnet.

An ENI can have:

  • private IPv4 address
  • secondary private IPv4 addresses
  • IPv6 addresses
  • MAC address
  • security groups

Most important SAA concept: a secondary ENI can be moved between EC2 instances, allowing its network identity to survive an EC2 instance failure.

docs.title: Primary ENI vs Secondary ENI
docs.text:
Every EC2 instance has a primary network interface, created automatically at launch.

The primary ENI is associated with that instance and is not used as the portable failover interface in the typical ENI failover pattern.

Additional ENIs can be attached to an instance.

The secondary ENI is the failover interface because it can be detached and attached to another compatible EC2 instance.

docs.title: ENI failover pattern
docs.text:
Example:

dashboard.internal.example.com
→ 10.0.1.50
→ secondary ENI
→ EC2 Instance A

If Instance A fails:

Secondary ENI
→ detach from A
→ attach to B

The client keeps using 10.0.1.50.

What moved:

Secondary ENI
├── private IP
├── MAC address
├── security groups
└── other ENI configuration

The EC2 instance itself was replaced.

docs.title: Important ENI limitation: Availability Zone
docs.text:
An ENI belongs to a subnet, and a subnet belongs to one Availability Zone.

Therefore:

An ENI can only be attached to an instance in the same Availability Zone.

Example:

AZ-A
├── Subnet A
│   └── Secondary ENI
└── EC2 Instance A

The ENI can move to another instance in AZ-A, but not directly to an instance in AZ-B.

For cross-AZ failover, use mechanisms such as:

  • Route 53
  • Elastic Load Balancing
  • application-level failover
  • other multi-AZ patterns

Exam clue: “Primary EC2 fails and replacement must immediately use the same private IP.” → Secondary ENI → detach → attach

docs.title: Multiple ENIs
docs.text:
Multiple ENIs are useful for:

  • separate network paths
  • management networks
  • traffic inspection appliances
  • network appliances
  • multi-homed instances

Example:

EC2 Instance
├── ENI 1 → Application network
└── ENI 2 → Management network

This is a multi-homed configuration.

docs.title: Elastic IP address
docs.text:
An Elastic IP (EIP) is a static public IPv4 address that can be associated with an AWS resource such as an EC2 instance.

The default public IPv4 address is not persistent across stop/start.

Exam clue: “Keep the same public IPv4 after stop/start.” → Elastic IP

An EIP can be remapped to another EC2 instance, including one in another AZ.

docs.title: EIP vs ENI
docs.text: Feature ENI Elastic IP Network identity Private/network interface Public IPv4 Typical use Private IP failover Stable public IPv4 Movable Secondary ENI can move Can be remapped Cross-AZ No; ENI is AZ-specific Yes Main exam use Preserve private network identity Preserve public IPv4

docs.title: Best practice
docs.text:
Avoid EIPs when an AWS-managed DNS/load-balancing solution is more appropriate.

Common alternatives:

  • Application Load Balancer
  • Network Load Balancer
  • Route 53
  • AWS Global Accelerator

docs.title: User data
docs.text:
EC2 user data is commonly used to run initialization commands when an instance launches.

Typical uses:

  • install packages
  • configure applications
  • download configuration
  • start services
  • bootstrap an instance

Example:

#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y nginx
systemctl enable --now nginx

Exam clue: “Automatically install/configure software when the instance launches.” → User data

Do not confuse user data with instance metadata.

docs.title: Instance metadata
docs.text:
EC2 Instance Metadata provides information about the running instance from inside the instance.

Metadata service:

http://169.254.169.254/

curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

Examples:

  • instance ID
  • Availability Zone
  • local IP information
  • IAM role credentials
  • placement information

docs.title: IMDSv2
docs.text:
IMDSv2 adds session-oriented protection to the metadata service and requires a token before metadata can be requested.

Exam clue: “Protect the EC2 metadata service against SSRF-style attacks.” → Require IMDSv2

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Linux OS needs to restart, but the EC2 instance must not enter stopped.

→ Reboot

Development environment runs only 9 AM–6 PM; stop paying EC2 compute charges outside hours; no memory preservation needed.

→ Stop → Start

Application takes minutes to initialize; shut it down during idle periods and restore its previous in-memory state on start.

→ EC2 Hibernation

Remember: Hibernation must be enabled when the instance is launched.

Unused EC2 instance is no longer needed and must be permanently removed.

→ Terminate

docs.title: Instance families and storage
docs.text:
NoSQL database already replicates data; highest priority is I/O throughput and sequential read/write performance.

→ Storage optimized EC2 instance + Instance Store

Why:

High I/O throughput
→ Storage optimized

Database already replicates data
→ Instance Store's ephemeral nature is acceptable

CPU-intensive calculations; no unusually large memory/storage requirement.

→ Compute optimized (C family)

Large in-memory dataset; substantial RAM required rather than high CPU.

→ Memory optimized (R family)

SAP HANA needs a very large memory footprint.

→ X family

Distributed database needs very high local disk I/O and low-latency NVMe.

→ Storage optimized (I family)

Large local HDD capacity; large sequential datasets.

→ D family

ML workload needs GPU acceleration for training.

→ P family

GPU acceleration mainly for graphics rendering or inference.

→ G family

Specialized AWS hardware optimized for ML inference rather than training.

→ Inf family

Linux app is ARM-compatible; wants better price-performance/lower compute cost.

→ Graviton-based instance (g suffix)

Highly variable CPU demand; usually low but occasionally bursts significantly.

→ T family

T-family instance performs well initially but later slows during sustained CPU-heavy processing.

→ CPU credits exhausted

T-family workload must continue bursting beyond accumulated credits.

→ T Unlimited, with possible additional charges

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Modern Nitro-based EC2 needs higher bandwidth, higher PPS, and lower inter-instance latency.

→ Enhanced Networking with ENA

Tightly coupled HPC workload needs very low-latency, high-throughput communication between supported EC2 instances.

→ Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)

Windows EC2 instance needs higher bandwidth, higher PPS, and lower inter-instance latency.

→ ENA, not EFA

Older Xen-based EC2 from a supported family needs enhanced networking.

→ Intel 82599 VF

Tightly coupled HPC cluster needs very low network latency and high network throughput.

→ Cluster Placement Group

For the strongest HPC networking setup:

→ Cluster Placement Group + EFA

"Cluster placement group gives 'insufficient capacity' when adding new instances."

→ Stop and restart all instances → then launch new ones

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text:
A newly created Windows EC2 instance has a public IP, Internet Gateway, and correct route table, but Remote Desktop cannot connect.

→ Allow inbound TCP 3389 in the Security Group

A Linux EC2 instance cannot be reached using SSH, and the network path is already correct.

→ Check inbound TCP 22 in the Security Group

Windows + RDP
→ TCP 3389

Linux + SSH
→ TCP 22

docs.title: Placement groups
docs.text:
Small number of critical EC2 instances; each must be on separate underlying hardware.

→ Spread Placement Group

Large Kafka cluster must separate groups of brokers across independent hardware failure domains.

→ Partition Placement Group

Tightly coupled distributed application needs the lowest possible network latency between EC2 instances.

→ Cluster Placement Group

docs.title: Purchasing and cost
docs.text:
Batch workload can be interrupted/restarted; minimizing EC2 cost is highest priority.

→ Spot Instances

Production workload cannot tolerate interruption and needs predictable compute capacity.

→ Do not use Spot. Consider On-Demand, Reserved Instances, or Savings Plans based on usage and commitment needs.

Predictable EC2 usage but instance configuration may change during the commitment.

→ Convertible Reserved Instance

Predictable EC2 usage; wants larger potential discount; no need to exchange RI configuration.

→ Standard Reserved Instance

Long-term savings with maximum flexibility across instance families, Regions, EC2, Fargate, and Lambda.

→ Compute Savings Plan

Long-term commitment tied to one EC2 instance family in one AWS Region.

→ EC2 Instance Savings Plan

EC2 capacity must be guaranteed in a specific AZ.

→ On-Demand Capacity Reservation or another appropriate zonal capacity reservation mechanism

Not merely:

→ Regional RI or Savings Plan

because those are primarily pricing commitments, not AZ-specific capacity reservations.

Decommissioned application no longer needs its EC2 instance, but an eligible unused Standard RI remains.

→ Terminate the unused EC2 instance and sell the eligible Standard RI through the Reserved Instance Marketplace

docs.title: Dedicated hardware
docs.text:
Software is licensed by physical CPU sockets/cores and physical-server visibility is required.

→ Dedicated Host

Only physical hardware isolation is required for compliance; no host-level visibility/control needed.

→ Dedicated Instance

docs.title: ENI and IP failover
docs.text:
EC2 instance fails; standby must immediately use the same private IP and security-group configuration.

→ Move a secondary ENI to the standby instance

Same private IP must move from one AZ to another.

→ Secondary ENI cannot do this because ENIs are AZ-specific. Use a multi-AZ DNS, load-balancing, or application-level failover architecture.

EC2 needs separate application and management interfaces.

→ Multiple ENIs / multi-homed configuration

EC2 must keep the same public IPv4 after stop/start.

→ Elastic IP

Public application needs a stable endpoint but does not specifically require a dedicated public IPv4 on the EC2 instance.

→ Prefer Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, Route 53, or Global Accelerator, depending on the requirement.

docs.title: User data and metadata
docs.text:
Install software/configuration automatically when a new EC2 instance launches.

→ User data

EC2 application needs instance ID, AZ, local IP information, or IAM role credentials.

→ Instance Metadata

Reduce SSRF risk against EC2 metadata service.

→ Require IMDSv2

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
• Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) → persistent block storage attached to EC2.
  • Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) → shared file storage accessible by multiple Linux-based clients.
  • Instance Store → very fast, temporary local storage physically attached to the EC2 host.

docs.title: EBS — Elastic Block Store
docs.text: Amazon EBS provides persistent block storage for EC2. Typical uses include operating system disks, databases, application files, logs, and persistent data.

docs.title: 1. An EBS volume belongs to one Availability Zone (AZ)
docs.text:
An EBS volume cannot be directly attached to an EC2 instance in another AZ.

EBS volume
    ↓
Snapshot
    ↓
Restore in destination AZ
    ↓
New EBS volume

For cross-Region migration, copy the snapshot to the destination Region before restoring it.

docs.title: 2. EBS is persistent
docs.text:
EBS data survives when an EC2 instance is stopped. Survival after termination depends on DeleteOnTermination.

Volume Default setting Survives termination? Root EBS volume DeleteOnTermination = true No Additional EBS volume Generally false Yes

Exam clue: The root volume must survive termination → set DeleteOnTermination = false.

docs.title: EBS volume attachment
docs.text: Normally, an EBS volume attaches to one EC2 instance at a time.

docs.title: EBS Multi-Attach
docs.text:
Supported io1 and io2 volumes can attach to up to 16 supported Nitro-based EC2 instances in the same AZ. The application must be designed to coordinate shared block storage.

Feature EBS Multi-Attach EFS Shared resource Block device File system Multi-instance access Yes Yes Multi-AZ access No; same AZ only Yes

Only io1 and io2 support Multi-Attach. gp3, st1, sc1, and Magnetic (standard) do not.

Exam clue: Multiple EC2 instances need the same block volume in one AZ, and the application is cluster-aware → io1/io2 Multi-Attach.

docs.title: Elastic Volumes
docs.text:
Elastic Volumes can increase volume size, change volume type, and adjust supported performance settings. An existing EBS volume cannot be shrunk.

Increase/grow → Yes | Shrink → No

docs.title: Modify EBS volumes and EC2 instance attributes
docs.text:
Do not confuse APIs that modify an EBS volume with APIs that modify the EC2 instance.

API What it modifies Example ModifyVolume EBS volume configuration Change supported volume type, size, or IOPS; reduce provisioned IOPS on an io2 volume within its allowed range ModifyInstanceAttribute EC2 instance attributes Change the EBS-optimized (ebsOptimized) setting, subject to instance-type support CloudWatch GetMetricData Retrieves monitoring metrics Analyze actual IOPS and throughput usage

Exam trap: ModifyInstanceAttribute is incorrect when the requirement is to change the provisioned IOPS of an individual EBS volume. Use ModifyVolume.

Can ModifyVolume be used while EC2 is running? Often yes. Supported modifications can be made to an attached, in-use volume without stopping the instance or detaching the volume, subject to applicable limitations. After increasing volume size, extend the filesystem to use the additional capacity. Wait for the previous modification to reach completed before starting another modification on the same volume.

docs.title: Create and mount a new EBS data volume
docs.text:
A newly attached EBS data volume is a block device; Linux does not automatically format or mount it.

Create volume → Attach to EC2 → Format → Mount
                                      ↓
                        Add to /etc/fstab for automatic mounting

Example:

mkfs -t xfs /dev/nvme1n1
mkdir /data
mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data

The exact device name depends on the instance and operating system.

Exam clue: An attached volume is missing from the expected directory → format and mount it; configure /etc/fstab if automatic mounting after reboot is required.

docs.title: EBS performance: IOPS vs Throughput
docs.text:
• IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second): Number of read/write operations per second. Important for databases, transactional systems, and small random operations.
  • Throughput: Amount of data transferred per second, usually MB/s or GB/s. Important for large sequential workloads, log processing, ETL, streaming, and big-data processing.
Workload requirement Think Many small/random operations High IOPS Large sequential reads/writes High throughput

docs.title: SSD
docs.text:
Used for random I/O, databases, boot volumes, and latency-sensitive workloads.

  • gp3 — general-purpose SSD.
  • io1 / io2 — provisioned IOPS SSD.

docs.title: HDD
docs.text:
Used primarily for large sequential workloads and throughput-oriented processing.

  • st1 — Throughput-Optimized HDD.
  • sc1 — Cold HDD.

Important: st1 and sc1 cannot be used as root/boot volumes.

docs.title: Magnetic (standard)
docs.text:
Magnetic is a previous-generation EBS volume type for small datasets accessed infrequently when performance is not the primary concern.

For current EBS choices, sc1 is the low-cost HDD option for infrequently accessed data.

Term Meaning Magnetic (standard) Previous-generation EBS; legacy terminology sc1 Current Cold HDD for low-cost, infrequently accessed data

Exam traps:

  • Spot is not an EBS volume type. Spot is an EC2 purchasing option.
  • SR-IOV is not an EBS volume type. It is an I/O virtualization technology.

docs.title: General Purpose SSD — gp3
docs.text:
gp3 is the general-purpose SSD option and a common default choice.

  • 3,000 baseline IOPS
  • 125 MB/s baseline throughput
  • IOPS and throughput can be provisioned independently of volume size.
  • Supports up to 80,000 IOPS.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A workload needs 10,000 IOPS and 100 GB of storage.

With gp3, you can configure:

100 GB
10,000 IOPS

You do not need to increase storage capacity just to obtain more IOPS.

Exam clue: More IOPS without increasing storage capacity → gp3.

docs.title: gp2 vs gp3
docs.text:
gp2 ties IOPS to volume size and also supports burst behavior.

  • gp2: baseline of 3 IOPS per GiB, subject to volume-size and burst rules.
  • gp3: baseline of 3,000 IOPS; IOPS and throughput can be configured independently of size.
Feature gp2 gp3 Baseline IOPS model Tied to size 3,000 baseline IOPS independent of size No Yes Throughput independent of size No Yes General-purpose SSD choice Previous model Common recommended choice

Exam clue: A company uses gp2 and needs more performance without paying for unnecessary storage → migrate to gp3.

Do not choose gp3 merely because the question mentions gp2; look for independent performance configuration or better price/performance.

docs.title: Provisioned IOPS SSD — io1 / io2
docs.text:
Use io1 or io2 when workloads require high, predictable IOPS and consistently low latency, especially for demanding databases and transactional applications.

Typical workloads:

  • High-performance relational databases.
  • High-performance NoSQL databases.
  • Demanding transactional applications.
  • Applications with strict I/O requirements.
Requirement Choice Normal database or general-purpose workload gp3 High, predictable IOPS io1 / io2 I/O-intensive database with strict latency requirements io1 / io2

Exam clues:

  • “Consistent, low-latency performance” → Provisioned IOPS.
  • “Highly I/O-intensive database” → io1 / io2.

Do not automatically choose Provisioned IOPS just because the workload is a database. Match the choice to the actual performance requirements.

docs.title: io2 Block Express
docs.text:
Amazon EBS io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS and provides very low latency.

Exam clues: “256,000 IOPS” or “sub-millisecond latency” → io2 Block Express.

docs.title: Throughput-Optimized HDD — st1
docs.text:
Use st1 for large sequential workloads where throughput matters more than random IOPS.

Typical workloads include:

  • Log processing.
  • Big-data workloads.
  • ETL.
  • Large sequential datasets.

Exam clue: Large sequential reads/writes and high throughput at lower cost → st1.

docs.title: Cold HDD — sc1
docs.text:
Use sc1 for infrequently accessed data when minimizing storage cost is the priority.

Exam clue: Infrequently accessed data on low-cost current-generation EBS HDD storage → sc1.

docs.title: Magnetic — standard
docs.text:
Magnetic (standard) is a previous-generation EBS volume type for small datasets, infrequent access, and workloads where performance is not the primary concern. Its performance is much lower and less consistent than that of modern SSD types.

Legacy exam wording: “Magnetic provides the lowest cost per GB and is suitable for infrequently accessed data.”

Recognize this as Magnetic (standard), not sc1.

docs.title: EBS decision guide
docs.text: Workload requirement EBS choice General-purpose SSD gp3 IOPS independent of volume size gp3 High, predictable IOPS io1 / io2 Up to 256,000 IOPS, extreme performance io2 Block Express Large sequential workload, throughput priority st1 Infrequently accessed, low-cost current HDD sc1 Legacy Magnetic volume requirement Magnetic (standard)

docs.title: EBS snapshots
docs.text:
An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume. Snapshots are stored in AWS-managed storage and are incremental after the first snapshot.

AWS stores the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot rather than making each snapshot a completely independent full copy.

Day 1 → Snapshot A
Day 2 → Snapshot B (changed blocks)
Day 3 → Snapshot C (changed blocks)

docs.title: Using an EBS volume while a snapshot is in progress
docs.text:
An EBS volume remains available while its snapshot is created. The volume can continue to be read from and written to, and the EC2 instance can continue normal operations.

EC2 → EBS volume
        ├── Read ✅
        ├── Write ✅
        └── Snapshot in progress ✅

Exam trap: “Can the EBS volume be used while the snapshot is in progress?” → Yes. A snapshot does not lock the volume or make it read-only.

docs.title: Cross-Region EBS backup
docs.text:
For disaster recovery in another Region:

EBS volume
    ↓
Create snapshot
    ↓
Copy snapshot to destination Region
    ↓
Restore volume there when needed

Exam clue: Back up EBS data to another AWS Region → create a snapshot and copy it to the destination Region.

docs.title: Snapshot Archive
docs.text:
EBS Snapshot Archive is intended for snapshots that are rarely accessed. It substantially reduces storage cost but has a slower restore process.

Exam clue: Snapshots are rarely restored, and lower backup storage cost matters more than fast recovery → Snapshot Archive.

docs.title: Recycle Bin
docs.text:
Amazon EBS Recycle Bin protects supported resources, including EBS snapshots, against accidental deletion. Retention rules keep deleted snapshots recoverable for a specified period.

Exam clue: Protect accidentally deleted EBS snapshots → Recycle Bin.

docs.title: Fast Snapshot Restore
docs.text:
Normally, data restored from an EBS snapshot is loaded on demand, potentially slowing initial reads while blocks are initialized.

Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) pre-initializes the restored volume so that it can provide full performance immediately.

Trade-off: Faster recovery and immediate performance, but additional cost.

Exam clue: A restored EBS volume must provide full performance immediately, without the initial read penalty → Fast Snapshot Restore.

docs.title: Data Lifecycle Manager — DLM
docs.text:
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates EBS snapshot lifecycle operations, including creation, retention, deletion, and selected cross-Region snapshot-copy workflows.

Example:

Create a snapshot daily
        ↓
Keep the last 7
        ↓
Delete older snapshots

Exam clue: Automatically create, retain, and delete EBS snapshots on a schedule → Amazon DLM.

For broader centralized backup management across multiple AWS services, consider AWS Backup.

docs.title: EBS encryption — AWS KMS
docs.text:
EBS encryption protects data at rest, data in transit between EC2 and EBS, and snapshots.

Scenario Result Encrypted EBS volume Data at rest is encrypted Data moving between EC2 and EBS Encrypted Snapshot of an encrypted volume Automatically encrypted Volume created from an encrypted snapshot Automatically encrypted Claim that only data in the volume is encrypted Incorrect Claim that a snapshot of an encrypted volume is unencrypted Incorrect Claim that a volume restored from an encrypted snapshot is unencrypted Incorrect

docs.title: EBS Encryption by Default
docs.text:
EBS Encryption by Default is a Region-level account setting that automatically encrypts new EBS volumes in that Region.

A new EBS volume restored from an unencrypted snapshot is also automatically encrypted when the setting applies.

Enable EBS Encryption by Default
               ↓
          AWS Region
               ↓
       New EBS volumes
               ↓
      Automatically encrypted

It does not automatically encrypt existing unencrypted EBS volumes or snapshots.

docs.title: Encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume
docs.text:
You cannot simply toggle an existing unencrypted volume to encrypted in place. Use:

Unencrypted EBS volume
        ↓
Create snapshot
        ↓
Copy snapshot with encryption enabled
        ↓
Create encrypted EBS volume
        ↓
Attach new volume

Exam clue: Encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume → snapshot → copy with encryption → create a new encrypted volume.

docs.title: EFS — Elastic File System
docs.text:
Amazon EFS is a managed, scalable, POSIX-compliant file system that primarily serves Linux-based workloads through NFSv4.

It grows and shrinks automatically as files are added or removed, and supports simultaneous access by multiple clients.

             EFS
              │
      ┌───────┼───────┐
      ↓       ↓       ↓
     EC2     EC2     EC2

All clients can access the same shared files.

docs.title: EFS vs EBS
docs.text: Feature EBS EFS Storage type Block File Shared by many instances Normally no Yes Multi-AZ Volume is AZ-specific Yes Access model Block device NFS file system Typical uses OS, databases, application disk Shared files Capacity management Provision volume size Grows/shrinks automatically Typical clients EC2 Multiple EC2 instances and compute clients

docs.title: EFS use cases
docs.text:
• User uploads.
  • Shared application files.
  • Content management systems.
  • WordPress content.
  • Shared configuration and data across Linux instances.
  • Applications behind an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) that require shared files.

Exam clue: Multiple EC2 instances in different AZs must access the same files → EFS.

docs.title: EFS and Windows
docs.text:
EFS is not the standard choice for native Windows file-sharing requirements involving SMB or Active Directory.

Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is the appropriate choice for Windows file shares requiring:

  • Server Message Block (SMB).
  • Windows file-sharing features.
  • Active Directory integration.

Exam clue: Windows + SMB + Active Directory → FSx for Windows File Server.

docs.title: EFS storage and cost
docs.text:
• EFS automatically grows and shrinks as data changes; you do not pre-provision a fixed capacity as with EBS.
  • EFS generally costs more per GB than EBS, but does not charge for unused provisioned capacity in the same way.
  • EFS lifecycle management can move less frequently accessed files into lower-cost storage classes.

docs.title: EFS performance modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior General Purpose Default and recommended for most workloads; prioritizes lower latency Max I/O Designed for very high concurrency and aggregate throughput where higher latency is acceptable

Exam clue: Thousands of concurrent clients, maximum aggregate throughput more important than latency → Max I/O.

For most applications, choose General Purpose.

docs.title: EFS throughput modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior Elastic Automatically scales throughput with workload demand; a modern default choice for many workloads Provisioned Explicitly configures throughput independently of stored data size Bursting Throughput depends on stored data and the EFS bursting model

Exam clue: Automatically adapts throughput to workload demand → Elastic throughput.

docs.title: EFS lifecycle management
docs.text:
EFS can move less frequently accessed files into lower-cost storage classes.

Frequently accessed → EFS Standard
Less frequently accessed → EFS IA
Very cold data → EFS Archive

Exam clue: Reduce costs for files that have not been accessed for a long time → EFS lifecycle management.

docs.title: Instance Store
docs.text:
Instance Store provides local storage physically attached to the EC2 host.

  • Very low latency.
  • Potentially extremely high I/O performance.
  • No network hop like network-attached EBS.
  • Ephemeral: data must be reproducible, disposable, or recoverable elsewhere.

docs.title: Instance Store data persistence
docs.text:
Instance Store data survives an EC2 reboot, but not a stop, hibernate, or termination.

EC2 action Instance Store data Reboot Survives Stop Lost Hibernate Lost Terminate Lost

Exam clue: Temporary cache, scratch space, or data replicated elsewhere → Instance Store.

docs.title: When Instance Store is appropriate
docs.text:
• Temporary files.
  • Scratch space.
  • Caching.
  • Intermediate processing data.
  • Data replicated by the application.
  • High-speed local processing.

For example, a Cassandra cluster can replicate data across multiple nodes. Losing one node's Instance Store data does not necessarily lose the application's data because other replicas exist.

docs.title: EBS vs Instance Store
docs.text:
Feature EBS Instance Store Location Network-attached AWS storage Physically local to host Persistent Yes No Survives stop Yes No Survives reboot Yes Yes EBS snapshots supported Yes No Can detach and attach elsewhere Yes, subject to AZ No Very high local IOPS Depends on volume and instance Excellent Typical use OS, databases, persistent data Cache, scratch, temporary processing

Exam clues:

  • “Fastest possible temporary storage” → Instance Store.
  • “High IOPS and data must persist” → EBS, typically io2 for extreme IOPS.

Do not choose Instance Store solely for its performance if the data must survive an EC2 stop.

docs.title: Main storage comparison
docs.text: Storage Best for EBS Persistent block storage attached to EC2 EFS Shared files across multiple Linux-based clients Instance Store Very fast temporary local storage FSx for Windows File Server Windows/SMB/Active Directory file shares FSx for Lustre High-performance parallel file systems Amazon S3 Object storage and large-scale durable data

docs.title: Question patterns
docs.text:
“Database needs 12,000 IOPS and does not require extreme I/O performance.”

→ gp3, provided its configured performance meets the requirements.

“The application needs more IOPS without increasing storage capacity.”

→ gp3.

“The application needs consistent, low-latency performance for an I/O-intensive relational or NoSQL database.”

→ io1 or io2.

“Database requires very high, predictable IOPS.”

→ io1/io2.

“Application requires 256,000 IOPS and extremely low latency.”

→ io2 Block Express.

“Large sequential processing of logs; throughput is the priority.”

→ st1.

“Data is rarely accessed and storage cost should be minimized.”

→ sc1.

“A legacy application uses Magnetic EBS for a small, infrequently accessed dataset where performance is not important.”

→ Magnetic (standard).

“An older question says Magnetic provides the lowest cost per GB for infrequently accessed data.”

→ Recognize Magnetic (standard) as a previous-generation EBS volume type. Do not confuse it with sc1, the current Cold HDD option.

“The company uses gp2 and wants more performance without paying for unnecessary storage.”

→ Migrate to gp3.

“Multiple EC2 instances in different AZs need access to the same files.”

→ EFS.

“Multiple EC2 instances in the same AZ need access to the same block volume.”

→ io1/io2 Multi-Attach.

“Up to 16 supported EC2 instances need simultaneous read/write access to the same block volume in one AZ.”

→ io1/io2 Multi-Attach.

“gp3 Multi-Attach provides multi-AZ resiliency.”

→ Incorrect. gp3 does not support Multi-Attach, and Multi-Attach is limited to the same AZ.

“A storage option called Spot provides the lowest EBS cost per GB.”

→ Incorrect. Spot is an EC2 purchasing option, not an EBS volume type.

“SR-IOV volume is suitable for boot volumes and small databases.”

→ Incorrect. SR-IOV is not an EBS volume type.

“Windows servers need an SMB file share integrated with Active Directory.”

→ FSx for Windows File Server.

“The application needs very fast temporary local storage.”

→ Instance Store.

“The application needs fast storage, and data must survive an EC2 stop.”

→ EBS.

“The root volume must survive EC2 termination.”

→ Set DeleteOnTermination = false.

“An EBS volume must be moved to another AZ.”

→ Snapshot → restore in the destination AZ.

“An EBS backup must be copied to another AWS Region.”

→ Copy the EBS snapshot to the destination Region.

“EBS volume configuration needs to change, including provisioned IOPS.”

→ Use ModifyVolume, not ModifyInstanceAttribute.

“The EC2 instance needs its EBS-optimized attribute changed.”

→ ModifyInstanceAttribute, subject to instance-type support.

“Determine actual IOPS and throughput usage from CloudWatch metrics.”

→ CloudWatch GetMetricData.

“All new EBS volumes, including volumes restored from unencrypted snapshots, must automatically be encrypted.”

→ Enable EBS Encryption by Default for the Region.

“Encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume.”

→ Snapshot → copy with encryption → create a new encrypted volume.

“An encrypted EBS volume must protect data at rest and while moving between EC2 and EBS.”

→ EBS encryption.

“A snapshot is created from an encrypted EBS volume.”

→ The snapshot is automatically encrypted.

“Create a volume from an encrypted EBS snapshot.”

→ The new volume is automatically encrypted.

“Automatically create and retain EBS snapshots on a schedule.”

→ Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM).

“Protect accidentally deleted EBS snapshots.”

→ EBS Recycle Bin.

“A restored EBS volume must provide full performance immediately.”

→ Fast Snapshot Restore.

“Multiple Linux instances in different AZs need access to the same shared file system.”

→ EFS.

“Linux instances need a POSIX-compliant shared file system across AZs.”

→ EFS.

“Windows + SMB + Active Directory.”

→ FSx for Windows File Server.

“Thousands of EFS clients; maximum aggregate performance matters more than latency.”

→ EFS Max I/O performance mode.

“Reduce EFS cost for files that are rarely accessed.”

→ EFS lifecycle management → IA / Archive.

“Data can be recreated, and the application needs the highest local storage performance.”

→ Instance Store.

docs.title: Section 5: Elastic Load Balancing & Auto Scaling
The idea
docs.text:
Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets.

Clients
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
EC2 instances

The load balancer performs health checks:

Healthy instance   → receives traffic ✅
Unhealthy instance → stops receiving traffic ❌

Auto Scaling Group (ASG) manages the number of EC2 instances.

High demand → scale out
Low demand  → scale in
Failure     → replace instance

Together:

Clients
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Auto Scaling Group
   ↓
EC2 instances

docs.title: OSI layers
docs.text:
Layer What it sees Example L3 IP 10.0.1.10 L4 IP + port + TCP/UDP TCP 443, UDP 5000 L7 HTTP details Path, host, headers 
URL/path/host/header routing
→ ALB

TCP/UDP, static IP, very high performance
→ NLB

docs.title: Load Balancers
docs.text:
Layer Main use Exam keyword ALB 7 HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC, content routing Path, host, header NLB 4 TCP/UDP/TLS, static IP, high performance UDP, fixed IP GWLB 3 Security appliances Firewall, IDS, IPS CLB 4/7 Legacy Usually avoid

ALB and NLB both support Weighted Target Groups.

docs.title: ALB — Application Load Balancer
docs.text:
Layer 7.

Supports routing based on:

  • URL path
  • Hostname
  • HTTP headers
  • Query strings

Examples:

/api/*       → API target group
/images/*    → Image target group

api.example.com
   ↓
API servers

admin.example.com
   ↓
Admin servers

docs.title: Important facts
docs.text:
• Targets can be EC2, IP addresses, Lambda, or containers.
  • Performs health checks.
  • Supports AWS WAF.
  • Uses a DNS name, not fixed static IPs.
  • Supports Weighted Target Groups.

docs.title: Weighted Target Groups
docs.text:
ALB
 ├── 80% → Version A
 └── 20% → Version B

Useful for:

  • Blue/green deployments
  • Canary deployments
  • A/B testing
  • Gradual migration

Weighted Target Groups = traffic split at the load balancer. Route 53 Weighted Routing = traffic split at DNS level.

docs.title: Client IP behind ALB
docs.text:
The original client IP is normally available through:

X-Forwarded-For

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text:
Keeps a client on the same target.

User → ALB → EC2-A

Useful when session state is stored locally.

A better architecture is often an external session store such as:

  • ElastiCache
  • DynamoDB

docs.title: ECS dynamic port mapping
docs.text: ALB can route to different container ports on the same EC2 instance.

docs.title: Fixed IP
docs.text:
ALB does not provide fixed static IPs.

Fixed IP requirement
→ NLB

docs.title: NLB — Network Load Balancer
docs.text:
Layer 4.

Supports:

  • TCP
  • UDP
  • TLS

Main characteristics:

  • Very high throughput
  • Very low latency
  • Static IP per AZ
  • Can use Elastic IPs
  • Preserves client source IP
  • Supports Weighted Target Groups

Use NLB for:

  • UDP applications
  • Gaming
  • IoT
  • Custom TCP protocols
  • Very high connection volumes
  • Fixed IP requirements

Example:

UDP gaming application requiring a fixed IP

→ NLB

docs.title: NLB Weighted Target Groups
docs.text:
NLB
 ├── 50% → AWS
 └── 50% → On-prem

Useful for:

  • Migration
  • Blue/green
  • Canary deployments

Important:

  • New connections use the new weights.
  • Existing connections are not immediately moved.
  • Weight 0 means no new connections to that target group.

docs.title: GWLB — Gateway Load Balancer
docs.text:
Used to pass traffic through security appliances.

Examples:

  • Firewalls
  • IDS
  • IPS
  • Traffic inspection appliances
Traffic
   ↓
GWLB
   ↓
Security appliance
   ↓
Application

Uses GENEVE on port 6081.

Firewall / IDS / IPS → GWLB

docs.title: CLB — Classic Load Balancer
docs.text:
Legacy generation.

For modern architectures, prefer:

  • ALB
  • NLB
  • GWLB

docs.title: ALB/NLB Weighted Target Groups
docs.text:
AWS app      → 80%
On-prem app  → 20%

Load-balancer-level splitting.

docs.title: Route 53 Weighted Routing
docs.text:
example.com
 ├── 80% → AWS
 └── 20% → On-prem

DNS-level splitting.

docs.title: Weighted vs Failover
docs.text:
Multiple resources receive traffic
→ Weighted

Primary + backup
→ Failover

docs.title: Direct Connect
docs.text:
Private connectivity between on-premises and AWS:

On-premises
     |
Direct Connect
     |
   AWS VPC

Private AWS ↔ data center connectivity → Direct Connect or VPN

docs.title: Cross-zone load balancing
docs.text:
Without cross-zone balancing, a load balancer node normally sends traffic to targets in its own AZ.

With cross-zone balancing, traffic can be distributed across targets in other AZs.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
• ALB: enabled by default.
  • NLB: disabled by default at the load balancer level.

Uneven traffic across AZs → check cross-zone load balancing.

docs.title: Deregistration delay
docs.text:
When a target is removed:

New requests
→ stop going to target

Existing connections
→ allowed to finish

Also called:

  • Deregistration delay
  • Connection draining

Errors during scale-in → deregistration delay

docs.title: SNI
docs.text:
SNI = Server Name Indication

Allows one HTTPS listener to serve multiple certificates based on hostname.

example.com
api.example.com
admin.example.com

Multiple HTTPS domains with different certificates → SNI

docs.title: TLS termination
docs.text:
The load balancer can terminate HTTPS:

Client
  ↓ HTTPS
ALB
  ↓ HTTP/HTTPS
EC2

Certificates are commonly stored in ACM.

docs.title: Auto Scaling Groups
docs.text:
An ASG manages a group of EC2 instances.

It uses a Launch Template to define how new instances are launched.

Launch Template can contain:

  • AMI
  • Instance type
  • Security groups
  • User data
  • Key pair

docs.title: Min / Desired / Max
docs.text:
min     = 2
desired = 4
max     = 10

docs.title: Self-healing
docs.text:
Instance fails
     ↓
ASG detects it
     ↓
Replace instance

docs.title: ECS scaling
docs.text:
With ECS using EC2:

Scaling Scales Purpose ECS Service Auto Scaling Tasks Application workload ECS Cluster Auto Scaling EC2 instances Container capacity Capacity Provider EC2 capacity for ECS Connects task demand to EC2 capacity 
High application load
→ More ECS tasks

Not enough EC2 capacity
→ More EC2 instances

                ECS
                /   \
             EC2    Fargate
              ↓        ↓
           Tasks     Tasks
              ↓        ↓
         Containers  Containers

docs.title: Target Tracking
docs.text:
Maintain a metric around a target.

Target CPU = 40%

Keep CPU around a specific value → Target Tracking

docs.title: Step Scaling
docs.text:
Different actions at different thresholds.

CPU 70% → +1
CPU 90% → +3

Different scaling actions by threshold → Step Scaling

docs.title: Scheduled Scaling
docs.text:
For predictable traffic.

09:00 → scale out
18:00 → scale in

Predictable schedule → Scheduled Scaling

docs.title: Predictive Scaling
docs.text:
Uses historical patterns to forecast demand.

Historical traffic
       ↓
Forecast
       ↓
Scale ahead of demand

Predict future demand → Predictive Scaling

docs.title: ASG Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text: Lifecycle hooks pause an instance during launch or termination.

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
Pending
   ↓
Pending:Wait
   ↓
Custom action
   ↓
Pending:Proceed
   ↓
InService

Custom setup before instance enters service → Pending:Wait

docs.title: Termination
docs.text:
Terminating
   ↓
Terminating:Wait
   ↓
Custom action
   ↓
Terminating:Proceed
   ↓
Terminated

Collect logs / cleanup before termination → Terminating:Wait

Typical pattern:

ASG
 ↓
Terminating:Wait
 ↓
EventBridge
 ↓
Lambda
 ↓
Collect logs
 ↓
Complete lifecycle action
 ↓
Terminate

docs.title: ASG health checks
docs.text:
By default, ASG uses EC2 health checks.

An instance can be:

EC2 = running ✅
Application = broken ❌

ASG may still consider it healthy.

Enable ELB health checks when the application itself must determine instance health.

ALB
 ↓
Unhealthy target
 ↓
ASG
 ↓
Replace instance

docs.title: ASG + SQS
docs.text:
For EC2 workers processing SQS jobs:

Application
    ↓
   SQS
    ↓
Workers

Scale based on queue metrics such as backlog per instance.

More pending jobs → more worker capacity.

docs.title: ASG Termination Policy
docs.text: When an ASG scales in, AWS must decide which instance to terminate.

docs.title: Default termination behavior
docs.text:
The default policy first tries to maintain AZ balance.

AZ-A = 10
AZ-B = 8
AZ-C = 7

Scale in
   ↓
Consider AZ-A first

Then it prefers instances with outdated/older launch configuration or launch template versions.

If candidates are still tied, it uses the instance closest to the next billing hour.

docs.title: Default shortcut
docs.text:
DEFAULT
   ↓
AZ with MOST instances
   ↓
Outdated configuration
   ↓
Closest to next billing hour

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Oldest configuration

with:

Oldest running instance

OldestInstance is a separate termination policy that specifically prefers the instance that has been running the longest.

docs.title: Useful termination policies
docs.text: Policy Meaning Default Maintain AZ balance + prefer outdated configuration + billing-hour criterion OldestInstance Terminate oldest running instance NewestInstance Terminate newest running instance OldestLaunchConfiguration Prefer instances using oldest launch configuration ClosestToNextInstanceHour Prefer instance closest to next billing hour

docs.title: Route 53 + Load Balancer + ASG
docs.text:
Different layers solve different problems:

Route 53
→ DNS-level routing

Load Balancer
→ stop traffic to unhealthy targets

ASG
→ replace failed instances

docs.title: Route 53 policies
docs.text:
Requirement Policy Split traffic by percentage Weighted Primary + standby Failover Lowest-latency Region Latency-Based Routing User location Geolocation Geographic distance + bias Geoproximity

Memory:

50/50
→ Weighted

Primary + Backup
→ Failover

Lowest latency
→ Latency

docs.title: Common question patterns
docs.text:
/api/* → one target group, /images/* → another → ALB path-based routing

Route based on hostname → ALB host-based routing

UDP + fixed IP → NLB

Very high TCP connection volume → NLB

Firewall / IDS / IPS → GWLB

Split traffic between two application versions → Weighted Target Groups

Route users to the lowest-latency Region → Route 53 Latency-Based Routing

Gradually migrate HTTP application from on-premises to AWS → ALB Weighted Target Groups or Route 53 Weighted Routing

Primary + standby application → Route 53 Failover

Load balancer says unhealthy but ASG does not replace instance → Enable ELB health checks

Traffic increases predictably every morning → Scheduled Scaling

Keep CPU around 40% → Target Tracking

Different scaling actions at different thresholds → Step Scaling

Predict future demand → Predictive Scaling

Multiple HTTPS certificates on one ALB → SNI

Errors when instances are removed during scale-in → Deregistration delay

Original client IP behind ALB → X-Forwarded-For

Fixed load balancer IP → NLB

Scale workers based on pending SQS jobs → SQS queue metrics

Terminate oldest running instance → OldestInstance policy

Collect logs before termination → Lifecycle hook + Terminating:Wait

Perform custom setup before launch completes → Lifecycle hook + Pending:Wait Default ASG scale-in termination behavior → Most-populated AZ → outdated configuration → closest to next billing hour

docs.title: Pocket Card
docs.text: Keyword Answer Path / host / header routing ALB HTTP / HTTPS / gRPC ALB WAF ALB Weighted Target Groups ALB or NLB UDP NLB Static IP / Elastic IP NLB Very high performance NLB Firewall / IDS / IPS GWLB GENEVE 6081 GWLB Multiple HTTPS certificates SNI Client IP behind ALB X-Forwarded-For Scale-in connection errors Deregistration delay Uneven AZ traffic Cross-zone load balancing Keep CPU at X% Target Tracking Different scaling steps Step Scaling Predictable traffic schedule Scheduled Scaling Forecast future demand Predictive Scaling Application health should replace EC2 ELB health checks on ASG Scale workers by jobs SQS metrics Oldest running instance OldestInstance Default ASG termination Most-populated AZ → outdated config → billing hour Before instance enters service Pending:Wait Before instance termination Terminating:Wait Lowest-latency Region Route 53 Latency Percentage traffic split Route 53 Weighted Primary + backup Route 53 Failover Replace failed EC2 ASG ECS application scaling Service Auto Scaling → tasks ECS EC2 capacity scaling Capacity Provider / Cluster Auto Scaling

docs.title: Trap
docs.text:
Oldest configuration ≠ oldest running instance.

"Terminate the instance that has been running the longest."

→ OldestInstance termination policy

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your private network inside AWS.

You control:

  • IP address ranges
  • Resource placement
  • Internet access
  • Communication between resources/networks
  • Routing
AWS Region
└── VPC
    ├── Subnet → EC2
    └── Subnet → Database

VPC = your AWS network

docs.title: Boxes in boxes
docs.text:
AWS Region
└── VPC
    ├── AZ-A
    │   ├── Public Subnet → EC2
    │   └── Private Subnet → EC2
    │
    └── AZ-B
        ├── Public Subnet → EC2
        └── Private Subnet → Database
  • VPC → one Region
  • Subnet → one AZ
  • Multi-AZ → multiple subnets
  • Subnets contain resources
  • Route tables determine traffic paths
  • newly created subnet is, by default, linked to the main route table of the VPC.

Route table = "Traffic to X goes through Y."

docs.title: Route tables
docs.text:
Example:

Destination       Target
0.0.0.0/0         Internet Gateway
10.0.0.0/16       local

The local route allows communication within the VPC CIDR, subject to security controls.

docs.title: Longest-prefix match
docs.text:
When multiple routes match, the most specific route wins.

10.0.0.0/16 → Transit Gateway
10.0.1.0/24 → VPC Peering

Traffic to 10.0.1.50 uses /24.

More specific route wins.

docs.title: Public vs private
docs.text:
A subnet is public when its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway (IGW).

0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway

A subnet is private when it has no route to an IGW.

Public subnet = route to IGW

Not the subnet name and not simply having a public IP.

docs.title: Internet Gateway
docs.text:
Provides internet connectivity:

EC2 ↔ IGW ↔ Internet

For IPv4, both directions are possible if routing, public IP addressing, and security rules allow it.

docs.title: Public subnet vs internet-reachable EC2
docs.text:
For IPv4 Internet reachability, an EC2 instance normally needs:

Public subnet
+
Public IPv4 / Elastic IP
+
Allowed SG/NACL traffic

Therefore:

Public subnet
= route to IGW

Internet-reachable EC2
= public subnet + public IP + allowed traffic

docs.title: Internet access components
docs.text: Component IP Traffic Purpose Internet Gateway IPv4 + IPv6 Two-way Internet access for public resources NAT Gateway IPv4 Outbound Private IPv4 → Internet Egress-Only IGW IPv6 Outbound Private IPv6 → Internet VPC Endpoint IPv4/IPv6 Private Access AWS services privately

docs.title: NAT Gateway — private IPv4 outbound
docs.text:
Used when private instances need:

  • OS/package updates
  • External APIs
  • Internet access
Private EC2
 ↓
NAT Gateway
 ↓
Internet Gateway
 ↓
Internet

Private EC2 → Internet ✅
Internet → Private EC2 ❌

docs.title: NAT Gateway placement
docs.text:
A traditional zonal NAT Gateway is in a public subnet.

Private subnet route:

0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway

NAT then uses the IGW.

docs.title: NAT availability
docs.text:
Traditional high-availability pattern:

AZ-A → NAT Gateway A
AZ-B → NAT Gateway B

Avoid making one AZ's NAT Gateway a dependency for another AZ.

docs.title: Current AWS nuance
docs.text:
AWS also provides Regional NAT Gateways, which automatically expand across AZs.

For SAA:

Traditional HA design → one zonal NAT Gateway per AZ

Regional NAT Gateway → managed cross-AZ expansion

docs.title: NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance
docs.text: NAT Gateway NAT Instance AWS-managed EC2 you manage Automatically scales You manage scaling/patching No security group Can use security group Hourly + data processing cost EC2-based cost — Disable source/destination checks

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
NAT Gateway is mainly an IPv4 solution.

For IPv6 outbound-only access:

Egress-Only Internet Gateway

IPv6 EC2
 ↓
Egress-Only IGW
 ↓
Internet

EC2 → Internet ✅
Internet → EC2 ❌

NAT Gateway → IPv4 outbound

Egress-Only IGW → IPv6 outbound

docs.title: CIDR essentials
docs.text:
CIDR describes an IP range.

10.0.0.0/16

IPv4 = 32 bits = 4 × 8-bit octets.

/16 means the first 16 bits are fixed:

10.0.X.X

Range:

10.0.0.0 → 10.0.255.255

Common sizes:

/16 → 65,536 addresses
/24 → 256 addresses

docs.title: Important facts
docs.text:
• VPC CIDR: /16 to /28
  • AWS reserves 5 IPv4 addresses per subnet
  • /24 subnet → 256 - 5 = 251 usable

docs.title: VPC DNS
docs.text:
A VPC provides DNS functionality for resources such as EC2 instances.

Two important VPC settings:

Setting Meaning DNS resolution Allows resources in the VPC to use the Amazon-provided DNS resolver DNS hostnames Allows AWS to assign DNS hostnames to resources such as EC2 instances

Example:

EC2
Private IP: 10.0.1.25
DNS hostname: ip-10-0-1-25.ec2.internal

Think:

DNS resolution
→ Can I resolve DNS names?

DNS hostnames
→ Does AWS give my EC2 a DNS hostname?

For a normal EC2 private DNS hostname:

DNS hostnames must be enabled.

You do not need Route 53 for the default EC2 private DNS hostname.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
EC2 has no private DNS hostname
→ Check VPC DNS hostnames

EC2 cannot resolve DNS names
→ Check VPC DNS resolution

docs.title: Lambda + VPC capacity
docs.text:
A VPC-connected Lambda function that scales heavily can run into ENI or subnet IP capacity limits.

Possible symptoms include:

  • EC2ThrottledException
  • SubnetIPAddressLimitReachedException
  • ENI/IP exhaustion during VPC initialization

Lambda + VPC + high concurrency → think ENIs + subnet IP capacity

Example:

10.31.0.0/27
→ 32 total IPv4 addresses
→ 27 usable AWS subnet IPs

A small subnet can therefore become a scaling bottleneck for a high-concurrency Lambda workload.

docs.title: No overlapping CIDRs
docs.text:
Networks that need to connect should use non-overlapping CIDRs.

Example:

VPC-A: 10.0.0.0/16
VPC-B: 10.0.0.0/16

Overlapping ranges cause problems with:

  • VPC Peering
  • Transit Gateway routing
  • VPN connectivity

Non-overlapping CIDRs make connectivity easier.

docs.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
docs.text: Security Group NACL Applies to ENI / instance Subnet Stateful Yes No Rules Allow only Allow + Deny Evaluation All applicable rules Lowest number first SG reference Yes No, CIDR-based

docs.title: Security Group
docs.text:
Security Groups are stateful.

EC2 → Database

If outbound traffic is allowed, the response is automatically allowed.

docs.title: Security Group references
docs.text:
A Security Group can use another Security Group as the source of an inbound rule.

Example:

App SG
  ↓ TCP 1433
DB SG

DB SG:

TCP 1433
Source: App SG

This means:

Allow traffic from resources that have App SG attached.

This is useful for Auto Scaling Groups because instance IPs change.

Dynamic EC2 fleet → reference the Security Group, not individual instance IPs/IDs.

docs.title: SG-to-SG example
docs.text:
ALB SG
 ↓
App SG
 ↓
DB SG

For MySQL:

DB SG:
TCP 3306
Source: App SG

For Microsoft SQL Server:

DB SG:
TCP 1433
Source: App SG

This is better than fixed IPs when application instance IPs change.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Security Groups cannot DENY.

Block a specific IP → NACL

docs.title: NACL
docs.text:
NACLs are stateless.

Both directions must be allowed:

Client → Server
Server → Client

Rules are evaluated from the lowest number upward; first match wins.

Example:

100 → DENY 10.0.0.5/32
200 → ALLOW 0.0.0.0/0

10.0.0.5 is denied by rule 100.

docs.title: Ephemeral ports
docs.text:
Responses commonly use ephemeral ports:

1024–65535

NACLs may need these ports for return traffic.

Request leaves but response does not return → check NACL / ephemeral ports

docs.title: NACL rule precedence
docs.text:
NACLs do not use rule specificity to choose a winner.

Lowest rule number → first matching rule wins → stop evaluation

Example:

100 → ALLOW  0.0.0.0/0
101 → DENY   110.238.109.37/32

Traffic from 110.238.109.37 is ALLOWED, because Rule 100 matches first.

If the rules are reversed:

100 → DENY   110.238.109.37/32
101 → ALLOW  0.0.0.0/0

The traffic is DENIED.

NACL: first matching rule wins — a more specific rule does not override an earlier rule.

IAM: explicit Deny overrides Allow.

docs.title: Security Group vs NACL memory
docs.text:
Security Group
= stateful
= instance / ENI
= allow only
= can reference another SG

NACL
= stateless
= subnet
= allow + deny
= CIDR
= lowest rule number first

docs.title: VPC Endpoints
docs.text:
VPC Endpoints provide a private path to AWS services without the public Internet.

Gateway Endpoint Interface Endpoint Main services S3, DynamoDB Many AWS services + SaaS Cost Free Paid Implementation Route table ENI On-prem / peering access No Yes

docs.title: Gateway Endpoint
docs.text:
Used for:

  • S3
  • DynamoDB
Private EC2
 ↓
Gateway Endpoint
 ↓
S3

No NAT required.

Private S3/DynamoDB + lowest cost → Gateway Endpoint

Gateway endpoints use route tables.

docs.title: Interface Endpoint
docs.text:
Uses an ENI in your subnet and AWS PrivateLink.

Supports many AWS services and SaaS and can be used through:

  • VPC Peering
  • Transit Gateway
  • VPN
  • On-premises connectivity

docs.title: Important nuance
docs.text:
S3 and DynamoDB also support Interface Endpoints.

S3/DynamoDB
+ normal VPC access + lowest cost
→ Gateway Endpoint

S3/DynamoDB
+ Interface Endpoint capabilities
→ Interface Endpoint

Gateway → S3/DynamoDB + cheap

Interface → ENI + PrivateLink + many services / advanced connectivity

docs.title: Connecting VPCs
docs.text:
VPC Peering
= direct VPC-to-VPC

Transit Gateway
= central networking hub

PrivateLink
= access to one service

docs.title: VPC Peering
docs.text:
Connects two VPCs directly.

VPC-A ←→ VPC-B
  • Cross-account supported
  • Cross-Region supported
  • Not transitive
  • CIDRs cannot overlap

docs.title: VPC Peering + Route Tables
docs.text:
Creating the peering connection does not automatically tell the route tables to use it.

Think:

Peering = build the connection

Route table = tell traffic to use the connection

Example:

VPC-A: 10.0.0.0/16
VPC-B: 10.1.0.0/16

After creating the peering connection:

VPC-A route table

Destination       Target
10.0.0.0/16       local
10.1.0.0/16       pcx-xxxx

This means:

"To reach VPC-B (10.1.0.0/16), use the peering connection."

The other VPC needs the reverse route:

VPC-B route table

Destination       Target
10.1.0.0/16       local
10.0.0.0/16       pcx-xxxx

pcx-xxxx = the VPC Peering Connection ID.

So for two VPCs to communicate:

1. Create VPC Peering
2. Add route to the other VPC's CIDR
3. Target = VPC Peering connection

Example:

EC2 in VPC-A
10.0.1.10
    ↓
Route table
10.1.0.0/16 → pcx-xxxx
    ↓
VPC Peering
    ↓
EC2 in VPC-B
10.1.1.10

Peering alone is not enough — the appropriate route must exist.

VPC Peering does not create:

VPC-A → VPC-B → VPC-C

automatically.

It is a direct connection:

VPC-A ←→ VPC-B

VPC Peering = direct, not transit

docs.title: Transit Gateway
docs.text:
Central hub for:

  • VPCs
  • Site-to-Site VPN
  • Direct Connect
VPC-A
   \
VPC-B — Transit Gateway — VPC-C
   /
 VPN
   |
On-premises
