docs.title: Cost Anomaly Detection vs Budgets
docs.text:
"Unexpected/unusual spending spike" → Cost Anomaly Detection

"Spending reaches 80% of budget" → AWS Budgets

The key difference is:

  • Budgets → predefined threshold
  • Anomaly Detection → unusual spending pattern

docs.title: Cost Explorer vs Savings Plans / Reserved Instances
docs.text:
Savings Plans and Reserved Instances are pricing/commitment mechanisms.

Cost Explorer can provide purchase recommendations based on your historical usage.

So:

"How much Savings Plan commitment should we purchase?"

→ Cost Explorer recommendations

docs.title: Billing Conductor
docs.text:
Billing Conductor is used to create customized billing views and rates, especially when an organization needs customized internal billing or chargeback.

It is much less common than the other tools in typical SAA questions.

docs.title: Quick decision table
docs.text: Question wording Answer Visualize or analyze AWS spending Cost Explorer Forecast spending Cost Explorer Programmatically access cost/usage data Cost Explorer API Generate automated custom cost reports Cost Explorer API Forecast costs programmatically Cost Explorer API Alert when spending reaches a threshold AWS Budgets Most detailed billing / line-item data CUR Query billing data with SQL CUR + Athena Unexpected spending spike Cost Anomaly Detection Rightsize an EC2/resource Compute Optimizer Track cost by team/department/project Cost Allocation Tags Savings Plan / RI purchase recommendation Cost Explorer Customized internal billing views Billing Conductor

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
AWS provides two main ways to connect an on-premises network to AWS:

  • Site-to-Site VPN → encrypted IPsec connection over a network/internet path
  • Direct Connect (DX) → dedicated network connection to AWS

The most important SAA skill is recognizing which AWS-side architecture the question is describing.

There are two especially important patterns:

SITE-TO-SITE VPN

On-premises
     │
     │ IPsec VPN
     ▼
   ┌─────┐
   │ VGW │ ──→ VPC
   └─────┘

or:

SITE-TO-SITE VPN + TRANSIT GATEWAY

On-premises
     │
     │ IPsec VPN
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

Direct Connect uses a different path:

DIRECT CONNECT + TRANSIT GATEWAY

On-premises
     │
 Direct Connect
     │
 Transit VIF
     │
     ▼
Direct Connect Gateway
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

docs.title: The key difference
docs.text:
VPN can attach directly to a Transit Gateway.

Direct Connect reaches a Transit Gateway through a Transit VIF + Direct Connect Gateway.

This distinction is extremely important for SAA questions.

docs.title: 1. Site-to-Site VPN
docs.text:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates an IPsec VPN connection between an on-premises network and AWS.

It normally uses an internet/network path rather than a dedicated Direct Connect circuit.

docs.title: Main characteristics
docs.text:
• Uses IPsec encryption
  • Usually faster to deploy than Direct Connect
  • Lower cost than dedicated connectivity
  • Network performance and latency depend on the underlying network path
  • Each VPN connection normally has two tunnels for redundancy
  • Can connect to either a Virtual Private Gateway or a Transit Gateway

docs.title: 2. VPN Architecture: VGW vs Transit Gateway
docs.text: This is the first major distinction to understand.

docs.title: A. VPN → Virtual Private Gateway → VPC
docs.text:
This is the traditional VPN architecture.

On-premises
     │
     │ IPsec VPN
     ▼
Customer Gateway
     │
     ▼
Virtual Private Gateway
     │
     ▼
    VPC

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Where Purpose Customer Gateway (CGW) On-premises side Represents the customer's router/firewall Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) AWS VPN endpoint attached to a VPC

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
On-premises needs a VPN connection to one VPC.

Think:

Site-to-Site VPN → VGW → VPC

docs.title: 3. VPN → Transit Gateway → VPCs
docs.text:
A Site-to-Site VPN can also be attached directly to a Transit Gateway.

On-premises
     │
     │ IPsec VPN
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

There is no Direct Connect Gateway here.

docs.title: Why use this architecture?
docs.text:
Transit Gateway acts as a central router.

For example:

                 Transit Gateway
                /       |       \
               /        |        \
             VPC A     VPC B     VPC C
               |
               |
        On-premises
             VPN

This is useful when the company has:

  • Many VPCs
  • Multiple AWS accounts
  • A centralized networking architecture
  • On-premises networks that need to communicate with many VPCs

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
On-premises needs VPN connectivity to multiple VPCs.

→ Site-to-Site VPN → Transit Gateway

Cross-Region VPCs connect with each other**. → Transit Gateway peering

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not think:

VPN → VGW → TGW

for this architecture.

Instead:

VPN → Transit Gateway

The VPN is itself a Transit Gateway attachment.

docs.title: 4. VPN: VGW vs Transit Gateway
docs.text: Requirement Architecture VPN → one VPC VPN → VGW → VPC VPN → many VPCs VPN → TGW → VPCs Central hub for many VPCs Transit Gateway Need higher aggregate VPN throughput TGW + ECMP + multiple VPN connections

docs.title: Easy memory
docs.text:
VGW = VPN to a VPC

TGW = VPN to many VPCs

docs.title: 5. Scaling VPN Throughput with ECMP
docs.text:
A common SAA requirement is:

"Existing VPN connectivity does not provide enough bandwidth. Increase the VPN throughput."

Use:

Transit Gateway + multiple VPN connections + ECMP

                 ┌── VPN Connection 1 ──┐
                 │                      │
On-premises ────┼── VPN Connection 2 ──┼── Transit Gateway
                 │                      │
                 └── VPN Connection 3 ─┘

ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) allows traffic to use multiple equal-cost paths.

docs.title: Important requirements
docs.text:
For Site-to-Site VPN ECMP:

  • VPN connections must be attached to a Transit Gateway
  • Use dynamic routing / BGP
  • Multiple VPN connections can be used to increase aggregate throughput
Multiple VPN connections
          +
    Transit Gateway
          +
      BGP / ECMP
          ↓
Higher aggregate VPN throughput

docs.title: Very important distinction
docs.text:
A single VPN connection already has two tunnels.

You do not simply create additional tunnels inside the same VPN connection to scale indefinitely.

For throughput scaling:

❌ One VPN connection
   → add arbitrary extra tunnels

✅ Multiple VPN connections
   → Transit Gateway
   → ECMP

docs.title: 6. Large Bandwidth Tunnels
docs.text:
AWS also supports Large Bandwidth Tunnels (LBT) for supported Site-to-Site VPN configurations.

A Large Bandwidth Tunnel can support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel in supported configurations.

The important exam distinction is:

Standard VPN tunnel
→ up to approximately 1.25 Gbps

Large Bandwidth Tunnel
→ up to 5 Gbps per tunnel

Large Bandwidth Tunnels are supported for VPN connections attached to Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN, not Virtual Private Gateway attachments.

Both tunnels in a VPN connection must use the same bandwidth configuration.

docs.title: Need even more aggregate bandwidth?
docs.text:
Use:

Multiple VPN connections
        ↓
Transit Gateway
        ↓
ECMP

For example:

VPN 1
├── 5 Gbps
└── 5 Gbps

VPN 2
├── 5 Gbps
└── 5 Gbps

        ↓
      ECMP

Higher aggregate bandwidth

The exact achievable throughput depends on the architecture and configuration. For SAA questions, the important pattern is:

Need higher aggregate VPN throughput → Transit Gateway + ECMP + multiple VPN connections

docs.title: 7. VPN Throughput vs VPN Redundancy
docs.text: Do not confuse these requirements.

docs.title: Need higher throughput
docs.text:
Transit Gateway
+
Multiple VPN connections
+
ECMP
+
BGP

docs.title: Need redundancy
docs.text:
Multiple VPN paths
→ failover / resilience

A second Customer Gateway or another VPN path can improve resilience.

But when the question specifically says:

Increase aggregate VPN bandwidth

look for:

Transit Gateway + ECMP

docs.title: 8. VPN CloudHub
docs.text:
VPN CloudHub is different from Transit Gateway.

VPN CloudHub allows multiple on-premises sites to communicate with each other through AWS using Site-to-Site VPN connections.

Example:

Office A
    │
    │ VPN
    ▼
   VGW
   ▲  ▲
  /    \
VPN    VPN
/        \
Office B  Office C

The sites can communicate through AWS without creating a direct VPN connection between every pair.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Office A ──┐
           │
Office B ──┼── AWS VPN CloudHub
           │
Office C ──┘

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
Several branch offices/data centers need to communicate with each other through AWS.

→ VPN CloudHub

docs.title: 9. VPN CloudHub vs Transit Gateway
docs.text:
These can look similar in exam questions, but the main idea is different.

VPN CloudHub Transit Gateway Main purpose Connect multiple on-premises sites Central hub for VPCs and networks Main technology Site-to-Site VPN + VGW Transit Gateway Key clue Branch office ↔ branch office Many VPCs/networks VPC connectivity Not the main purpose Major use case VPN throughput scaling Not the main pattern ECMP

docs.title: Easy rule
docs.text:
Multiple on-premises sites need to communicate through AWS → VPN CloudHub

Many VPCs/networks need a central routing hub → Transit Gateway

docs.title: 10. Client VPN
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN is different from Site-to-Site VPN.

It provides secure access for individual users/devices.

Employee laptop
       │
       │ Client VPN
       ▼
      AWS

docs.title: Remember
docs.text: Requirement Service Entire on-premises network → AWS Site-to-Site VPN Individual laptop/user → AWS Client VPN

docs.title: 11. Direct Connect
docs.text:
AWS Direct Connect (DX) provides a dedicated network connection between an on-premises location and AWS.

On-premises
     │
     │ Direct Connect
     ▼
    AWS

docs.title: Main characteristics
docs.text:
• Dedicated connectivity
  • Does not use the public internet for the Direct Connect path
  • More consistent network performance than internet-based VPN
  • Suitable for large and steady data transfers
  • Requires physical/network-provider connectivity
  • Usually takes longer to provision than VPN
  • Does not encrypt traffic by default

Common dedicated connection capacities include:

  • 1 Gbps
  • 10 Gbps
  • 100 Gbps

docs.title: 12. Direct Connect Is Private, Not Encrypted
docs.text:
This is one of the most important exam traps.

Private connectivity does not automatically mean encryption.

Direct Connect provides a private network path, but Direct Connect traffic is not encrypted by default.

If the requirement says:

"Traffic must be encrypted."

You need an appropriate encryption mechanism, such as VPN/IPsec.

Remember:

Direct Connect
= private connectivity

VPN / IPsec
= encryption

docs.title: 13. Direct Connect Virtual Interfaces
docs.text:
A Virtual Interface (VIF) determines how traffic is routed through a Direct Connect connection.

The three important VIF types are:

VIF Main purpose Private VIF Private connectivity to VPC resources Public VIF AWS public services Transit VIF Transit Gateway connectivity through a Direct Connect Gateway

docs.title: 14. Private VIF
docs.text:
A Private VIF is used for private connectivity to VPC resources.

Example:

On-premises
     │
     │ Direct Connect
     ▼
Private VIF
     │
     ▼
    VPC

Typical clue:

On-premises application needs private connectivity to EC2 instances in a VPC.

→ Private VIF

A private VIF can be used with a Virtual Private Gateway or a Direct Connect Gateway, depending on the architecture.

docs.title: 15. Public VIF
docs.text:
A Public VIF is used to access AWS public services through Direct Connect.

Examples:

  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • Other AWS public endpoints

Example:

On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Public VIF
     │
     ▼
AWS public services

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"On-premises needs Direct Connect access to S3."

→ Public VIF

docs.title: 16. Transit VIF
docs.text:
A Transit VIF is used when Direct Connect needs to reach a Transit Gateway.

The architecture is:

On-premises
     │
     │ Direct Connect
     ▼
 Transit VIF
     │
     ▼
Direct Connect Gateway
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

docs.title: This is the critical Direct Connect architecture
docs.text:
You do not connect the Direct Connect connection directly to the Transit Gateway.

Instead:

Direct Connect
      ↓
Transit VIF
      ↓
Direct Connect Gateway
      ↓
Transit Gateway

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Connect on-premises to many VPCs through an existing Direct Connect connection and Transit Gateway."

→ Transit VIF + Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway

docs.title: 17. Why Does Direct Connect Need a Direct Connect Gateway?
docs.text:
This is the easiest way to remember it.

A Transit Gateway can accept several types of connectivity, including:

VPC
VPN
Direct Connect Gateway

But the Direct Connect connection itself is not a Transit Gateway attachment.

Therefore the Direct Connect path is:

Direct Connect connection
        ↓
    Transit VIF
        ↓
Direct Connect Gateway
        ↓
   Transit Gateway

By contrast, VPN can attach directly:

Site-to-Site VPN
        ↓
   Transit Gateway

docs.title: Memorize this exact comparison
docs.text:
VPN + TGW

VPN ─────────────→ TGW

DX + TGW

DX
 ↓
Transit VIF
 ↓
DX Gateway
 ↓
TGW

This is one of the most useful architecture patterns in this section.

docs.title: 18. Direct Connect Gateway
docs.text:
A Direct Connect Gateway (DXGW) allows Direct Connect connectivity to be extended to AWS networks.

It is useful when an organization has:

  • Multiple VPCs
  • Multiple AWS accounts
  • Multiple Regions
  • Transit Gateway architecture

The architecture can be:

On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Transit VIF
     │
     ▼
Direct Connect Gateway
     │
     ▼
AWS network

The DX Gateway can be associated with:

  • Transit Gateway
  • Virtual Private Gateway(s)

depending on the architecture.

docs.title: 19. Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway
docs.text:
For a large multi-account environment:

                    On-premises
                         │
                  Direct Connect
                         │
                    Transit VIF
                         │
                         ▼
               Direct Connect Gateway
                         │
                         ▼
                  Transit Gateway
                  /      |      \
                 /       |       \
             Account A Account B Account C
                 │         │         │
                VPC       VPC       VPC

This allows multiple VPCs/accounts to use the same Direct Connect connectivity to reach on-premises resources.

For example, the on-premises network contains:

  • Active Directory
  • DNS
  • Internal applications

and several AWS accounts need access to them.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Multiple AWS accounts need access to on-premises resources through an existing Direct Connect connection."

Think:

DX → Transit VIF → DXGW → TGW → VPCs

docs.title: 20. Direct Connect Gateway vs Transit Gateway
docs.text:
These services have different jobs.

Service Main job Direct Connect Gateway Connects Direct Connect to AWS networks Transit Gateway Central router for VPCs and networks

Think of them as different layers:

On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
     ▼
DX Gateway
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
     │
 ┌───┼───┐
VPC  VPC  VPC

docs.title: Easy rule
docs.text:
DX Gateway = Direct Connect side

Transit Gateway = AWS network routing side

docs.title: 21. VPN + Transit Gateway vs DX + Transit Gateway
docs.text: This is the most important comparison in this section.

docs.title: VPN
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
     │ Internet / IPsec
     ▼
   VPN
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   / | \
 VPC VPC VPC

VPN attaches directly to the Transit Gateway.

docs.title: Direct Connect
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
     │ Direct Connect
     ▼
Transit VIF
     │
     ▼
DX Gateway
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   / | \
 VPC VPC VPC

Direct Connect reaches the Transit Gateway through the Direct Connect Gateway.

docs.title: One-line memory
docs.text:
VPN → TGW directly

DX → Transit VIF → DXGW → TGW

docs.title: 22. Direct Connect vs VPC Peering
docs.text:
VPC Peering provides point-to-point connectivity between VPCs.

VPC A ←────────→ VPC B

With many VPCs, this can become difficult to manage:

VPC A ←→ VPC B
  ↕  ╲   ↗
VPC C ←→ VPC D

Transit Gateway provides a centralized architecture:

          Transit Gateway
          /      |      \
        VPC A   VPC B   VPC C

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Many VPCs need centralized connectivity."

→ Transit Gateway

Not a large VPC peering mesh.

docs.title: 23. Multi-Account Transit Gateway
docs.text:
A Transit Gateway can be shared with other AWS accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM).

Example:

                 Transit Gateway
                /       |       \
               /        |        \
          Account A  Account B  Account C
              │          │          │
             VPC        VPC        VPC

This is common in organizations with a centralized networking account.

Combined with Direct Connect:

On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Transit VIF
     │
DX Gateway
     │
Transit Gateway
     │
    RAM
     │
Multiple AWS accounts

docs.title: 24. Direct Connect + VPN Backup
docs.text:
A common exam requirement is:

"The company already has Direct Connect and needs a cost-effective backup."

Use:

Direct Connect as primary + Site-to-Site VPN as backup

                    ┌── Direct Connect ──→ AWS
On-premises ────────┤
                    └── Site-to-Site VPN → AWS
                              backup

The VPN provides an alternative path if Direct Connect becomes unavailable.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Cost-effective backup for Direct Connect"

→ Site-to-Site VPN

docs.title: 25. Direct Connect + VPN Encryption
docs.text:
Direct Connect itself is private but does not encrypt traffic by default.

If encryption is required, VPN/IPsec can be used as an encryption layer.

Conceptually:

On-premises
     │
     │ encrypted VPN traffic
     │
     ▼
Direct Connect
     │
     ▼
AWS

This is different from ordinary Site-to-Site VPN over the public internet.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Normal Site-to-Site VPN
→ VPN traffic uses an internet/network path
→ IPsec encryption

VPN over Direct Connect / private IP VPN
→ VPN encryption runs over private Direct Connect connectivity

So if the question specifically says:

"Use Direct Connect but also encrypt the traffic."

Think about a VPN/IPsec encryption layer over the private Direct Connect path, where supported.

docs.title: 26. Two Direct Connect Connections
docs.text:
For stronger Direct Connect resilience, an organization can use multiple Direct Connect connections.

              ┌── DX connection 1 ──→ AWS
On-premises ──┤
              └── DX connection 2 ──→ AWS

Ideally, the connections should use independent physical/network paths where possible.

docs.title: Trade-off
docs.text:
More resilience
      ↓
More infrastructure
      ↓
More cost

docs.title: 27. VPN First, Direct Connect Later
docs.text:
Direct Connect can take longer to provision.

A company can establish VPN connectivity first:

Phase 1

On-premises
     │
     VPN
     │
     ▼
    AWS

Then add Direct Connect:

Phase 2

On-premises
     │
     ├── Direct Connect ──→ AWS
     │
     └── VPN ─────────────→ AWS

The VPN can later become a backup path.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"The company needs connectivity immediately while waiting for Direct Connect."

→ Site-to-Site VPN

docs.title: 28. Choosing VPN vs Direct Connect
docs.text:
The decision usually comes down to these requirements:

Requirement Usually points to Need connectivity quickly Site-to-Site VPN Need IPsec encryption Site-to-Site VPN Lower-cost connectivity Site-to-Site VPN Dedicated physical connectivity Direct Connect More predictable network performance Direct Connect Large, steady data transfers Direct Connect Cost-effective backup for DX Site-to-Site VPN Individual users/laptops Client VPN

docs.title: 29. Architecture Decision Table
docs.text:
This is the table to use when solving SAA questions.

Scenario Architecture On-prem → one VPC using VPN VPN → VGW → VPC On-prem → many VPCs using VPN VPN → TGW → VPCs VPN needs higher aggregate throughput Multiple VPNs → TGW + ECMP Multiple on-premises sites need to communicate VPN CloudHub Individual users need VPN access Client VPN On-prem → one VPC using DX DX + Private VIF On-prem → AWS public services using DX DX + Public VIF On-prem → many VPCs using DX + TGW DX + Transit VIF + DXGW + TGW Multiple AWS accounts need DX connectivity DXGW + TGW Need dedicated/private connectivity Direct Connect Need encryption over DX VPN/IPsec over DX Need DX backup DX + Site-to-Site VPN Need central VPC/network hub Transit Gateway Need point-to-point VPC connectivity VPC Peering

docs.title: 30. The Four Most Important Architectures
docs.text: If you remember only four diagrams, remember these.

docs.title: Architecture 1 — VPN to one VPC
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
     │ VPN
     ▼
    VGW
     │
     ▼
    VPC

Think: VPN + one VPC

docs.title: Architecture 2 — VPN to many VPCs
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
     │ VPN
     ▼
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

Think: VPN + many VPCs

docs.title: Architecture 3 — Direct Connect to one VPC
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Private VIF
     │
     ▼
    VPC

Think: DX + Private VIF

docs.title: Architecture 4 — Direct Connect to many VPCs through TGW
docs.text:
On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Transit VIF
     │
DX Gateway
     │
Transit Gateway
   /    |    \
 VPC   VPC   VPC

Think: DX + Transit VIF + DXGW + TGW

docs.title: 31. The Critical Difference
docs.text:
When you see a question involving Transit Gateway, first ask:

Is the on-premises connection VPN or Direct Connect?

Then choose the path.

docs.title: If VPN:
docs.text:
VPN
 ↓
Transit Gateway
 ↓
VPCs

docs.title: If Direct Connect:
docs.text:
Direct Connect
 ↓
Transit VIF
 ↓
Direct Connect Gateway
 ↓
Transit Gateway
 ↓
VPCs

docs.title: Never confuse these:
docs.text:
❌ Direct Connect → Transit Gateway

✅ Direct Connect → Transit VIF → DX Gateway → Transit Gateway

✅ VPN → Transit Gateway

docs.title: 32. Exam Question Patterns
docs.text:
"The company needs connectivity to AWS within days."

→ Site-to-Site VPN

"The company needs a dedicated connection with more consistent network performance for large, steady data transfers."

→ Direct Connect

"On-premises needs VPN connectivity to several VPCs."

→ Site-to-Site VPN → Transit Gateway

"On-premises needs connectivity to several VPCs using an existing Direct Connect connection."

→ Transit VIF → Direct Connect Gateway → Transit Gateway

"VPN throughput is insufficient. Increase aggregate VPN bandwidth."

→ Multiple VPN connections + Transit Gateway + ECMP + BGP

"Several branch offices need to communicate with each other through AWS."

→ VPN CloudHub

"Remote employees need secure access to AWS from their laptops."

→ Client VPN

"The company needs a cost-effective backup for Direct Connect."

→ Site-to-Site VPN

"Direct Connect traffic must be encrypted."

→ VPN/IPsec over the Direct Connect connectivity

Remember:

Direct Connect is private, but not encrypted by default.

"On-premises needs access to S3 through Direct Connect."

→ Public VIF

"On-premises needs private access to VPC resources through Direct Connect."

→ Private VIF

"On-premises must reach VPCs attached to a Transit Gateway through Direct Connect."

→ Transit VIF + Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway

"Many AWS accounts need access to on-premises DNS and Active Directory through an existing Direct Connect connection."

→ Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway

"The company wants a central routing hub for many VPCs."

→ Transit Gateway

"Two VPCs need simple point-to-point connectivity."

→ VPC Peering

docs.title: VPN
docs.text: Keyword Answer Encrypted IPsec connection Site-to-Site VPN Fast to deploy Site-to-Site VPN VPN → one VPC VPN → VGW → VPC VPN → many VPCs VPN → TGW → VPCs VPN throughput too low TGW + ECMP + multiple VPN connections ECMP VPN routing BGP / dynamic routing One VPN connection 2 tunnels Multiple on-premises sites ↔ each other VPN CloudHub Individual users/laptops Client VPN

docs.title: Direct Connect
docs.text: Keyword Answer Dedicated private connectivity Direct Connect Consistent network performance Direct Connect Large steady transfers Direct Connect DX encryption by default ❌ No Encrypt DX traffic VPN/IPsec over DX Private VPC resources Private VIF AWS public services Public VIF DX → Transit Gateway Transit VIF + DXGW + TGW DX → many VPCs Transit VIF + DXGW + TGW DX backup Site-to-Site VPN

docs.title: Transit Gateway
docs.text: Requirement Answer Central hub for many VPCs Transit Gateway VPN → many VPCs VPN → TGW DX → many VPCs DX → Transit VIF → DXGW → TGW VPN throughput scaling TGW + ECMP Multiple AWS accounts TGW + AWS RAM

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
AWS Transit Gateway (TGW) is a centralized network router for connecting multiple VPCs and other networks.

It is useful when an organization has:

  • many VPCs
  • multiple AWS accounts
  • on-premises networks
  • Site-to-Site VPN connections
  • Direct Connect
  • a need for transitive routing
  • a need to centrally control network traffic

docs.title: VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway
docs.text:
VPC Peering connects two VPCs directly.

VPC A ←→ VPC B

VPC Peering is not transitive.

VPC A ←→ VPC B ←→ VPC C

VPC A ❌→ VPC C

If many VPCs need connectivity, the number of peering connections can grow rapidly.

With Transit Gateway:

           Transit Gateway
          /       |       \
       VPC A    VPC B    VPC C

Each VPC connects to the Transit Gateway, and the Transit Gateway can route traffic between the attached networks.

docs.title: Easy rule
docs.text:
VPC Peering = direct VPC-to-VPC connection

Transit Gateway = centralized hub for many networks

docs.title: What can connect to Transit Gateway?
docs.text:
Transit Gateway supports several attachment types.

Attachment Purpose VPC Connect a VPC to the Transit Gateway Site-to-Site VPN Connect on-premises networks through VPN Direct Connect Connect through a Direct Connect Gateway and Transit VIF Transit Gateway peering Connect two Transit Gateways Other supported network attachments Connect supported AWS/network resources

docs.title: Typical architecture
docs.text:
Transit Gateway
                    /        |        \
                   /         |         \
                VPC A      VPC B      VPC C
                   │
                VPN / DX
                   │
            On-premises network

docs.title: Transit Gateway routing
docs.text:
Transit Gateway uses Transit Gateway route tables to control how traffic is routed between attachments.

This allows centralized routing and segmentation.

For example:

                 Transit Gateway
                /               \
           Prod route table    Dev route table
               /                    \
          Prod VPCs              Dev VPCs

You can configure routing so that:

  • Production VPCs can communicate with on-premises
  • Development VPCs can communicate with on-premises
  • Production VPCs cannot route to development VPCs

docs.title: Important idea
docs.text: Transit Gateway route tables can be used to segment traffic between groups of VPCs.

docs.title: AWS RAM and Transit Gateway
docs.text:
AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) allows supported AWS resources to be shared across AWS accounts.

A major SAA use case is sharing a Transit Gateway with VPCs in other AWS accounts.

Example:

Central networking account
          │
          │ creates
          ▼
    Transit Gateway
          │
          │ AWS RAM
      ┌───┴────┐
      ▼        ▼
 Account A   Account B
    VPC         VPC

This allows a central networking account to manage the Transit Gateway while other AWS accounts attach their VPCs to it.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Transit Gateway = connects the networks

AWS RAM = allows the Transit Gateway to be shared across accounts

RAM does not perform the network routing itself.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"A central networking account has a Transit Gateway and wants VPCs in other AWS accounts to use it."

→ Share the Transit Gateway using AWS RAM

docs.title: Transit Gateway + Direct Connect
docs.text:
For on-premises connectivity through Direct Connect, the typical architecture is:

On-premises
     │
Direct Connect
     │
Transit VIF
     │
Direct Connect Gateway
     │
Transit Gateway
     │
 ┌───┼────┐
VPC A VPC B VPC C

The services have different roles:

Service Role Direct Connect Dedicated connectivity from on-premises to AWS Direct Connect Gateway Connects Direct Connect to supported AWS networks Transit Gateway Central routing hub for multiple VPCs/networks AWS RAM Shares the Transit Gateway across AWS accounts

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Existing Direct Connect + many VPCs/accounts need access to on-premises services."

→ Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway

For multi-account architectures, the Transit Gateway can be shared using AWS RAM.

docs.title: Transit Gateway + Site-to-Site VPN
docs.text:
Transit Gateway can also be used as the central endpoint for multiple VPN connections.

On-premises A
     │
    VPN
     │
     ▼
Transit Gateway
     ▲
     │
    VPN
     │
On-premises B

This is useful when several offices or on-premises networks need centralized connectivity to AWS.

docs.title: Transit Gateway Peering
docs.text:
You can connect two Transit Gateways using Transit Gateway peering.

Example:

Region A                         Region B

VPC A ─┐                     ┌─ VPC D
VPC B ─┼─ TGW A ←→ TGW B ───┼─ VPC E
VPC C ─┘                     └─ VPC F

This is useful when different regions have separate Transit Gateways that need connectivity.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"Connect two Transit Gateways in different Regions."

→ Transit Gateway peering

docs.title: Appliance mode
docs.text:
Appliance mode is used when traffic must pass through a network appliance such as:

  • firewall
  • IDS/IPS
  • inspection appliance
  • security appliance

It helps maintain symmetric traffic flows, meaning both directions of a flow can pass through the same network appliance.

Example:

VPC A
  │
  ▼
Transit Gateway
  │
  ▼
Inspection VPC
  │
Firewall
  │
  ▼
Destination

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"All traffic must pass through the same firewall in both directions."

→ Transit Gateway with appliance mode

docs.title: Multicast
docs.text:
Transit Gateway supports IP multicast.

This is useful for applications that need one-to-many network communication.

docs.title: Exam clue
docs.text:
"The application requires IP multicast."

→ Transit Gateway

For SAA, remember:

Multicast → Transit Gateway

docs.title: Transit Gateway vs VPC Peering
docs.text: Feature VPC Peering Transit Gateway Connects two VPCs directly ✅ — Central hub ❌ ✅ Transitive routing ❌ ✅ Many VPCs Possible, but many connections may be required ✅ Centralized routing ❌ ✅ Segmentation with TGW route tables ❌ ✅ Cross-account architecture Possible ✅ Cross-region connectivity Supported Supported through TGW peering Typical use Small/simple VPC-to-VPC connectivity Large/multi-VPC network architecture

docs.title: When should you prefer VPC Peering?
docs.text: For a small number of VPCs that simply need direct communication, VPC Peering can be simpler and may have lower cost because it does not have Transit Gateway attachment/hourly charges.

docs.title: When should you prefer Transit Gateway?
docs.text:
Use Transit Gateway when you need:

  • many VPCs
  • centralized routing
  • transitive connectivity
  • centralized network segmentation
  • multiple accounts
  • VPN connectivity
  • Direct Connect integration
  • centralized inspection

docs.title: Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink
docs.text: These solve very different problems.

docs.title: Transit Gateway
docs.text:
Provides network-level connectivity.

VPC A
  │
  ▼
Transit Gateway
  │
  ▼
VPC B

The connected networks can route to each other according to the configured route tables.

docs.title: AWS PrivateLink
docs.text:
Provides private access to a specific service.

Consumer VPC
     │
     ▼
Interface Endpoint
     │
     ▼
Service

The consumer does not receive general network access to the provider VPC.

docs.title: Easy rule
docs.text:
Need network-to-network connectivity → Transit Gateway

Need access to one specific service → PrivateLink

docs.title: PrivateLink exam clues
docs.text:
Use PrivateLink when the question emphasizes:

  • expose a specific service
  • many consumer VPCs
  • consumers should not access the entire provider VPC
  • overlapping CIDR ranges

docs.title: Cost considerations
docs.text:
Transit Gateway charges for:

  • Transit Gateway attachments
  • data processed

VPC Peering does not have a Transit Gateway-style hourly attachment charge, although data transfer charges still apply.

Therefore:

Small/simple VPC connectivity → VPC Peering may be simpler and cheaper

Large/multi-VPC architecture → Transit Gateway provides centralized connectivity and routing

Do not choose Transit Gateway only because it is more scalable; consider the actual number of VPCs and connectivity requirements.

docs.title: Question patterns
docs.text:
"25 VPCs and an on-premises datacenter need centralized connectivity."

→ Transit Gateway

"VPC A peers with B, and B peers with C, but A cannot reach C."

→ VPC Peering is non-transitive

If transitive connectivity is required:

→ Transit Gateway

"Production VPCs must not communicate with development VPCs, but both need access to on-premises."

→ Transit Gateway with separate route tables / routing policies

"The application requires IP multicast."

→ Transit Gateway

"Only two VPCs need simple direct communication."

→ VPC Peering

"A central networking account needs to share a Transit Gateway with many AWS accounts."

→ AWS RAM

"Connect Transit Gateway in Region A to Transit Gateway in Region B."

→ Transit Gateway peering

"All traffic between VPCs must pass through a firewall appliance."

→ Transit Gateway with appliance mode

"Existing Direct Connect must provide connectivity to many VPCs."

→ Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway

"Multiple AWS accounts need to use a central Transit Gateway."

→ AWS RAM + Transit Gateway

"Expose one service to many customer VPCs without providing general VPC-to-VPC connectivity."

→ AWS PrivateLink
