docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
This section covers AWS certificate management and TLS/HTTPS patterns that commonly appear as specific-use-case questions.

Requirement → keyword → answer

Requirement / keyword Answer Need a new public TLS / HTTPS certificate ACM TLS / HTTPS certificates ACM Third-party certificate that must be imported ACM Third-party certificate import alternative IAM certificate store CloudFront TLS certificate ACM in us-east-1 ALB TLS certificate ACM in the same Region as the ALB Regional API Gateway TLS certificate ACM in the same Region as the API Edge-optimized API Gateway certificate ACM in us-east-1 Multiple unrelated domains on one ALB HTTPS listener Multiple ACM certificates + SNI Multiple subdomains of one domain Wildcard certificate Multiple names in one certificate SAN certificate Certificate expiring soon ACM expiration events / DaysToExpiry

docs.title: ACM — AWS Certificate Manager
docs.text:
ACM = TLS/SSL certificate management for AWS services.

ACM can:

  • Request and issue new public certificates
  • Import existing certificates from third-party Certificate Authorities (CAs)
  • Manage certificates for supported AWS services

Common integrations:

  • Application Load Balancer (ALB)
  • CloudFront
  • API Gateway

docs.title: Common signal
docs.text: HTTPS / TLS certificate → ACM

docs.title: ACM can request / issue certificates
docs.text:
ACM can request a new public TLS certificate for your domain.

Typical flow:

You
 ↓
ACM: Request certificate
 ↓
Prove domain ownership
 ↓
ACM issues certificate
 ↓
Use with ALB / CloudFront / API Gateway

Domain ownership can be validated using:

  • DNS validation
  • Email validation

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
ACM can create/issue a new public certificate for you.

So don't think of ACM only as a place where you import certificates.

It can either:

Need a new certificate
→ ACM requests/issues it

or:

Already have a certificate from another CA
→ Import it into ACM

docs.title: Public ACM certificates
docs.text:
Public ACM certificates are available at no additional certificate charge.

ACM can automatically renew eligible ACM-issued certificates when the renewal requirements are met.

docs.title: Importing third-party certificates
docs.text:
You can import a certificate obtained from an external Certificate Authority (CA), such as a commercial third-party CA, into ACM.

When importing, you provide:

  • Certificate
  • Private key
  • Certificate chain, when applicable

Example:

Third-party CA
      ↓
Certificate + private key + chain
      ↓
     ACM
      ↓
ALB / other supported AWS service

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Imported certificates are not automatically renewed by ACM.

You must obtain the renewed certificate from the CA and import the new certificate.

This is different from an ACM-issued public certificate, which ACM can automatically renew when the certificate is eligible.

docs.title: IAM certificate store
docs.text:
AWS IAM also provides a server certificate store where third-party certificates can be uploaded.

For SAA purposes:

ACM = modern/default certificate management choice

IAM certificate store = older/alternative certificate store

A question may therefore list both:

  • AWS Certificate Manager
  • AWS IAM certificate store

as valid places where a third-party certificate can be imported.

For an ALB, ACM is normally the preferred AWS-native solution.

docs.title: S3 is not an ALB certificate store
docs.text:
You could technically store certificate files in an S3 bucket, but that does not make S3 a certificate management service.

For example:

certificate.pem
private-key.pem
certificate-chain.pem

can exist as S3 objects, but an ALB does not simply use an S3 object as its HTTPS listener certificate.

Typical pattern:

Third-party certificate
        ↓
       ACM
        ↓
ALB HTTPS listener

Do not choose S3 merely because the question says the certificate must be stored securely.

docs.title: ACM and EC2
docs.text:
You generally cannot use an ACM public certificate's private key directly on an EC2 server in the same way that you would with a certificate file you manage yourself.

For an ALB / CloudFront / API Gateway architecture, the common pattern is:

Internet
   ↓
ALB / CloudFront / API Gateway
   ↓
ACM certificate
   ↓
Application

The TLS certificate is associated with the AWS service that terminates HTTPS.

docs.title: ACM Regional behavior
docs.text:
ACM certificates are generally Regional resources.

For services such as ALB:

ALB in us-east-1
→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

A regional service normally uses a certificate in the same Region.

docs.title: CloudFront special case
docs.text:
A certificate used by CloudFront must be in:

us-east-1

Even if the rest of your infrastructure is deployed in another Region.

Common exam trap:

ALB
→ ACM certificate in the SAME REGION as the ALB

CloudFront
→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

docs.title: API Gateway certificate region
docs.text: API Gateway has an important Regional vs Edge-optimized distinction.

docs.title: Regional API Gateway
docs.text:
Regional API in us-east-2
→ ACM certificate in us-east-2

The certificate must be in the same Region as the Regional API.

docs.title: Edge-optimized API Gateway
docs.text:
An Edge-optimized API Gateway endpoint uses an API Gateway-managed CloudFront distribution.

Therefore:

Edge-optimized API Gateway
→ API Gateway-managed CloudFront
→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

docs.title: SAA memory
docs.text:
ALB
→ ACM same Region as ALB

Regional API Gateway
→ ACM same Region as API

CloudFront
→ ACM us-east-1

Edge-optimized API Gateway
→ ACM us-east-1

Do not use the broad rule:

"API Gateway → ACM us-east-1"

First check whether the API is Regional or Edge-optimized.

docs.title: ACM-issued public certificate
docs.text:
ACM requests and issues the certificate.

ACM
 ↓
Public certificate

ACM can automatically renew eligible certificates.

docs.title: ACM private certificate
docs.text:
Used for internal/private PKI scenarios.

AWS Private CA
      ↓
Private certificate
      ↓
ACM / supported AWS service

docs.title: Imported certificate
docs.text:
You already obtained the certificate from another CA.

DigiCert / other CA
        ↓
   Import into ACM
        ↓
Use with supported AWS service

Important:

Imported certificate → you handle renewal and re-import.

docs.title: Certificate expiration monitoring
docs.text:
When the requirement is:

"Notify me before an ACM certificate expires."

Think of two important AWS patterns.

docs.title: 1. ACM expiration events → EventBridge
docs.text:
ACM provides certificate expiration events through Amazon EventBridge.

Typical pattern:

ACM certificate
      ↓
Approaching-expiration event
      ↓
Amazon EventBridge
      ↓
SNS / Lambda / other target

The event includes information such as DaysToExpiry.

This is the most direct event-driven approach.

docs.title: 2. DaysToExpiry metric → scheduled checking
docs.text:
ACM also publishes the DaysToExpiry CloudWatch metric.

It indicates how many days remain before a certificate expires.

Possible pattern:

ACM
 ↓
DaysToExpiry
 ↓
Scheduled daily checking
 ↓
Find certificates reaching 30 days
 ↓
SNS notification

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Do not think:

EventBridge itself is a CloudWatch metric alarm.

A scheduled EventBridge rule provides the trigger for a process that checks the metric and then sends the notification.

For SAA questions, the intended concept is:

ACM expiration events → EventBridge

or

DaysToExpiry metric → periodic monitoring/checking

docs.title: AWS Health
docs.text:
AWS Health can also provide ACM-related renewal/expiration events, particularly around renewal status and situations requiring customer action.

Useful exam distinction:

ACM EventBridge expiration event
→ approaching certificate expiration

AWS Health
→ renewal / renewal-status / action-required events

docs.title: Exam memory
docs.text:
Need notification before ACM certificate expires
        ↓
ACM expiration events → EventBridge → SNS
        OR
DaysToExpiry metric → scheduled checking → SNS

docs.title: ALB HTTPS Certificates & SNI
docs.text:
SNI (Server Name Indication) allows an ALB HTTPS listener to use multiple certificates on the same listener.

The client includes the requested hostname during the TLS handshake, allowing the ALB to select the appropriate certificate.

Example:

ALB :443
 ├── i-love-manila.com      → Certificate A
 ├── i-love-boracay.com     → Certificate B
 ├── i-love-cebu.com        → Certificate C
 └── another-domain.com     → Certificate D

Useful when multiple unrelated domains share one ALB.

A new domain can be supported by adding another certificate to the listener rather than replacing the existing certificate.

docs.title: Exam pattern
docs.text: Many unrelated domains + one ALB HTTPS listener → SNI

docs.title: Wildcard vs SAN vs SNI
docs.text: Requirement Best fit Multiple subdomains of one domain Wildcard certificate Multiple names in one certificate SAN certificate Multiple unrelated domains on one ALB listener Multiple certificates + SNI

docs.title: Wildcard certificate
docs.text:
A wildcard covers multiple subdomains under the same domain.

Example:

*.example.com

Can cover:

www.example.com
api.example.com
shop.example.com

A wildcard is not intended for unrelated domains such as:

i-love-manila.com
i-love-boracay.com
i-love-cebu.com

docs.title: SAN certificate
docs.text:
A SAN (Subject Alternative Name) certificate can contain multiple domain names in one certificate.

Useful when multiple names should be covered by one certificate.

docs.title: SNI
docs.text:
SNI is different from SAN.

SNI allows the ALB listener to have multiple certificates, with the ALB selecting the correct certificate based on the hostname requested by the client.

Think:

Wildcard
→ one certificate covers many subdomains

SAN
→ one certificate contains many names

SNI
→ one listener uses multiple certificates

docs.title: Common Question Patterns
docs.text:
"Need a new public HTTPS/TLS certificate."

→ AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)

"Need HTTPS certificate for an Application Load Balancer."

→ ACM

Use the ACM certificate in the same Region as the ALB.

"Need a TLS certificate for CloudFront."

→ ACM in us-east-1

"A Regional API Gateway needs a custom HTTPS domain."

→ ACM certificate in the same Region as the API

"An Edge-optimized API Gateway needs a custom HTTPS domain."

→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

"A company obtained a certificate from a third-party CA and needs to import it into AWS."

→ ACM → IAM certificate store can also be a valid certificate-store answer depending on the choices.

"Multiple unrelated domains share one ALB HTTPS listener."

→ Multiple certificates + SNI

"Several subdomains belong to one domain."

→ Wildcard certificate

"One certificate must cover multiple domain names."

→ SAN certificate

"Security team wants an alert 30 days before ACM certificates expire."

→ ACM expiration events → EventBridge → SNS

or

→ DaysToExpiry metric → scheduled checking → SNS

docs.title: ACM Region trap
docs.text:
ALB
→ ACM certificate in same Region

Regional API Gateway
→ ACM certificate in same Region

CloudFront
→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

Edge-optimized API Gateway
→ ACM certificate in us-east-1

docs.title: ACM issue vs import
docs.text:
Need a new public certificate
→ ACM requests/issues it

Already have a third-party certificate
→ Import into ACM

docs.title: Imported certificate trap
docs.text:
Third-party certificate
→ Import into ACM
→ ACM does NOT automatically renew it
→ Renew it externally and import the replacement

docs.title: Certificate expiration trap
docs.text:
Approaching ACM expiration
→ EventBridge expiration events

Days remaining as a metric
→ CloudWatch DaysToExpiry

Need notification
→ SNS

Need a daily metric-based check
→ scheduled process / EventBridge schedule

docs.title: ALB certificate trap
docs.text:
Many unrelated domains
+
One ALB HTTPS listener
→ Multiple certificates + SNI

Do not confuse:

Subdomains of one domain
→ Wildcard

Multiple names in one certificate
→ SAN

Multiple unrelated domains on one ALB
→ SNI

docs.title: Certificate Pocket Card
docs.text: Keyword Answer Need a new public TLS certificate ACM TLS / SSL certificate ACM HTTPS ACM Third-party certificate import ACM Third-party certificate store alternative IAM certificate store Imported certificate renewal Manual / re-import ALB certificate ACM in same Region as ALB Regional API Gateway certificate ACM in same Region as API CloudFront certificate ACM in us-east-1 Edge-optimized API Gateway certificate ACM in us-east-1 Certificate expiring soon ACM EventBridge / DaysToExpiry Alert before certificate expiry EventBridge → SNS Metric showing days remaining DaysToExpiry Multiple unrelated domains on one ALB SNI + multiple certificates Multiple subdomains of one domain Wildcard certificate Multiple names in one certificate SAN certificate S3 certificate storage Not an ALB certificate store

docs.title: Q1 — Certificate expiration notification
docs.text:
Scenario: A company uses ACM certificates on ALBs and wants to notify the security team 30 days before expiration. Which approaches can satisfy the requirement?

Correct concepts:

1. ACM certificate expiration events → EventBridge → SNS

ACM
 ↓
Approaching-expiration event
 ↓
EventBridge
 ↓
SNS

2. DaysToExpiry → scheduled checking → SNS

ACM
 ↓
DaysToExpiry metric
 ↓
Scheduled daily check
 ↓
SNS

docs.title: Exam trap
docs.text:
Do not automatically choose:

AWS Config
Trusted Advisor
Private CA

when the question is simply asking for ACM expiration notification.

docs.title: Q2 — Which certificate location?
docs.text:
Scenario: An ALB is deployed in eu-west-1 and needs an ACM certificate.

Answer:

ALB: eu-west-1
→ ACM certificate: eu-west-1

docs.title: Q3 — CloudFront certificate
docs.text:
Scenario: A CloudFront distribution needs an ACM certificate.

Answer:

CloudFront
→ ACM in us-east-1

docs.title: Q4 — Multiple domains on one ALB
docs.text:
Scenario: One ALB must serve several unrelated domain names over HTTPS.

Answer:

One ALB HTTPS listener
+
Multiple ACM certificates
+
SNI

docs.title: Q5 — Several subdomains
docs.text:
Scenario: A company needs HTTPS for:

api.example.com
www.example.com
shop.example.com

Answer:

Wildcard certificate
→ *.example.com

docs.title: Q6 — One certificate, many names
docs.text:
Scenario: A single certificate must contain several different domain names.

Answer:

SAN certificate

docs.title: Section 37C: Data Lakes, ETL & Data Integration
The idea
docs.text:
These are AWS services that commonly appear in SAA questions involving data lakes, ETL, metadata, schema discovery, data preparation, incremental processing, and bulk operations on S3 objects.

You generally don't need deep knowledge of each one.

The best strategy is:

Read the requirement → identify the unique keyword → choose the service.

Serverless ETL + data catalog
→ AWS Glue

Automatically discover schema in S3
→ Glue Crawler

Store table/schema metadata
→ Glue Data Catalog

Transform CSV → Parquet
→ Glue ETL

Visual / drag-and-drop Glue ETL jobs
→ Glue Studio

Clean / mask / anonymize data with minimal custom code
→ AWS Glue DataBrew

Athena query performance on large S3 data
→ Parquet / ORC

Prevent Glue from reprocessing previously processed data
→ Glue Job Bookmark

Data lake + fine-grained permissions
→ Lake Formation

Aurora/JDBC → S3 data lake with predefined ingestion workflow
→ Lake Formation Blueprint

Salesforce → S3
→ AppFlow

Find/subscribe to third-party datasets
→ AWS Data Exchange

Discover sensitive data in S3
→ Amazon Macie

Bulk operation on millions of existing S3 objects
→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: What is a data lake?
docs.text:
Data lake = a central place to store large amounts of raw data in different formats for later processing and analytics.

In AWS, Amazon S3 is commonly used as the storage for a data lake.

                    DATA LAKE
                       ↓
                      S3
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ↓              ↓              ↓
     CSV files      JSON files      Images
     Logs           Parquet         IoT data
     Database data  Video           etc.

Simple idea:

S3
= actual data

Data lake
= the overall collection of data used for analytics

Other services can then process or query it:

S3
 ↓
Glue / Athena / EMR
 ↓
Process / query / analyze

docs.title: What is Lake Formation?
docs.text:
AWS Lake Formation = governance and fine-grained access control for a data lake.

It does not store the actual data.

Think:

S3
= stores the data

Lake Formation
= controls who can access what

For example:

Sales team
→ sales table

Finance team
→ financial table

Regional manager
→ only rows for their region

Analyst
→ only selected columns

Lake Formation can provide fine-grained permissions at the table, row, and column level.

docs.title: Common pattern
docs.text:
S3
 ↓
Glue Crawler
 ↓
Glue Data Catalog
 ↓
Lake Formation permissions
 ↓
Athena / EMR / other analytics

docs.title: SAA memory
docs.text:
Data lake = data

S3 = common data lake storage

Lake Formation = who can access what

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Data lake + fine-grained permissions → AWS Lake Formation

docs.title: Lake Formation Blueprints & Workflows
docs.text:
Lake Formation Blueprint = predefined ingestion recipe.

A blueprint can create a workflow containing Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers to ingest data into the S3 data lake.

For a relational database such as Aurora MySQL, the incremental database blueprint can load data from a JDBC source into S3.

Aurora MySQL
     ↓
Lake Formation Blueprint
     ↓
Workflow
     ↓
Glue jobs / crawler / triggers
     ↓
S3 data lake

The workflow copies the actual data into S3; the Glue Data Catalog stores metadata about the resulting tables.

docs.title: Incremental database blueprint
docs.text:
The first run loads the selected data and establishes bookmarks.

Later runs use the bookmarks to identify new rows.

First run
→ existing data → S3

Later runs
→ new rows → S3

This is best when data is primarily append-only and existing rows are not continually updated.

docs.title: Blueprint vs workflow
docs.text:
Blueprint
= recipe/template

Workflow
= actual generated process

Aurora/JDBC → S3 data lake with minimal ingestion orchestration → Lake Formation Blueprint

docs.title: Lake Formation Tag-Based Access Control (LF-TBAC)
docs.text:
LF-TBAC = use tags to control access to many data resources.

Instead of manually granting permissions to each table, database, or column, you attach LF-Tags to resources and grant permissions based on those tags.

Example:

Sales data
→ LF-Tag: department=sales

DevOps data
→ LF-Tag: department=devops

HR data
→ LF-Tag: department=hr

Then:

DevOps team
→ permission for department=devops
→ gets access to matching resources

This is useful when:

  • there are many datasets
  • data is spread across multiple AWS accounts
  • fine-grained access control is required
  • minimal operational overhead is important

docs.title: Why LF-TBAC?
docs.text:
Without tags:

Table 1 → manually grant
Table 2 → manually grant
Table 3 → manually grant
Table 4 → manually grant
...

With LF-TBAC:

Tag resources
      ↓
Grant permission to the tag
      ↓
Matching resources are covered

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
Many datasets + fine-grained access + cross-account sharing + minimal operational overhead

→ Lake Formation Tag-Based Access Control (LF-TBAC)

docs.title: Exam shortcut
docs.text: Lake Formation + scalable fine-grained authorization → LF-TBAC

docs.title: AWS Glue
docs.text:
AWS Glue = serverless ETL and Data Catalog service.

ETL means:

Extract
Transform
Load

Glue can:

  • discover data
  • catalog schemas
  • transform data
  • prepare data for analytics
  • track previously processed data with job bookmarks

It is especially useful when the requirement is serverless ETL with low operational overhead, especially for larger data-processing workloads.

Glue Studio → visual / drag-and-drop interface for creating Glue ETL jobs.

docs.title: Main Glue components
docs.text:
AWS Glue
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────────┐
      ↓         ↓             ↓
   Crawler    Catalog         ETL
  discover    metadata      transform
                                │
                                ↓
                         Job Bookmark
                         track progress

docs.title: Glue Crawler
docs.text:
Glue Crawler = automatically discovers the structure/schema of data.

It can inspect data sources such as S3 and determine things like:

customer_id → integer
name        → string
price       → decimal

It then updates the Glue Data Catalog.

docs.title: Typical flow
docs.text:
S3 files
   ↓
Glue Crawler
   ↓
Discover schema
   ↓
Glue Data Catalog

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Automatically discover the schema of files in S3."

→ Glue Crawler

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Crawler discovers. It does not perform the ETL transformation.

For example, a crawler can determine that a CSV contains:

customer_id
name
price

But it does not perform:

CSV → Parquet

That is the job of Glue ETL.

docs.title: Glue Data Catalog
docs.text:
Glue Data Catalog = centralized metadata store.

It stores information about datasets rather than the actual dataset itself.

It can store:

  • table definitions
  • columns
  • data types
  • data locations
  • schema

Think:

Actual data
→ S3

Information ABOUT the data
→ Glue Data Catalog

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Store metadata/schema/table definitions."

→ Glue Data Catalog

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Data Catalog stores metadata. It does not transform or store the actual data.

docs.title: Glue ETL
docs.text:
Glue ETL = performs the actual data transformation.

For example:

CSV
 ↓
Glue ETL
 ↓
Parquet

It can perform common transformations such as:

  • format conversion
  • filtering
  • joining
  • cleaning
  • restructuring

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Convert CSV files to Parquet."

→ Glue ETL

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Glue Crawler
= discovers schema

Glue Data Catalog
= stores metadata

Glue ETL
= transforms data

docs.title: AWS Glue DataBrew
docs.text:
AWS Glue DataBrew = visual, no-code/low-code data preparation and cleaning service.

It is useful when the requirement is to clean, normalize, transform, or anonymize data without developing custom code.

Typical operations include:

  • cleaning data
  • replacing values
  • masking sensitive information
  • removing unwanted data
  • standardizing data
  • preparing datasets for analytics or development

docs.title: Typical pattern
docs.text:
Amazon RDS
    ↓
DataBrew
    ↓
Clean / mask / transform data
    ↓
Amazon S3
    ↓
Development / analytics

docs.title: Strong SAA signal
docs.text:
"Clean or sanitize data with minimal custom code."

→ AWS Glue DataBrew

Especially when the question says:

  • remove or replace personal identifiers
  • mask sensitive values
  • prepare a copy of production data for development
  • reduce custom code
  • minimize operational overhead

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A company exports customer data from RDS every week to create development data.

Customer names and personal identifiers must be removed or replaced with random values.

RDS
 ↓
DataBrew
 ↓
Replace / mask sensitive values
 ↓
S3
 ↓
Development environment

→ DataBrew

docs.title: DataBrew vs Glue ETL
docs.text:
Both can transform data, but the exam distinction is:

Glue ETL
→ Serverless ETL
→ More general / programmable data transformation

DataBrew
→ Visual data preparation
→ Little/no custom code
→ Cleaning / masking / standardizing data

docs.title: DataBrew vs Macie
docs.text:
This is an important SAA trap.

Macie
→ Discover sensitive data in S3

DataBrew
→ Clean / transform / mask data

Do not choose Macie just because the question mentions PII.

If the requirement is:

"Find/discover sensitive data in S3."

→ Macie

If the requirement is:

"Remove, replace, mask, or clean sensitive data with minimal code."

→ DataBrew

docs.title: DataBrew vs Athena
docs.text:
Athena
→ Query/analyze data in S3 using SQL

DataBrew
→ Visually clean/transform data

If you need to write SQL/regular expressions to perform the transformation, that usually means more operational overhead than DataBrew.

docs.title: Exam shortcut
docs.text:
Clean / mask / anonymize data + minimal code → DataBrew

Discover sensitive data in S3 → Macie

Query S3 data with SQL → Athena

docs.title: Parquet for Athena
docs.text:
Apache Parquet = columnar file format optimized for analytics.

When Athena queries a large dataset in S3, Parquet can reduce the amount of data that needs to be read because Athena can read only the required columns.

Typical pattern:

Large JSON dataset in S3
        ↓
Convert to Parquet
        ↓
Amazon Athena
        ↓
Less data scanned
        ↓
Faster / cheaper queries

docs.title: Common exam signal
docs.text:
Athena queries are slow because a large amount of JSON data is stored in S3.

→ Convert the data to Parquet or another columnar format such as ORC.

docs.title: Security connection
docs.text:
If the S3 data is governed by Lake Formation, the performance improvement does not require removing the Lake Formation controls.

For data access through Lake Formation, the relevant IAM permission can include:

lakeformation:GetDataAccess

So the common exam combination is:

Athena + large JSON dataset
→ Parquet

Lake Formation-controlled data access
→ lakeformation:GetDataAccess

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Parquet / ORC
→ query-performance optimization

Lake Formation
→ data lake access control

docs.title: Glue Job Bookmarks
docs.text:
Glue Job Bookmarks = track what a Glue ETL job has already processed.

They are useful for incremental ETL because they help Glue avoid processing the same old data again on later runs.

docs.title: Typical problem
docs.text:
Suppose an S3 bucket contains:

Day 1:
A
B
C

The Glue job processes all three objects.

Later:

Day 2:
A
B
C
D
E

Without a mechanism to track previous progress, the job may process:

A B C D E

again.

With job bookmarks, Glue can track what was already processed and focus on the newly relevant data.

Day 1:
S3 → A B C
     ↓
Glue processes A B C
     ↓
Bookmark records progress


Day 2:
S3 → A B C D E
     ↓
Bookmark knows A B C were already processed
     ↓
Glue processes new/relevant data

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Glue ETL keeps reprocessing old data from previous runs."

→ Enable Glue Job Bookmarks

docs.title: Main benefit
docs.text:
Operational efficiency.

You do not need to build custom logic just to remember which data was already processed.

docs.title: Typical question
docs.text:
"A daily AWS Glue ETL job reads data from S3, but old data from previous runs is being reprocessed. What is the most operationally efficient solution?"

→ Enable Job Bookmarks

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Job Bookmark
= remember what the Glue job processed

Crawler
= discover schema

Catalog
= store metadata

ETL
= transform data

docs.title: Glue Job Bookmarks vs Other Solutions
Job Bookmarks vs deleting old data
docs.text:
Do not create custom Lambda logic just to delete previously processed source data unless the requirement explicitly calls for deletion.

Deleting source data can:

  • destroy historical data
  • create additional operational complexity
  • make recovery harder
  • require extra monitoring and permissions

If the problem is simply:

"Don't process the same data again."

→ Glue Job Bookmarks

docs.title: Job Bookmarks vs partitioning
docs.text:
Partitioning and bookmarks solve different problems.

Partitioning
= organize data for more efficient querying/processing

Job Bookmark
= track previously processed data

For example:

S3 data organized by:
year/month/day
→ Partitioning

Glue remembers which data was already processed
→ Job Bookmark

They can be used together.

docs.title: Complete Glue Example
docs.text:
Suppose CSV files arrive in an S3 bucket every day.

A typical serverless data-processing workflow can look like:

S3 source bucket
      ↓
Glue Crawler
      ↓
Discover schema
      ↓
Glue Data Catalog
      ↓
Store metadata/table definition
      ↓
Glue ETL job
      ↓
Job Bookmark checks previous progress
      ↓
Process new/relevant data
      ↓
CSV → Parquet
      ↓
S3 transformed bucket

This separates the roles:

Crawler
→ Understand the structure

Catalog
→ Remember the structure

ETL
→ Transform the data

Job Bookmark
→ Remember what the ETL job already processed

docs.title: Glue ETL + S3
docs.text:
A typical serverless solution can look like:

S3
 ↓ Object Created
EventBridge
 ↓
Glue ETL job
 ↓
Job Bookmark
 ↓
CSV → Parquet
 ↓
S3 transformed bucket

Or the process can use a scheduled Glue job.

Glue is useful when the requirement is:

  • serverless ETL
  • low operational overhead
  • processing larger datasets
  • preparing data for analytics
  • incremental processing without custom tracking

docs.title: Glue vs Lambda
docs.text:
Lambda
→ lightweight event-driven processing

Glue
→ larger/serverless ETL and data preparation

docs.title: Glue vs EC2 + Spark vs EMR vs Lambda
docs.text: A common SAA question may give several ways to process data.

docs.title: EC2 + Spark
docs.text:
EC2 + Spark
→ You manage the servers

You are responsible for more infrastructure management.

docs.title: EMR
docs.text:
EMR
→ Managed big-data / Spark infrastructure

Amazon EMR is covered more deeply in the analytics section.

docs.title: Lambda
docs.text:
Lambda
→ Better for lightweight event-driven processing

Lambda can be useful for smaller, short-running transformations triggered by events.

docs.title: Glue
docs.text:
Glue
→ Serverless ETL

Glue is the natural choice when the question emphasizes serverless ETL rather than generic compute.

docs.title: Glue Job Bookmark
docs.text:
Glue Job Bookmark
→ Incremental processing

If the question specifically says that previously processed data keeps getting processed again, the key feature is the Job Bookmark, not simply Glue itself.

docs.title: AWS Glue Service Comparison
docs.text: Glue component Main job Signal Glue Crawler Discover schema Automatically discover schema Glue Data Catalog Store metadata Tables / schema / metadata Glue ETL Transform data CSV → Parquet / ETL Glue Studio Visual ETL job creation Drag-and-drop ETL Glue DataBrew Visual data preparation Clean / mask / anonymize with little code Glue Job Bookmark Track processing progress Prevent reprocessing previously read data

docs.title: Quick memory
docs.text:
Discover
→ Crawler

Store
→ Catalog

Transform
→ ETL

Visual ETL
→ Glue Studio

Clean / mask / anonymize with little code
→ DataBrew

Remember previous processing
→ Job Bookmark

docs.title: Amazon AppFlow
docs.text:
Amazon AppFlow = transfer data between SaaS applications and AWS services without writing the integration yourself.

It is designed for data integration between supported applications and AWS destinations/sources.

Examples include:

Salesforce
    ↓
AppFlow
    ↓
S3

or:

Salesforce
    ↓
AppFlow
    ↓
Amazon Redshift

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Salesforce/SaaS → S3 or Redshift → AppFlow

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company wants to move Salesforce data into Amazon S3 without custom integration code."

→ Amazon AppFlow

docs.title: Important idea
docs.text:
AppFlow is about data transfer/integration between applications and AWS services.

It is not primarily an ETL engine like Glue.

AppFlow
= move data between SaaS and AWS

Glue
= discover / catalog / transform data

docs.title: AWS Data Exchange
docs.text:
AWS Data Exchange = discover, subscribe to, share, and use third-party datasets in AWS.

It provides a way for data providers to make datasets available and for data recipients to discover and subscribe to them.

Typical use case:

Third-party data provider
          ↓
   AWS Data Exchange
          ↓
      Subscriber
          ↓
   AWS analytics / ML

Example:

"A company wants to find and subscribe to a third-party dataset for use in its analytics workload."

→ AWS Data Exchange

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Find / subscribe to third-party datasets → AWS Data Exchange

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
AppFlow
= move data between supported SaaS applications and AWS

Data Exchange
= discover / subscribe to external datasets

docs.title: Amazon Macie
docs.text:
Amazon Macie = discover and identify sensitive data in Amazon S3.

Macie uses pattern matching and machine learning techniques to help identify sensitive data and provide visibility into data security risks.

Typical examples include:

  • personal information
  • credentials
  • financial information
  • other sensitive-data patterns

docs.title: Typical pattern
docs.text:
S3
 ↓
Macie
 ↓
Discover sensitive data

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
"Discover sensitive data in S3."

→ Amazon Macie

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Macie is primarily about discovery and visibility, not general-purpose data cleaning.

Macie
→ Find sensitive data

DataBrew
→ Clean / transform / mask data

Athena
→ Query data

docs.title: SAA trap
docs.text:
A question may mention:

customer names / personal identifiers / PII

Do not automatically choose Macie.

Ask:

Does the requirement say to discover the sensitive data, or to transform/remove it?

Discover PII in S3
→ Macie

Remove / replace / mask PII with minimal code
→ DataBrew

docs.title: S3 Batch Operations
docs.text:
S3 Batch Operations = perform an operation on many existing S3 objects.

For example, it can perform supported operations such as:

  • copy objects
  • restore objects
  • add tags
  • invoke Lambda
  • perform other supported object-level operations

The key idea is bulk operations on existing objects.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Millions of existing objects
        ↓
S3 Batch Operations
        ↓
Apply the operation

docs.title: Important S3 Encryption Trap
docs.text:
A bucket's default encryption setting does not retroactively change old objects.

Suppose:

S3 bucket
↓
Millions of existing objects

You change the bucket's default encryption configuration.

That does not automatically reprocess all existing objects.

When the question instead asks you to:

Perform an operation on millions/billions of existing S3 objects

→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company has millions of existing S3 objects and needs to apply an operation to all of them."

→ S3 Batch Operations

The exact operation might be:

  • copying objects
  • tagging objects
  • restoring objects
  • invoking Lambda
  • another supported object-level operation

The important clue is the large number of existing objects.

docs.title: S3 Batch Operations vs EventBridge / Lambda
docs.text: Do not confuse bulk processing of existing objects with processing a newly created object.

docs.title: New object arrives
docs.text:
S3 Object Created
→ EventBridge / Lambda / other event-driven solution

docs.title: Millions of existing objects
docs.text:
Existing objects
→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
New event
→ Event-driven processing

Huge number of existing objects
→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: Data Lake Architecture Example
docs.text:
A larger architecture can combine several services:

                    SaaS applications
                         │
                         ↓
                      AppFlow
                         │
                         ↓
S3 data lake ──────────────────────────────────┐
   │                                            │
   ↓                                            ↓
Glue Crawler                             Lake Formation
   │                                      permissions
   ↓                                            │
Glue Data Catalog                              │
   │                                            │
   ↓                                            │
Glue ETL ───────────────→ transformed data ←───┘
   │
   ↓
Job Bookmark
tracks incremental processing

For a relational source such as Aurora:

Aurora / JDBC
      ↓
Lake Formation Blueprint
      ↓
Generated workflow
      ↓
Glue jobs + crawler + triggers
      ↓
S3 data lake
      ↓
Lake Formation permissions
      ↓
Athena / QuickSight

For data preparation / anonymization:

RDS export
    ↓
DataBrew
    ↓
Clean / mask / replace sensitive values
    ↓
S3
    ↓
Development environment

The roles remain different:

AppFlow
= bring data from SaaS

Lake Formation Blueprint
= predefined ingestion workflow

S3
= store the actual data

Glue Crawler
= discover schema

Glue Data Catalog
= store metadata

Glue ETL
= transform data

DataBrew
= visually clean / mask / prepare data

Glue Job Bookmark
= track previously processed data

Lake Formation
= control data lake access

Macie
= discover sensitive data in S3

docs.title: Common Question Patterns
docs.text:
"Serverless ETL and a central data catalog are required."

→ AWS Glue

"Automatically discover the schema of data files in S3."

→ Glue Crawler

"Store table/schema metadata for analytics."

→ Glue Data Catalog

"Convert CSV files into Parquet."

→ Glue ETL

"Create Glue ETL jobs using a visual interface instead of building the job entirely in code."

→ Glue Studio

"Clean, mask, or anonymize customer data with minimal custom code."

→ AWS Glue DataBrew

"A weekly copy of RDS customer data is needed for development, but names and personal identifiers must be removed or replaced."

→ AWS Glue DataBrew

"Athena queries are slow because a large amount of JSON data is stored in S3."

→ Transform the data into Apache Parquet (or another columnar format such as ORC)

"A Glue ETL job keeps processing old S3 data from previous runs."

→ Enable Glue Job Bookmarks

"A daily Glue job should process newly arrived data without repeatedly processing old data."

→ Glue Job Bookmarks

"A company wants to build a data lake with fine-grained access control over tables, rows, and columns."

→ Lake Formation

"A company stores its raw analytics data in S3 and wants to control which users can access specific tables, rows, or columns."

→ Lake Formation

"Aurora/JDBC data must be ingested into an S3 data lake with minimal custom orchestration."

→ Lake Formation Blueprint / Workflow

"Aurora data should be incrementally loaded into the data lake."

→ Lake Formation Incremental Database Blueprint

"A company wants Aurora data in S3 and column-level access for marketing users, then wants to query it from QuickSight."

→ Lake Formation Blueprint → S3 → Lake Formation Data Filter → Athena → QuickSight

"Move Salesforce data to S3 without custom integration code."

→ AppFlow

"Transfer data from a SaaS application to Amazon Redshift without building the integration from scratch."

→ AppFlow

"A company wants to find and subscribe to a third-party dataset for analytics."

→ AWS Data Exchange

"A company wants to discover sensitive data patterns in an S3 bucket."

→ Amazon Macie

"Apply an operation to millions of existing S3 objects."

→ S3 Batch Operations

"Millions/billions of existing S3 objects need to be processed in bulk."

→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: Glue Job Bookmark vs Partitioning
docs.text:
Do not confuse these.

Partitioning
= organize data to improve query/processing efficiency

Job Bookmark
= track what the Glue job already processed

Exam trigger:

Data is hard to query efficiently
→ Think partitioning / columnar formats such as Parquet

Glue keeps reprocessing old data
→ Think Job Bookmark

docs.title: Parquet vs GZIP
docs.text:
Do not treat compression and columnar storage as the same thing.

Parquet
= columnar format
= analytics/query optimization

GZIP
= compression
= reduces file size

For Athena performance questions involving large JSON datasets:

Convert to Parquet/ORC

rather than simply compressing the JSON with GZIP.

docs.title: DataBrew vs Macie
docs.text:
This is one of the most useful distinctions in this section.

Macie
→ Discover sensitive data in S3

DataBrew
→ Clean / transform / mask / anonymize data

Exam trigger:

Find PII
→ Macie

Remove / replace / mask PII
→ DataBrew

docs.title: DataBrew vs Athena
docs.text:
Athena
→ Query/analyze S3 data using SQL

DataBrew
→ Visually clean/transform data

If the question emphasizes minimal custom code for cleaning or preparing data, DataBrew is usually the better fit.

docs.title: AppFlow vs Data Exchange
docs.text:
SaaS application → AWS
→ AppFlow

Third-party dataset → discover/subscribe/use
→ AWS Data Exchange

docs.title: S3 Batch Operations vs normal S3 events
docs.text:
One newly created object
→ event-driven processing

Millions of existing objects
→ S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: Job Bookmarks vs custom Lambda cleanup
docs.text:
Do not overengineer a Glue incremental-processing problem.

Glue reprocesses old data
→ Job Bookmark

Delete old source objects
→ Not the default solution

If the question asks for the most operationally efficient way to prevent reprocessing, Job Bookmarks are usually the direct answer.

docs.title: Blueprint vs Glue Data Catalog
docs.text:
Do not confuse ingestion with metadata.

Lake Formation Blueprint / Workflow
→ copies/ingests actual data into S3

Glue Data Catalog
→ stores metadata about that data

docs.title: Glue + DataBrew + Macie + Athena
docs.text:
A useful way to separate the services:

             S3 data
                │
      ┌─────────┼───────────┐
      ↓         ↓           ↓
   Macie     DataBrew    Athena
      │         │           │
   DISCOVER   CLEAN       QUERY
   sensitive   / MASK      / ANALYZE
     data      data         data

And for ETL:

S3
 ↓
Glue Crawler
 ↓
Glue Data Catalog
 ↓
Glue ETL
 ↓
Transformed data

So:

Crawler
→ discover

Catalog
→ metadata

ETL
→ transform

DataBrew
→ visually clean / mask

Macie
→ discover sensitive data in S3

Athena
→ query

docs.title: Pocket Card
docs.text: Keyword Answer Serverless ETL / data catalog AWS Glue Discover schema Glue Crawler Automatically discover S3 file schema Glue Crawler Store metadata Glue Data Catalog Store table/schema definitions Glue Data Catalog Transform data Glue ETL CSV → Parquet Glue ETL Visual / drag-and-drop ETL Glue Studio Clean / mask / anonymize data + minimal code AWS Glue DataBrew Discover sensitive data in S3 Amazon Macie Query S3 data with SQL Amazon Athena Athena + large JSON dataset Parquet / ORC Reduce Athena data scanned Parquet / ORC Glue reprocesses old data Glue Job Bookmark Incremental Glue ETL processing Glue Job Bookmark Data lake + fine-grained permissions Lake Formation Data lake + many datasets + scalable permissions Lake Formation LF-TBAC S3 = actual data in the data lake Amazon S3 Lake Formation = data lake access AWS Lake Formation Lake Formation data access lakeformation:GetDataAccess Table/row/column permissions Lake Formation Cross-account fine-grained access Lake Formation LF-TBAC Aurora/JDBC → S3 data lake Lake Formation Blueprint Predefined ingestion recipe Lake Formation Blueprint Blueprint → actual process Lake Formation Workflow Incremental Aurora/JDBC ingestion Incremental Database Blueprint Blueprint actual data destination S3 Blueprint metadata Glue Data Catalog SaaS → S3 AppFlow SaaS → Redshift AppFlow Find/subscribe to third-party datasets AWS Data Exchange Bulk operation on existing S3 objects S3 Batch Operations Millions/billions of existing objects S3 Batch Operations

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Match the requirement to the unique service keyword.

Requirement / keyword Service Spark / Hadoop Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce) SQL directly on S3 Amazon Athena Query S3 data from Redshift without loading it Amazon Redshift Spectrum BI + standard SQL + analytical workloads Amazon Redshift Apache Flink / real-time stream processing Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Interactive Flink streaming analysis Flink Studio Kafka Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) RabbitMQ Amazon MQ BI dashboards Amazon QuickSight Search / logs / OpenSearch dashboards Amazon OpenSearch Service Prometheus metrics dashboards Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus + Grafana Serverless Spark / Hive batch processing Amazon EMR Serverless File-based video transcoding AWS Elemental MediaConvert Legacy video transcoding Amazon Elastic Transcoder

docs.title: Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce)
docs.text:
Amazon EMR = managed big-data processing using frameworks such as Apache Spark and Hadoop.

Use it for:

  • large-scale data processing
  • Spark jobs
  • Hadoop workloads

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Spark / Hadoop → Amazon EMR

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Large data in S3 must be processed with Apache Spark:

S3
 ↓
Amazon EMR
 ↓
Spark processing
 ↓
Processed data

→ Amazon EMR

docs.title: Spot Instances with EMR
docs.text: You can use Spot Instances for suitable EMR task nodes to reduce cost when the workload can tolerate interruption and the task nodes are suitable for Spot capacity.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Large-scale Spark/Hadoop processing → Amazon EMR

docs.title: EMR Node Types
docs.text:
A node = a server/instance(EC2) that is part of the EMR cluster.

A cluster usually contains multiple nodes that work together:

EMR Cluster
├── Server
├── Server
├── Server
└── Server

EMR gives these servers different roles.

                    EMR CLUSTER
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ↓              ↓              ↓
       PRIMARY          CORE           TASK
        "boss"       "workers"     "extra workers"

docs.title: Primary node
docs.text:
Primary node = manages/co-ordinates the cluster.

It handles cluster management and coordinates the work of the other nodes.

Think:

Primary = boss / manager

Example:

You submit a Spark job
        ↓
    Primary
        ↓
coordinates the work
      ↙   ↘
   Core   Task

docs.title: Core nodes
docs.text:
Core nodes = workers that do computation and can store data in HDFS.

Think:

Core = worker + storage

Example:

Primary
   │
   ├── Core 1 → compute + HDFS
   ├── Core 2 → compute + HDFS
   └── Core 3 → compute + HDFS

Because core nodes can store HDFS data, losing them can affect data availability.

Core → usually On-Demand

docs.title: Task nodes
docs.text:
Task nodes = extra workers that provide compute capacity but do not store HDFS data.

Think:

Task = extra worker / extra compute

Example:

Primary
   │
   ├── Core 1 → compute + HDFS
   ├── Core 2 → compute + HDFS
   ├── Task 1 → compute only
   ├── Task 2 → compute only
   └── Task 3 → compute only

Task nodes are useful when you temporarily need more processing capacity.

Because they do not store HDFS data:

Task → often Spot

If a Spot task node is interrupted, you mainly lose compute capacity, not HDFS data stored on the core nodes.

docs.title: Node type memory
docs.text: Node Simple meaning Main role Primary Boss Manages/co-ordinates the cluster Core Worker + storage Compute + HDFS data Task Extra worker Compute only

docs.title: Common cost-saving pattern
docs.text:
Primary → On-Demand
Core    → On-Demand
Task    → Spot

Core → On-Demand because it can store HDFS data.

Task → Spot because it is compute-only and can tolerate interruption more easily.

docs.title: Important
docs.text: Many EMR workloads use Amazon S3 for their main data storage rather than HDFS. The Core-node/HDFS distinction matters when the cluster is using HDFS.

docs.title: EMR Cluster Lifecycle
docs.text: These are lifecycle patterns, not node types.

docs.title: Transient EMR Cluster
docs.text:
Create cluster
    ↓
Run job
    ↓
Job finishes
    ↓
Cluster terminates

Good for periodic or batch jobs.

Transient = create → run → terminate

docs.title: Long-Running EMR Cluster
docs.text:
Create cluster
    ↓
Cluster stays running
    ↓
Many jobs over time

Good for continuous or repeatedly used workloads.

Long-running = stays running

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Lifecycle
→ Transient
→ Long-running

Node types
→ Primary
→ Core
→ Task

For periodic batch processing, transient EMR is often more cost-effective than keeping a cluster running.

docs.title: Amazon EMR Serverless
docs.text:
Amazon EMR Serverless = run Spark or Hive jobs without managing an EMR cluster or EC2 nodes.

Submit job
   ↓
EMR Serverless
   ↓
AWS automatically provisions/scales resources
   ↓
Job completes

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Serverless Spark/Hive + no cluster management → Amazon EMR Serverless

docs.title: Simple distinction
docs.text:
Amazon EMR
→ You use/manage an EMR cluster
→ can integrate with Apache Ranger 

EMR Serverless
→ No cluster/node management
→ AWS automatically handles resources
→ can not integrate with Apache Ranger

Use EMR Serverless for batch processing when you do not want to provision and manage an EMR cluster.

docs.title: Amazon EMR vs Amazon Redshift
docs.text: Amazon EMR Amazon Redshift Managed big-data processing Managed data warehouse Spark / Hadoop Analytical SQL Process / transform large datasets BI / reporting / analytics

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
Spark / Hadoop → Amazon EMR

BI + standard SQL + analytical workloads → Amazon Redshift

A question can require both.

docs.title: EMR + Redshift Pattern
docs.text:
S3 data lake
     ↓
Amazon EMR
(Spark / Hadoop)
     ↓
Amazon Redshift
     ↓
BI tools + standard SQL

EMR
→ processes the large dataset

Redshift
→ stores/analyzes processed data
  for analytical SQL and BI

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company stores large datasets in S3 and wants to use big-data processing frameworks to process the data. Business users then need high-performance access using BI tools and standard SQL queries."

→ Amazon EMR + Amazon Redshift

docs.title: Amazon Athena
docs.text:
Amazon Athena = serverless interactive SQL queries directly against data in S3.

Use it when CSV, JSON, Parquet, or similar data is already in S3.

S3
 ↓
Amazon Athena
 ↓
SQL query

No database server needs to be provisioned just to query the data.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: SQL + S3 → Amazon Athena

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Amazon Athena = SQL ON S3

docs.title: Athena + QuickSight Reporting
docs.text:
Pattern: S3 data + weekly reporting + visualization + cost-effective → Glue Crawler + Athena + QuickSight

S3
 ↓
Glue Crawler
 ↓
Glue Data Catalog
 ↓
Athena
 ↓
QuickSight
Service Role Glue Crawler Discovers the S3 data schema Athena Serverless SQL directly on S3 QuickSight Dashboards / visualization

A company is preparing a solution that the sales team can use for generating weekly revenue reports. The team must be able to run analysis on sales records stored in Amazon S3 and visualize the results of queries.

How can the solutions architect meet the requirement in the most cost-effective way possible?

→ Use AWS Glue crawler to build tables in AWS Glue Data Catalog. Run queries using Amazon Athena. Use Amazon QuickSight for visualization.

docs.title: Exam signal
docs.text: S3 + SQL + occasional/weekly reporting + visualization → Glue + Athena + QuickSight

docs.title: Amazon Redshift
docs.text:
Amazon Redshift = managed cloud data warehouse for analytical workloads.

Use it for:

  • analytical SQL queries
  • high-performance analytics
  • BI / reporting
  • data warehousing

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: BI + standard SQL + analytical workloads → Amazon Redshift

docs.title: Redshift Cross-Region Snapshots
docs.text:
Redshift Cross-Region Snapshot Copy automatically copies snapshots of a Redshift cluster to another AWS Region.

Use it for disaster recovery from an entire Region outage.

Redshift Cluster (Region A)
        ↓
Cross-Region Snapshot Copy
        ↓
Snapshot (Region B)
        ↓
Restore Redshift Cluster

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
Redshift cluster + Region outage → Cross-Region Snapshot Copy

Automated snapshots alone are not enough for Regional DR because the snapshot needs to be available in another Region.

docs.title: Amazon Redshift Spectrum
docs.text:
Amazon Redshift Spectrum = query data stored in S3 directly from Redshift without loading the data into Redshift tables.

Use it when:

  • you already use Amazon Redshift
  • some data remains in S3
  • you want to query that S3 data using Redshift
Amazon Redshift
      ↓
Redshift Spectrum
      ↓
S3 data

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Query S3 data from Redshift without loading it → Redshift Spectrum

docs.title: Key distinction
docs.text:
Athena
→ SQL directly on S3

Redshift Spectrum
→ SQL on S3 from Redshift

docs.title: Athena vs Redshift vs Redshift Spectrum
docs.text: Requirement Service Query data directly in S3 with SQL Amazon Athena Query S3 data using an existing Redshift environment Redshift Spectrum Dedicated analytical data warehouse Amazon Redshift BI / reporting / high-performance warehouse analytics Amazon Redshift

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Athena
= QUERY S3

Redshift
= ANALYTICAL DATA WAREHOUSE

Redshift Spectrum
= QUERY S3 FROM REDSHIFT

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
"Analysts need to query files already stored in S3 using SQL, with no need to provision a database."

→ Amazon Athena

"Business users need high-performance analytical SQL queries against a data warehouse."

→ Amazon Redshift

"The company already uses Redshift but wants to query additional datasets stored in S3 without loading them into Redshift."

→ Redshift Spectrum

docs.title: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
docs.text:
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink = managed real-time stream processing with Apache Flink.

Use it for:

  • real-time analytics
  • streaming ETL
  • continuous event processing
  • stream transformations
  • detecting patterns in streams

Typical sources:

  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
  • Amazon MSK / Apache Kafka

Typical pattern:

Kinesis / Kafka
      ↓
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
      ↓
Real-time processing
      ↓
Kinesis / S3 / other destinations

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Apache Flink + real-time streaming analytics → Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company receives continuous streaming data from Amazon Kinesis and needs to perform real-time analytics using Apache Flink."

→ Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

docs.title: Flink use cases
docs.text:
Continuous event stream
        ↓
Flink
        ↓
Transform / aggregate / analyze
        ↓
Real-time results

Examples:

  • real-time analytics
  • streaming ETL
  • continuous event processing
  • stream transformations
  • detecting patterns in streams

docs.title: Flink Studio
docs.text:
Flink Studio = interactive environment for developing and analyzing Apache Flink streaming workloads.

Use it for interactive querying, exploration, development, or streaming analysis.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Interactive Flink development / streaming analysis → Flink Studio

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company wants to interactively query and analyze streaming data using Apache Flink."

→ Flink Studio

docs.title: Flink Studio vs Managed Service for Apache Flink
docs.text: Requirement Answer Run managed production Flink stream-processing applications Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Interactive Flink development Flink Studio Interactive streaming analysis Flink Studio

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Production stream processing
→ Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

Interactive development / exploration / analysis
→ Flink Studio

docs.title: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)
docs.text:
Amazon MSK = managed Apache Kafka.

Use it for Kafka-compatible workloads without managing the underlying Kafka infrastructure yourself.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Kafka → Amazon MSK

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"An existing application uses Apache Kafka and the company wants a managed Kafka service on AWS."

→ Amazon MSK

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: MSK = MANAGED KAFKA

docs.title: MSK vs Managed Service for Apache Flink
docs.text:
Kafka
→ Amazon MSK

Process streaming data with Apache Flink
→ Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

Typical architecture:

Applications
    ↓
Amazon MSK
(Kafka)
    ↓
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
    ↓
Real-time processing
    ↓
S3 / Kinesis / other destination

docs.title: Distinction
docs.text: Service Role Amazon MSK Streaming platform / Kafka Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Stream processing

docs.title: Amazon QuickSight
docs.text:
Amazon QuickSight = business intelligence and dashboards.

Use it for:

  • dashboards
  • charts
  • reports
  • business visualizations

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Business dashboard → Amazon QuickSight

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Business users need dashboards and visual reports based on analytical data."

→ Amazon QuickSight

docs.title: Analytics architecture
docs.text:
Data
 ↓
Processing / warehouse
 ↓
Amazon Redshift
 ↓
Amazon QuickSight
 ↓
Dashboards / reports

QuickSight is the visualization / BI layer, not the primary big-data processing engine.

docs.title: OpenSearch + Kibana / OpenSearch Dashboards
docs.text:
Amazon OpenSearch Service = search, log analysis, and operational analytics.

Use it when data is loaded/indexed into OpenSearch and you want to search it and visualize the results.

Kibana = visualization UI for Elasticsearch

OpenSearch Dashboards = visualization UI for OpenSearch

Records / logs
      ↓
Amazon OpenSearch Service
      ↓
Search / queries
      ↓
OpenSearch Dashboards

For older Elasticsearch questions:

Elasticsearch
      ↓
Kibana

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Logs + search + OpenSearch dashboards → Amazon OpenSearch Service

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Athena
→ SQL directly on S3

OpenSearch
→ data is indexed/loaded into OpenSearch
→ search/query there
→ visualize with OpenSearch Dashboards

docs.title: OpenSearch vs Grafana vs QuickSight
docs.text: Requirement Service Search logs / indexed data / operational dashboards OpenSearch + OpenSearch Dashboards Prometheus / metrics dashboards Prometheus / AMP + Grafana Business BI / reports / dashboards QuickSight

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Load application logs into an OpenSearch cluster, run searches, and visualize the results."

→ Amazon OpenSearch Service + OpenSearch Dashboards

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text:
Grafana = dashboard / visualization tool mainly used for metrics.

Common pattern:

Prometheus / AMP
      ↓
Grafana
      ↓
Metrics dashboards

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Prometheus / PromQL + dashboards → Grafana

docs.title: Simple distinction
docs.text:
OpenSearch
→ logs / search
→ OpenSearch Dashboards

Prometheus / AMP
→ metrics
→ Grafana

docs.title: AWS Elemental MediaConvert
docs.text:
AWS Elemental MediaConvert = managed file-based video transcoding service.

Use it to convert/process video files for on-demand delivery.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: File-based video transcoding → AWS Elemental MediaConvert

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Video file
    ↓
MediaConvert
    ↓
Transcoded video

Example: create multiple resolutions or formats for on-demand playback.

docs.title: MediaConvert vs MediaLive
docs.text: Requirement Service File-based video transcoding AWS Elemental MediaConvert Live video encoding AWS Elemental MediaLive

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
MediaConvert = FILE-BASED VIDEO

MediaLive = LIVE VIDEO

docs.title: Legacy Service: Amazon Elastic Transcoder
docs.text:
Amazon Elastic Transcoder = older managed video/audio transcoding service.

It was discontinued on November 13, 2025. AWS recommends AWS Elemental MediaConvert for file-based transcoding workflows.

docs.title: Exam memory
docs.text:
Video transcoding → MediaConvert

Old question mentioning Elastic Transcoder → recognize it as the legacy service

Current file-based video transcoding
→ MediaConvert

Legacy service
→ Elastic Transcoder

Do not select Elastic Transcoder for a new modern AWS architecture.

docs.title: Amazon Timestream
docs.text:
Amazon Timestream = fully managed time-series database for data that changes over time.

Typical use cases:

  • IoT sensor data
  • application / infrastructure metrics
  • monitoring data
  • device telemetry

Example:

10:00 → CPU = 45%
10:01 → CPU = 52%
10:02 → CPU = 61%

docs.title: Signal

Primary

Core

Task

→ create → run job → terminate

Long-running

Redshift

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
These AWS AI/ML services usually appear in SAA questions as very specific use cases.

You generally don't need deep knowledge of how the machine-learning models work.

The best strategy is:

Identify what type of input you have → identify what the question wants to do with it → choose the unique service.

For example:

Images / video
→ Rekognition

Audio / speech → text
→ Transcribe

Text → speech
→ Polly

Text → another language
→ Translate

Text analysis / sentiment
→ Comprehend

Medical / clinical text / PHI
→ Comprehend Medical

Scanned documents / tables / forms
→ Textract

Search company documents
→ Kendra

Recommendations
→ Personalize

Time-series forecasting
→ Forecast

Chatbot
→ Lex

Build your own ML model
→ SageMaker

docs.title: AI / ML Service Family
docs.text: Service What it does Signal Amazon Rekognition Looks at images and videos and detects things such as faces, objects, people, and unsafe content Faces, objects, video Amazon Transcribe Takes audio/speech and turns it into written text Call recording → transcript Amazon Polly Takes written text and turns it into spoken audio App reads text aloud Amazon Translate Takes text in one language and translates it into another language English → French Amazon Comprehend Takes text and analyzes its meaning, such as sentiment, entities, and key phrases Positive/negative review Amazon Comprehend Medical Analyzes clinical/medical text and detects medical information and PHI Medical text / PHI Amazon Textract Takes scanned documents/images and extracts text, tables, and form fields Invoice/form → structured data Amazon Kendra Searches company documents and finds relevant answers using natural-language queries Find vacation policy Amazon Personalize Uses user/item behavior to generate personalized recommendations Customers also bought Amazon Forecast Uses historical time-series data to predict future values Predict future sales/demand Amazon Lex Lets you build conversational chatbots that understand user messages and respond Customer-service chatbot Amazon SageMaker Lets data scientists build, train, tune, and deploy their own ML models Train your own ML model

docs.title: Amazon Rekognition
docs.text:
Amazon Rekognition = image and video analysis.

It can analyze:

  • images
  • videos
  • faces
  • objects
  • people
  • unsafe or inappropriate content

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Faces / objects / people / image / video analysis → Rekognition

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company needs to automatically detect faces and objects in uploaded images."

→ Amazon Rekognition

Another example:

"A company needs to identify unsafe content in uploaded videos."

→ Amazon Rekognition

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Image / video
→ Rekognition

docs.title: Amazon Transcribe
docs.text:
Amazon Transcribe = speech-to-text.

It takes audio or speech and converts it into written text.

Audio
 ↓
Transcribe
 ↓
Text

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• call-center recordings
  • meeting recordings
  • voice recordings
  • audio transcription

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Speech → text → Transcribe

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company records customer-service calls and wants to automatically create text transcripts."

→ Amazon Transcribe

docs.title: Amazon Polly
docs.text:
Amazon Polly = text-to-speech.

It takes written text and generates spoken audio.

Text
 ↓
Polly
 ↓
Speech / audio

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Text → speech → Polly

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A mobile application needs to read articles aloud to users."

→ Amazon Polly

docs.title: Transcribe vs Polly
docs.text:
These are opposites.

Speech
   ↓
Transcribe
   ↓
Text

Text
   ↓
Polly
   ↓
Speech

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Transcribe = speech → text

Polly = text → speech

docs.title: Amazon Translate
docs.text:
Amazon Translate = text translation between languages.

It takes text in one language and translates it into another language.

English
   ↓
Translate
   ↓
French

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Translate text between languages → Amazon Translate

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"An application receives English customer messages and needs to provide them in French."

→ Amazon Translate

docs.title: Amazon Comprehend
docs.text:
Amazon Comprehend = natural-language processing and text analysis.

It can analyze text for things such as:

  • sentiment
  • entities
  • key phrases
  • language
  • other text insights

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Understand the meaning or sentiment of text → Comprehend

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company wants to determine whether customer reviews are positive, negative, or neutral."

→ Amazon Comprehend

docs.title: Another example
docs.text:
"A company wants to automatically identify names, organizations, and locations in customer feedback."

→ Amazon Comprehend

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Text
 ↓
Comprehend
 ↓
Meaning / sentiment / entities / key phrases

docs.title: Amazon Comprehend Medical
docs.text:
Amazon Comprehend Medical = analyze clinical and medical text.

It is designed for healthcare-related text and can identify medical information and Protected Health Information (PHI).

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
Clinical / medical text → Comprehend Medical

PHI detection → Comprehend Medical

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A hospital needs to identify patient names, addresses, and other PHI in clinical reports."

→ Amazon Comprehend Medical

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
General text analysis
→ Comprehend

Medical / clinical text
→ Comprehend Medical

Medical PDF
→ Textract
→ Comprehend Medical

So:

PDF report
   ↓
Textract
   ↓
Extracted text
   ↓
Comprehend Medical
   ↓
PHI detection

docs.title: Amazon Textract
docs.text:
Amazon Textract = extract text, tables, and form fields from scanned documents and images.

It is especially useful when the input is a document, such as:

  • invoices
  • forms
  • scanned documents
  • receipts
  • identity documents
  • tables

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Scanned document → text / tables / forms → Textract

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company needs to automatically extract names, fields, tables, and values from scanned invoices."

→ Amazon Textract

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Do not confuse Textract with Rekognition.

Rekognition
= image / video analysis

Textract
= document / text / table / form extraction

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Scanned invoice
       ↓
   Textract
       ↓
Text + fields + tables

docs.title: Rekognition vs Textract
docs.text: This is a common conceptual distinction.

docs.title: Rekognition
docs.text:
Use it when the question is about understanding what is in an image or video.

Image
→ faces
→ objects
→ people
→ unsafe content
→ Rekognition

docs.title: Textract
docs.text:
Use it when the question is about extracting structured information from a document.

Scanned invoice
→ text
→ tables
→ form fields
→ Textract

docs.title: Amazon Kendra
docs.text:
Amazon Kendra = intelligent enterprise search.

It can search company documents and return relevant information using natural-language queries.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Search internal company documents using natural-language queries → Kendra

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose employees have thousands of internal documents.

An employee asks:

"What is our vacation policy?"

Kendra can search the organization's indexed content and return relevant information.

→ Amazon Kendra

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:

        ↓
Natural-language search
        ↓
Relevant information

docs.title: Amazon Personalize
docs.text:
Amazon Personalize = personalized recommendations based on user and item behavior.

It can use information such as:

  • user behavior
  • item interactions
  • preferences
  • historical activity

to generate personalized recommendations.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Recommendations based on user behavior → Personalize

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"An online store wants to recommend products based on each customer's previous activity."

→ Amazon Personalize

Another common example:

"Customers who purchased this item may be interested in similar items."

→ Amazon Personalize

User behavior

Personalize
      ↓
Personalized recommendations

docs.title: Amazon Forecast
docs.text:
Amazon Forecast = time-series forecasting.

It uses historical time-series data to predict future values.

Common examples include:

  • sales
  • demand
  • inventory requirements
  • resource usage

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Predict future values from historical time-series data → Forecast

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company wants to predict next month's product demand based on historical sales data."

→ Amazon Forecast

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Historical time-series data
          ↓
       Forecast
          ↓
Future values

docs.title: Simple signal
docs.text: Future demand / sales prediction → Forecast

docs.title: Amazon Lex
docs.text:
Amazon Lex = conversational chatbot service.

It lets you build applications that understand user messages and interact conversationally.

It is commonly used for:

  • customer-service chatbots
  • conversational interfaces
  • voice or text interactions

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Build a conversational chatbot → Lex

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company wants to build a customer-service chatbot that can understand customer requests."

→ Amazon Lex

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
User
 ↓
Conversational interface
 ↓
Lex

Application response

docs.text: Chatbot → Lex

docs.title: Amazon SageMaker
docs.text:
Amazon SageMaker = build, train, tune, and deploy your own machine-learning models.

It is the service to think about when the question is about custom machine learning development, rather than simply calling a prebuilt AI capability.

Data scientists can use it to:

  • build models
  • train models
  • tune models
  • deploy models
  • manage ML workflows

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Build/train/deploy your own ML model → SageMaker

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Data scientists need to build and train a custom machine-learning model using the company's own dataset."

→ Amazon SageMaker

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Use a ready-made AI capability
→ Specialized AI service

Build your own ML model
→ SageMaker

For example:

Image / video analysis
→ Rekognition

Speech → text
→ Transcribe

Custom ML model
→ SageMaker

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
These AWS services commonly appear in SAA questions involving instance management, secure access, command execution, patching, operational issues, right-sizing, AWS operational events, automated remediation, and Prometheus-compatible monitoring.

Best strategy:

Read the requirement → identify the unique keyword → choose the service.

Secure shell access to private EC2 without SSH
→ AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

Run the same command on hundreds of EC2 instances
→ AWS Systems Manager Run Command

Automatically patch hundreds of EC2 instances
→ AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager

Manage / inspect EC2 instances
→ AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager

Centrally track and investigate operational issues
→ AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter

Automatically perform operational remediation
→ AWS Systems Manager Automation

Recommend optimal size for EC2 / ASG / EBS / Lambda
→ AWS Compute Optimizer

AWS event specifically associated with your account/resources
→ AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health
   (older SAA material: Personal Health Dashboard)

docs.title: AWS Systems Manager
docs.text:
AWS Systems Manager (SSM) = a collection of tools for managing and operating AWS and supported hybrid infrastructure.

Most important SAA services:

  • AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
  • AWS Systems Manager Run Command
  • AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
  • AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager
  • AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter
  • AWS Systems Manager Automation
Session Manager = ACCESS
Run Command     = RUN
Patch Manager   = PATCH
Fleet Manager   = MANAGE / INSPECT
OpsCenter       = TRACK / INVESTIGATE ISSUES
Automation      = FIX / AUTOMATE

docs.title: Session Manager
docs.text:
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager = secure interactive shell access to managed EC2 instances without traditional SSH.

You can avoid:

  • a bastion host
  • inbound port 22
  • exposing SSH to the Internet

Typical pattern:

Admin
  ↓
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
  ↓
Private EC2

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Secure access to private EC2 without SSH → AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Administrators need secure shell access to private EC2 instances without opening port 22 or maintaining a bastion host."

→ AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Session Manager = ACCESS instances

docs.title: Run Command
docs.text:
AWS Systems Manager Run Command = execute commands or scripts on one or many managed instances.

Example:

500 EC2 instances
      ↓
AWS Systems Manager Run Command
      ↓
Run the same script

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Run a command/script across many EC2 instances → AWS Systems Manager Run Command

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
"Execute the same shell script on hundreds of EC2 instances."

→ AWS Systems Manager Run Command

"Execute a script across a fleet of EC2 instances."

→ AWS Systems Manager Run Command

docs.title: Signal

docs.title: Examples

"Apply security patches to 500 EC2 instances every month."

→ AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager

"Apply security patches to EC2 instances on a regular schedule."

→ AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager

docs.title: Memory

  • Services
  • Windows Registry
  • Instance information

docs.title: Example

→ AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager

→ AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter

docs.text:

docs.title: AWS Health / Personal Health Dashboard
docs.text: AWS Health Dashboard provides AWS Health information for both public service events and account-specific events. Older SAA material may refer to the account-specific view as the AWS Personal Health Dashboard (PHD).

docs.title: Public / Service Health
docs.text:
AWS Health Dashboard – Service health = public/general AWS service events.

Example:

Is Amazon EC2 experiencing
a service issue in this Region?

Public events are not specific to an AWS account and can describe a Regional service issue even when you do not use that service there.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: General AWS service status → AWS Health Dashboard – Service health

docs.title: Account-Specific / Your Account Health
docs.text:
The signed-in AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health shows events specific to your account, including upcoming scheduled changes and affected resources.

Older SAA material commonly calls this the AWS Personal Health Dashboard (PHD).

AWS event
specific to your account/resources
        ↓
AWS Health Dashboard
Your account health

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: AWS event specifically associated with my account/resources → AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
PUBLIC
= general AWS service / Regional event
= not specific to my account

ACCOUNT-SPECIFIC
= specific to my account / organization
= affected resources may be identified

The distinction is not whether the event could affect resources generally. Public events can also affect users. The distinction is whether the event is specific to your account.

docs.title: EventBridge + AWS Health
docs.text:
Amazon EventBridge can detect and route AWS Health events so you can automate actions.

Typical pattern:

AWS Health event
      ↓
Amazon EventBridge
      ↓
Automation / target action

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
AWS Health
= provides the health event

Amazon EventBridge
= detects / routes / triggers from the event

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Automatically react when AWS reports an event that may affect resources in the account."

→ AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health + Amazon EventBridge

This matches the older SAA wording:

→ Personal Health Dashboard + EventBridge

docs.title: Service Health vs Account-Specific Health
docs.text:
General AWS service / Regional status
→ AWS Health Dashboard – Service health

Event specific to my account/resources
→ AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health
  (older term: Personal Health Dashboard)

docs.title: EventBridge
docs.text:
Amazon EventBridge
= detect / route / trigger

docs.title: AWS Health Question Patterns
docs.text:
"An EC2 instance may be affected by an upcoming AWS event specific to the company's account."

→ AWS Health Dashboard – Your account health

"A company wants general information about the status of an AWS service."

→ AWS Health Dashboard – Service health

"Automatically take action when an AWS Health event occurs."

→ Amazon EventBridge

docs.title: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus
docs.text:
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) = managed, Prometheus-compatible monitoring and alerting.

Especially relevant to:

  • Amazon EKS
  • Amazon ECS
  • AWS Fargate
  • Kubernetes
  • container workloads

Uses the Prometheus data model and PromQL.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Prometheus / PromQL + container/Kubernetes metrics → Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
"A company uses Kubernetes and wants Prometheus and PromQL for monitoring without managing Prometheus infrastructure."

→ Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)

"The company needs managed Prometheus-compatible metrics for EKS workloads."

→ Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)

docs.title: Prometheus Metrics
docs.text:
Examples of Prometheus metrics are simple numerical measurements collected over time:

cpu_usage_percent = 72
memory_usage_bytes = 4294967296
http_requests_total = 154320
http_request_duration_seconds = 0.42
http_errors_total = 37
active_connections = 128

For Kubernetes:

pod_cpu_usage
pod_memory_usage
container_restarts_total
container_network_receive_bytes

Think:

Prometheus metrics = numbers about how your application/infrastructure is behaving over time.

Prometheus then stores and queries these metrics using PromQL.

docs.title: Typical AMP Architecture
docs.text:
Container / Kubernetes workloads
             ↓
       Prometheus metrics
             ↓
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)
             ↓
         PromQL queries
             ↓
     Amazon Managed Grafana
             ↓
         Dashboards

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)
= metrics + Prometheus querying

Amazon Managed Grafana
= visualization
