docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
These are smaller AWS application-development services that commonly appear in SAA questions as specific application requirements.

You generally don't need deep knowledge of each one.

The best strategy is:

Read the requirement → identify the unique keyword → choose the service.

For example:

Long-running batch jobs
→ AWS Batch

GraphQL
→ AWS AppSync

GraphQL + real-time subscriptions
→ AWS AppSync

GraphQL + offline synchronization
→ AWS AppSync

Multiple data sources / multiple DynamoDB tables in one GraphQL operation
→ AWS AppSync Pipeline Resolver

Quick web/mobile application development
→ AWS Amplify

Application needs to send email
→ Amazon SES

docs.title: AWS Batch
docs.text:
AWS Batch = run large batch jobs without managing the job scheduler yourself.

It is designed for batch computing workloads where jobs can run for a long time and may need significant compute resources.

AWS Batch manages the scheduling and provisioning of compute resources needed to run batch jobs.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Long-running batch jobs / containers → AWS Batch

docs.title: Typical pattern
docs.text:
Thousands of jobs
      ↓
   AWS Batch
      ↓
Compute capacity
      ↓
Run batch workloads

AWS Batch can provision and manage compute resources for the jobs rather than requiring you to build and maintain your own batch scheduling system.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company needs to run thousands of long-running data-processing jobs and does not want to manage the job scheduler."

→ AWS Batch

docs.title: AWS Batch vs Lambda
docs.text: A common SAA comparison is between AWS Batch and Lambda.

docs.title: Lambda
docs.text:
Lambda
= short event-driven functions

Lambda is designed for individual function executions triggered by events.

docs.title: AWS Batch
docs.text:
AWS Batch
= long-running batch workloads

It is appropriate for workloads where jobs may run for significantly longer periods and require dedicated compute capacity.

docs.title: Simple memory
docs.text:
Lambda
= short event-driven function

AWS Batch
= long-running batch job

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company has thousands of computationally intensive jobs that may run for hours."

→ AWS Batch

The question is describing a batch-computing workload rather than a typical Lambda function.

docs.title: AWS Batch with Containers
docs.text:
AWS Batch is commonly used for containerized batch workloads.

A typical architecture can look like:

Job submissions
      ↓
AWS Batch
      ↓
Containerized jobs
      ↓
EC2 / Spot capacity

The important SAA signal remains:

Large-scale / long-running batch processing → AWS Batch

docs.title: AWS Batch and Spot Instances
docs.text:
AWS Batch can use suitable Spot capacity to reduce the cost of batch workloads.

This can be useful when jobs can tolerate interruptions.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Batch workload
+
Cost optimization
+
Interruptible jobs
→ Spot capacity can be appropriate

The exact compute environment can vary, but you generally do not need to memorize the infrastructure details for SAA.

docs.title: AWS AppSync
docs.text:
AWS AppSync = managed GraphQL API service.

Use it when the question says:

  • GraphQL
  • real-time subscriptions
  • real-time application updates
  • offline synchronization for applications
  • multiple data sources / multiple DynamoDB tables in one GraphQL operation

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: GraphQL → AppSync

docs.title: Typical pattern
docs.text:
Mobile / Web application
          ↓
       AppSync
          ↓
      Data sources

AppSync provides a managed GraphQL API layer between the application and backend data sources.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL allows clients to request the data they need through a GraphQL API.

So when the SAA question explicitly says:

GraphQL

Think:

→ AWS AppSync

This is one of the strongest service keywords to memorize.

docs.title: AppSync Real-Time Subscriptions
docs.text:
AppSync supports real-time subscriptions, which are useful when clients need to receive updates as backend data changes.

Example:

User A updates data
       ↓
    AppSync
       ↓
Real-time update
       ↓
User B

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: GraphQL + real-time subscriptions → AppSync

docs.title: AppSync Offline Synchronization
docs.text:
AppSync can also support offline synchronization for applications.

This is particularly useful for mobile or other clients that may temporarily lose connectivity.

The application can continue working with local data and synchronize changes when connectivity is restored.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: GraphQL + offline synchronization → AppSync

docs.title: AppSync Pipeline Resolvers
docs.text:
An AppSync pipeline resolver allows multiple resolver functions to be executed in sequence as part of a single GraphQL operation.

Each function can interact with a different data source, such as DynamoDB, Lambda, or other supported AppSync data sources.

Typical pattern:

Client
  ↓
AppSync
  ↓
Pipeline Resolver
  ├── Function 1 → DynamoDB Table A
  ├── Function 2 → DynamoDB Table B
  └── Function 3 → DynamoDB Table C
  ↓
Response

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
Multiple data sources / multiple DynamoDB tables in one GraphQL operation → AppSync Pipeline Resolver

This can be useful when a single API request needs to coordinate several backend operations.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A healthcare application needs to efficiently retrieve and write data from multiple DynamoDB tables."

→ AWS AppSync Pipeline Resolver

A pipeline resolver can coordinate multiple resolver functions and data-source operations as part of the GraphQL request.

docs.title: AppSync Examples
docs.text:
"A mobile application needs a managed GraphQL API with real-time subscriptions."

→ AWS AppSync

"A mobile application needs GraphQL and offline data synchronization."

→ AWS AppSync

"A serverless application needs to retrieve and write data across multiple DynamoDB tables through one GraphQL operation."

→ AWS AppSync Pipeline Resolver

docs.title: AppSync Memory
docs.text:
AppSync
= GRAPHQL
= REAL-TIME SUBSCRIPTIONS
= OFFLINE SYNCHRONIZATION
= PIPELINE RESOLVERS

The strongest keyword remains:

GraphQL → AppSync

For pipeline questions, remember:

Multiple data sources / multiple operations → AppSync Pipeline Resolver

docs.title: AWS Amplify
docs.text:
AWS Amplify = tools for quickly building and deploying web/mobile applications.

It helps developers connect frontend applications with AWS backend services.

Amplify is designed to make it easier to build and deploy application frontends and integrate them with AWS services.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Quick full-stack web/mobile development → Amplify

docs.title: Typical use case
docs.text:
A developer wants to quickly build a web or mobile application and connect it to AWS services without manually configuring every backend component.

Web / Mobile frontend
        ↓
     Amplify
        ↓
AWS backend services

Amplify can help with application development and deployment workflows.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A development team wants to quickly build and deploy a web and mobile application using AWS backend services."

→ AWS Amplify

docs.title: Amplify vs AppSync
docs.text:
These services can appear together, but they solve different problems.

AppSync
= managed GraphQL API

Amplify
= tools for building and deploying web/mobile applications

They can also be used together:

Web / Mobile app
      ↓
   Amplify
      ↓
   AppSync
      ↓
  Data sources

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
GraphQL → AppSync

Quick web/mobile application development → Amplify

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
Amazon SES (Simple Email Service) = send application emails.

It is designed for sending email from applications.

Common examples include:

  • receipts
  • verification emails
  • notifications
  • marketing emails

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Application needs to send email → SES

docs.title: Verification email
docs.text:
User signs up
     ↓
Application
     ↓
SES
     ↓
Verification email

docs.title: Receipt
docs.text:
Purchase
   ↓
Application
   ↓
SES
   ↓
Email receipt

docs.title: Notification
docs.text:
Application event
      ↓
     SES
      ↓
Email notification

docs.title: SES vs SNS
docs.text:
This is an important SAA distinction.

SNS
= notifications / pub-sub

SES
= email sending

docs.title: SNS
docs.text:
SNS is primarily used for:

  • pub/sub messaging
  • notifications
  • fan-out
  • delivering messages to supported subscribers

Example:

Application
    ↓
   SNS
   ├── SQS
   ├── Lambda
   └── other subscribers

docs.title: SES
docs.text:
SES is specifically for sending email.

Application
    ↓
   SES
    ↓
  Email

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
SNS = notifications / pub-sub

SES = email

docs.title: SES vs SNS Exam Trap
docs.text:
A question may say:

"A web application needs to send an email to a customer after a purchase."

→ SES

Not SNS merely because the question says "notification."

The actual delivery mechanism is email.

"A service needs to publish a notification to multiple subscribers."

→ SNS

The key is the required communication pattern.

docs.text:
Lambda

AWS Batch

Think about the workload model, not simply whether a container is involved.

→ AppSync

Build/deploy web or mobile application
→ Amplify

They can be used together.

docs.text:
AppSync Pipeline Resolver
= request-time data orchestration

AWS CodePipeline

Email
→ SES

Notifications / pub-sub

→ AWS Batch

→ AWS Amplify

→ Amazon SES

"Application needs to send receipts and notification emails."

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
These are smaller AWS services that usually appear in SAA questions as specific use cases that do not fit neatly into the main service families.

You generally don't need deep knowledge of each one.

The best strategy is:

Read the requirement → identify the unique keyword → choose the service.

For example:

File-based video transcoding
→ AWS Elemental MediaConvert

AWS compliance reports
→ AWS Artifact

Software license limits
→ AWS License Manager

Share AWS resources across accounts
→ AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)

Stream desktop applications to users
→ Amazon AppStream 2.0

Create a fast copy of an Aurora database for testing
→ Aurora Cloning

docs.title: AWS Artifact
docs.text:
AWS Artifact = access AWS compliance documents and reports.

It is a document portal for AWS compliance information.

Examples include AWS compliance documentation such as:

  • SOC
  • PCI
  • ISO-related reports

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Auditor needs AWS compliance reports → Artifact

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"An auditor needs access to AWS compliance reports for the company's audit."

→ AWS Artifact

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Artifact is a document portal.

It is not:

  • a monitoring service
  • a logging service
  • a security monitoring service
  • a compliance monitoring engine

Think:

AWS compliance documents
        ↓
    AWS Artifact

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Artifact = COMPLIANCE DOCUMENTS

docs.title: AWS License Manager
docs.text:
AWS License Manager = track and control software licenses used by AWS resources.

Use it when a company has a limited number of software licenses, such as Windows Server licenses for EC2.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Software licenses + track usage + enforce license limit → AWS License Manager

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A company has 50 Windows Server licenses.

The licenses are counted based on the vCPU count of EC2 instances.

50 licenses
    ↓
AWS License Manager
    ↓
Track EC2 license usage
    ↓
Limit reached?
 ├─ No → EC2 launch allowed
 └─ Yes → Prevent additional launch

Enable license limit enforcement to prevent usage from exceeding the available licenses.

Amazon SNS can be used for notifications.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Software licenses + EC2 + enforce license limit → License Manager

docs.title: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
docs.text:
AWS RAM = share supported AWS resources across AWS accounts.

It is commonly used in multi-account AWS environments.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Share AWS resources across accounts → AWS RAM

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A company has multiple AWS accounts and wants them to use a shared VPC subnet or Transit Gateway.

AWS Account A
      │
      ├── Share resource
      ↓
    AWS RAM
      ↓
AWS Account B

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
RAM can be used to share supported resources such as:

  • VPC subnets
  • Transit Gateways
  • Route 53 Resolver rules

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: RAM = SHARE AWS RESOURCES ACROSS ACCOUNTS

docs.title: AWS ParallelCluster
docs.text:
AWS ParallelCluster = deploy and manage HPC (High Performance Computing) clusters on AWS.

Commonly used with:

  • EC2 → compute nodes
  • Slurm → job scheduler
  • FSx for Lustre → high-performance shared storage
  • EFS → shared file storage

Typical use cases:

  • Scientific simulations
  • Engineering workloads
  • Genomics
  • Weather modeling
  • Large-scale numerical processing

Remember:

ParallelCluster = deploy and manage HPC clusters

docs.title: Amazon AppStream 2.0
docs.text:
Amazon AppStream 2.0 = stream desktop applications to users from AWS.

The application runs on AWS, while the user accesses it remotely through a browser or compatible client.

docs.title: Typical pattern
docs.text:
User's laptop
     ↓
   Browser
     ↓
AppStream 2.0
     ↓
Application runs on AWS

docs.title: Use it when
docs.text:
You need to give users access to applications without requiring the applications to be installed locally on their computers.

Common situations include:

  • desktop applications
  • Windows applications
  • centralized application access
  • remote application streaming

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Users need to access a desktop application without installing it locally → AppStream 2.0

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Users need to access a Windows application from their laptops without installing the application locally."

→ Amazon AppStream 2.0

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
AppStream 2.0 streams applications to users.

Think:

Application runs in AWS
        ↓
Stream the application
        ↓
User interacts remotely

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: AppStream 2.0 = STREAM DESKTOP APPLICATIONS

docs.title: Aurora Cloning
docs.text:
Aurora Cloning = create a fast copy of an Amazon Aurora database for testing, development, or other purposes.

It allows you to create a new Aurora cluster from an existing Aurora cluster without initially making a full physical copy of all the underlying data.

This makes cloning much faster and more storage-efficient than a traditional full database copy.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: Create a fast copy of an Aurora database for testing → Aurora Cloning

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A production Aurora database contains a large amount of data.

Developers need a separate environment for testing.

Instead of creating a complete physical copy:

Production Aurora
       ↓
   Aurora Clone
       ↓
Testing / Development

→ Aurora Cloning

docs.title: Why use it?
docs.text:
Typical use cases include:

  • testing
  • development
  • experimentation
  • creating temporary database environments

docs.title: Memory

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
These are smaller AWS networking and infrastructure services that usually appear as specific-use-case questions.

Requirement → unique keyword → service

Requirement / keyword Answer IPv6 outbound-only Internet access Egress-Only Internet Gateway On-premises → AWS DNS queries Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint AWS → on-premises DNS queries Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint AWS infrastructure in your own data center AWS Outposts Very low latency for a specific metropolitan area AWS Local Zones 5G / mobile edge AWS Wavelength

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Route 53 Resolver connects DNS between your AWS VPC and your on-premises/corporate network.

You need it when:

AWS VPC  ↔  On-premises / Corporate network

and one side needs to resolve DNS names that are known only by the other side.

docs.title: First: What problem does it solve?
docs.text:
DNS converts a hostname into an IP address:

database.company.local
        ↓
    10.20.30.40

Your company may have a corporate DNS server that knows internal names such as:

payroll.company.local
git.company.local
database.company.local

AWS has its own DNS resolution inside a VPC.

Now imagine AWS and your corporate network are connected through:

VPN
or
Direct Connect

You can have:

Corporate network
        ↕
   VPN / Direct Connect
        ↕
      AWS VPC

The networks can communicate, but DNS still needs to know where to send queries.

That's where Route 53 Resolver endpoints come in.

docs.title: There are TWO directions
docs.text:
The easiest way to understand Resolver is to look at where the DNS query starts.

On-premises → AWS

uses:

Inbound Resolver endpoint

AWS → On-premises

uses:

Outbound Resolver endpoint

docs.title: What does it do?
docs.text:
It allows DNS queries coming from on-premises into AWS.

Example:

Your AWS VPC has a private service:

database.internal
        ↓
   10.20.5.30

Your on-premises server wants to know:

"What IP address is database.internal?"

Your corporate DNS does not know the AWS private name.

The query can go:

On-premises
      ↓
Corporate DNS
      ↓
Inbound Resolver Endpoint
      ↓
AWS DNS / Route 53
      ↓
10.20.5.30

docs.title: Why is it called "inbound"?
docs.text:
The DNS query is coming into AWS:

ON-PREM → AWS

Therefore:

Inbound Resolver Endpoint

docs.title: What does it do?
docs.text:
It allows DNS queries originating in AWS to reach on-premises DNS servers.

Example:

Your company has:

payroll.company.local
        ↓
    10.10.5.20

Your corporate DNS knows this name.

An EC2 instance in AWS asks:

"What IP is payroll.company.local?"

AWS's normal DNS does not know the corporate name.

The query can go:

EC2
 ↓
AWS DNS
 ↓
Outbound Resolver Endpoint
 ↓
Corporate DNS
 ↓
10.10.5.20

docs.title: Why is it called "outbound"?
docs.text:
The DNS query is leaving AWS:

AWS → ON-PREM

Therefore:

Outbound Resolver Endpoint

docs.title: The most important Resolver diagram
docs.text:
AWS
             ┌─────────────────┐
             │                 │
             │      VPC        │
             │                 │
             │      EC2        │
             │        ↓        │
             │   AWS DNS       │
             │                 │
             └─────────────────┘
                ↑           ↓
                │           │
          INBOUND        OUTBOUND
                │           │
                ↓           ↓
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │   Corporate Network     │
        │                         │
        │   Corporate DNS         │
        └─────────────────────────┘

The simple version:

On-prem → AWS
= INBOUND

AWS → On-prem
= OUTBOUND

docs.title: What does Resolver actually transfer?
docs.text:
The Resolver endpoint forwards DNS queries.

It is not primarily for:

  • transferring application data
  • routing normal network traffic
  • replacing VPN
  • replacing Direct Connect

Think of it as a DNS bridge.

Network connectivity
        +
DNS Resolver endpoints
        =
AWS and on-prem can resolve each other's names

docs.title: Resolver does NOT create network connectivity
docs.text:
You still need network connectivity such as:

VPN

or:

Direct Connect

For example:

          VPN
AWS  <------------>  On-prem
 │                       │
 │                       │
 └── Resolver ───────────┘
       DNS queries

The VPN or Direct Connect allows the networks to communicate.

The Resolver endpoint handles the DNS part.

docs.title: Scenario 1
docs.text:
On-premises servers need to resolve private DNS names in AWS.

Think:

On-prem → AWS

Answer:

Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint

docs.title: Scenario 2
docs.text:
EC2 instances need to resolve internal corporate DNS names.

Think:

AWS → On-prem

Answer:

Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint

docs.title: Scenario 3
docs.text:
AWS and on-premises are connected through Direct Connect, but AWS workloads cannot resolve internal corporate hostnames.

Think:

AWS → Corporate DNS

Answer:

Resolver outbound endpoint

docs.title: Scenario 4
docs.text:
On-premises applications cannot resolve private Route 53 names hosted in AWS.

Think:

On-prem → AWS

Answer:

Resolver inbound endpoint

docs.title: Don't confuse DNS direction with network ownership
docs.text:
The names inbound/outbound are from AWS's perspective.

So:

On-prem → AWS
= INBOUND to AWS

AWS → On-prem
= OUTBOUND from AWS

Always ask:

"Is the DNS query entering AWS or leaving AWS?"

docs.title: Route 53 Hosted Zones vs Resolver
docs.text: These are different things.

docs.title: Route 53 Hosted Zone
docs.text:
Stores DNS records such as:

www.example.com → 10.20.30.40

Think:

Where are the DNS records?

docs.title: Route 53 Resolver
docs.text:
Handles DNS queries and forwarding between DNS environments.

Think:

Where should this DNS query go?

docs.title: Quick comparison
docs.text: Requirement Answer Store/manage DNS records Route 53 Hosted Zone On-prem DNS → AWS DNS Resolver inbound endpoint AWS DNS → on-prem DNS Resolver outbound endpoint Connect AWS network to on-prem network VPN / Direct Connect

docs.title: Egress-Only Internet Gateway
docs.text:
Egress-Only Internet Gateway = outbound-only Internet access for IPv6.

It allows IPv6 instances to initiate outbound Internet connections while preventing unsolicited inbound connections.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
IPv6 + outbound Internet + block unsolicited inbound

→ Egress-Only Internet Gateway

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
IPv6 instance
      ↓
Egress-Only Internet Gateway
      ↓
Internet

Allowed:

EC2 → Internet

Not allowed:

Internet → EC2

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Internet Gateway (IGW) = normal Internet connectivity.

Egress-Only Internet Gateway = specifically for IPv6 outbound-only access.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Egress-Only IGW = IPv6 OUTBOUND ONLY

docs.title: AWS Outposts
docs.text:
AWS Outposts = AWS infrastructure physically installed in your own data center.

Use it when:

  • workloads must physically remain on-premises
  • very low latency to local systems is required
  • local workloads need AWS APIs/services
  • the company wants AWS-style infrastructure in its own facility

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
Your data center
       ↓
   AWS Outposts
       ↓
AWS infrastructure

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: AWS infrastructure on-premises → Outposts

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A company must keep workloads in its own data center but wants to use AWS infrastructure and APIs."

→ AWS Outposts

docs.title: AWS Local Zones
docs.text:
AWS Local Zones = AWS infrastructure placed closer to users in a specific metropolitan area.

Use it when an application needs very low latency for users in a particular city or metropolitan area.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: City-level low latency → Local Zones

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
Main AWS Region
       ↓
Local Zone
       ↓
Users in nearby metropolitan area

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"An application requires very low latency for users in a specific metropolitan area."

→ AWS Local Zones

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Local Zones = AWS CLOSER TO A CITY

docs.title: AWS Wavelength
docs.text:
AWS Wavelength = AWS infrastructure inside a telecommunications provider's 5G network.

It places AWS compute and storage at the edge of a telecom 5G network.

Use it for:

  • mobile applications
  • 5G applications
  • extremely low-latency mobile workloads
  • processing data close to mobile users

docs.title: Signal
docs.text: 5G → Wavelength

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
Mobile device
      ↓
5G network
      ↓
Wavelength Zone
      ↓
AWS resources at telecom edge

This minimizes network distance between mobile users and the application.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"A mobile application needs extremely low-latency processing over a 5G network."

→ AWS Wavelength

docs.title: AWS SAA-C03 — 20 Last-Minute Elimination Rules
docs.text:
Use these as elimination rules, not absolute "always choose X" rules.

The goal is to quickly eliminate answers that violate the scenario, then choose the simplest solution that satisfies the exact requirements.

docs.title: 1. LEAST operational overhead
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • EC2 that you must patch/manage
  • Custom infrastructure-management scripts
  • Manual failover
  • Manual scaling
  • Self-managed servers

Think:

Managed services / serverless / AWS-managed operations

Do not memorize:

Least operational overhead = Lambda

The real rule is:

Remove infrastructure management whenever the workload allows it.

docs.title: 2. Cost-effective + unpredictable or variable workload
docs.text:
Distrust:

  • Permanently provisioned capacity
  • Large always-running EC2 fleet
  • Overprovisioning for peak traffic

Think:

Serverless / autoscaling / pay-per-use

docs.title: 3. Predictable, steady workload for years
docs.text:
Distrust:

  • Pure On-Demand when a long-term commitment is clearly appropriate

Think:

Savings Plans / Reserved Instances

The key is steady and predictable usage.

docs.title: 4. High availability
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Single AZ
  • Single EC2 instance
  • Single database instance
  • Manual recovery

Think:

Multi-AZ + redundancy + automatic failover

docs.title: 5. Fault tolerant
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Solutions requiring humans to recover the system
  • Single points of failure
  • Manual replacement

Think:

Automatic failure detection + automatic recovery/failover

docs.title: 6. Scalable / elastic
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Fixed server count
  • Manual scaling
  • Architectures that cannot react automatically to demand

Think:

ASG / managed scaling / serverless

docs.title: 7. Static website
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • EC2 web servers
  • Self-managed web infrastructure

Think:

S3 + CloudFront

Especially when the requirement is simply to serve static files.

docs.title: 8. EC2 needs private access to S3
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • NAT Gateway when the only requirement is private S3 access
  • Internet Gateway/public internet path

Think:

S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint

docs.title: 9. Private access to an AWS service
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Unnecessary public internet routing
  • NAT Gateway when a suitable VPC endpoint solves the requirement

Think:

VPC Endpoint

Then distinguish:

  • Gateway endpoint → S3, DynamoDB
  • Interface endpoint → most other AWS services

docs.title: 10. Shared filesystem across Linux EC2 instances
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • EBS as shared storage between multiple instances

Think:

EFS

Remember:

EBS = block storage for an instance EFS = shared file storage

docs.title: 11. Windows shared file system
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • EFS when Windows-specific SMB functionality is required

Think:

FSx for Windows File Server

docs.title: 12. Relational data / SQL / joins / transactions
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • DynamoDB when the application genuinely needs relational capabilities

Think:

RDS / Aurora

Look for:

  • SQL
  • joins
  • relational schema
  • complex queries
  • transactions

docs.title: 13. Massive key-value scale / very low latency
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • RDS/Aurora when relational features are unnecessary

Think:

DynamoDB

Typical clues:

  • Key-value access
  • Massive scale
  • Very high request volume
  • Single-digit millisecond performance
  • Serverless database

docs.title: 14. Decouple producer and consumer
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Direct synchronous communication
  • Producer calling consumer directly

Think:

SQS

Typical architecture:

Producer → SQS → Consumer

The queue absorbs traffic spikes and allows asynchronous processing.

docs.title: 15. One message → many subscribers
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • A single consumer/queue when multiple independent subscribers need the message

Think:

SNS fan-out

Typical architecture:

             → SQS
Producer → SNS → Lambda
             → SQS

docs.title: 16. Event routing based on rules
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Custom Lambda routing when AWS already provides event routing
  • Complex SNS-only architecture when event rules/filtering are the requirement

Think:

EventBridge

Typical clues:

  • Event bus
  • Event rules
  • AWS service events
  • SaaS events
  • Route events to different targets

docs.title: 17. HTTP path/host routing
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • NLB when Layer 7 HTTP routing is explicitly required

Think:

ALB

Typical clues:

  • /api/*
  • /images/*
  • Host-based routing
  • HTTP headers
  • HTTP redirects

docs.title: 18. Static IPs required for the load balancer
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • ALB when fixed/static IP addresses are explicitly required

Think:

NLB

NLB supports static IP addresses and can use Elastic IPs.

docs.title: 19. Global entry point + static anycast IP + traffic acceleration
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • Route 53 alone
  • Regional load balancer alone

Think:

Global Accelerator

Typical clues:

  • Global users
  • Static anycast IPs
  • Faster path to regional applications
  • Automatic traffic routing/failover

docs.title: 20. Who did what?
docs.text:
Eliminate:

  • CloudWatch when the question asks who made an AWS API change
  • AWS Config when the question is about API activity

Think:

CloudTrail

Remember the three-way distinction:

Service Main question CloudWatch How is it performing? CloudTrail Who did what? AWS Config What is the resource's configuration/compliance state?

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Memorize:

Object → S3 Block → EBS Shared file → EFS Windows file → FSx for Windows HPC filesystem → FSx for Lustre

If an answer uses EBS as shared storage across multiple EC2 instances, be suspicious.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Memorize:

SQL / joins / relational transactions → Aurora/RDS Key-value / massive scale → DynamoDB Cache → ElastiCache

Do not choose DynamoDB simply because the question says high performance.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Memorize:

Layer 7 HTTP routing → ALB Layer 4 TCP/UDP + static IP → NLB Global static anycast IP → Global Accelerator DNS routing → Route 53 Web application filtering → WAF DDoS protection → Shield

These services can all appear in the same question as distractors.

docs.title: Users need AWS access
docs.text: IAM Identity Center / federation

docs.title: Roles must never exceed a maximum permission set
docs.text: Permissions boundary

docs.title: Organization-wide guardrail
docs.text: SCP

docs.title: Who created/deleted/changed something?
docs.text: CloudTrail

docs.title: What is the current resource configuration?
docs.text: AWS Config

docs.title: CPU / memory / disk / application metrics and logs
docs.text:
CloudWatch

For EC2 memory and filesystem utilization:

CloudWatch Agent

docs.title: The "Unnecessary Architecture" Rule
docs.text:
When two answers both technically work, eliminate the one that adds unnecessary components.

Example:

Requirement:

Encrypt S3 objects at rest.

Do not automatically choose:

S3
+ KMS
+ custom key policies
+ Lambda
+ key rotation logic

when a simpler AWS-managed encryption option satisfies the requirement.

Think:

Use the simplest architecture that fully satisfies the requirement.

docs.title: Step 1 — Read the last sentence
docs.text:
Look for:

  • LEAST
  • MOST
  • COST
  • OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD
  • HIGH AVAILABILITY
  • FAULT TOLERANCE
  • MINIMAL CHANGES
  • MOST SECURE
  • LOWEST LATENCY
  • COST OPTIMIZATION

The last sentence often tells you what to optimize for.

docs.title: Step 2 — Find the hard requirement
docs.text:
Ask:

What requirement would make an option impossible?

Examples:

  • Static IP?
  • Shared filesystem?
  • SQL?
  • Asynchronous processing?
  • Global?
  • Private?
  • Multi-AZ?
  • Minimal changes?
  • Cheapest?

docs.title: Step 3 — Eliminate contradictions
docs.text:
Do not ask:

"Which service do I remember?"

Ask:

"Which answers clearly violate the requirement?"

docs.title: Step 4 — Remove unnecessary complexity
docs.text:
Among the survivors:

Prefer the solution that satisfies the requirement with fewer unnecessary components and less management.

docs.title: Final Mental Model
docs.text:
When stuck between two answers, think:

Does it satisfy the exact requirement?
        ↓
Does it introduce unnecessary management?
        ↓
Does it introduce unnecessary components?
        ↓
Is there a more AWS-managed solution?
        ↓
Does it meet the required scale / availability / security?
        ↓
Choose the remaining answer.

docs.title: One rule to remember above everything else
docs.text:
SAA questions usually aren't asking "What AWS service can do this?"

They are asking:

"Which architecture satisfies these exact requirements with the requested trade-off?"
